div.p: 2 ASK FOR McDOUCALL'S PATENT SELF RAISINC FLOUR IT THE TBEST
IN THE COURTS
THEFT CHARGE DIbMISSED.

At the Liverpool County Sessions on Tuesday, Arthur Banyan (25), a colliery drawer, was found not guilty of stealing £l3, the property of Mary Ann Harrison, at klaydock, on March 30th, and was discharged.

div.head: OVER THE WALL. Former Employee Found on Brewery Premises.
div.p: OVER THE WALL. Former Employee Found on Brewery Premises.

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday, before the Mayor (in the chair); and other magistrates. Ernest Willett, unhairer, 48, Marshhouse-lane, was charged with being found on the enclosed premises of Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, Ltd., Dallam-lane. on Saturday afternoon, with intent to commit a felony. Prisoner said he was guilty of climbing over the wall but not of felonious intentions. The Chief Constable said that P.C. Berry was on duty at 4 o'clock and saw prisoner loitering about Stamford- street. About 4.15 the officer saw Mr. Booth, the foreman of the Brewery, coming out of the brewery yard, alone' with the prisoner. In answer to the officer Booth said he bad found the prisoner in the yard, where he had not the least right to be. The prisoner told the officer he was trying to get a job. As a matter 'of fact, continued the Chief, he was at present earning 28s. per week at the glace kid works, Longford. The prisoner had been taken round to the front entrance of the brewery, but the man at the door said he had not been round that way. Prisoner was previously employed at the brewery and consequently knew the • runs" of the place. The brewery was closed at that time in the afternoon, and there was the fact, that the prisoner had climbed over the wall. Joseph Booth, foreman, after corroborating the Chief's statement, said prisoner did not appear to realise the seriousness of the offence when he was discovered. He was quite sober. Prisoner said he was afraid the pickets might keep him back if he went to the front ccor. He had heard the Brewery wanted men badly, and was alter employ- ment. Mr. Booth had told him, to go on Monday morn- ing and see Mr. Hutton about getting a job. A Magistrate : Do you mean to say the pickets would have tried to stop you if you had gone round by the front entrance? Prisoner : Yes. The Chief Constable: As a matter of fact, he was talking to a picket before be got over Uri wall, and there was a picket not far away from the spot where he got over. The Mayor : Why were you after work if you were earning 28s. per week? Prisoner: We are slack at present. The Chief Constable :I did not intend to bring this in, but the prisouer knew it was impossible to obtain work there, as he was discharged two years ago. Prisoner said the pickets did not see him go over the wall. He thought they would be working overtime at the brewery. Willett, who had been once previously before the Court on three charges of obtaining money from children by means of a trick in 1900, was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days' imprisonment.

div.head: BLIND CHILD'S EDUCATION. ---- A Question of Cost.
div.p: BLIND CHILD'S EDUCATION. ---- A Question of Cost.

At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, before Councillor H. Roberts in the chair and other magis- trates, Mr. R. B. Roberts (assistant director at educa- tion) applied for an order to send Florence Williams Watkins, aged 11 years, daughter of George Watkins, 80, Ellesmere-street, to tt,e Thomason Memorial School for the Blind, Bolton. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the mother of the girl. Mr. Roberts explained that three sears ago the child had a very unfortunate accident which left her too blind to be instructed in an ordinary elementary school. It was the duty of the Education authority to provide adequate instruction for the child at a suitable institu- tion, and at the first it was intended to send tier to Henshaw's Blind Asylum, Old Trafford, Manchester. Mrs. Watkins was equally desirous that the child sheuld go away to a school. Arrangements had practically been made for the child to go to Old Trafford, but on the 7th April it was observed that the eharges at that institution had been increased from £2.6 to .£36 per year The Committee therefore decided on an equally efficient school at Bolton, where the charge was £3O per annum. Mrs. Watkins did not agree to that wirings, so therefore they had no alternative but to bring the case before the magistrates. Mr. Browne said the father of the girl was paralysed and bad not worked for three ,ears. Mra. Watkins, therefore, had to go out to work. The parents were desirous that the child should go to the Hensbaw School and the girl herself would be very disappointed Haile was not sent there. Mrs. Watkins had agreed to pay 2s. per week whilst the girl was in the home. Mr. Roberts said the whole question was one as to the charge made. . The Chairman : There would be a difference of .£24 taken over the four years. Mr. hoberts : Warrington is not the only education authority who have refused to pay the increased charge of the Henshaw Asylum. The Chairman said the child's education would cost the rates £lOO. Both institutions were exceptionally good. They made an order for the child to go to the Thomason school at Bolton.

div.head: ATTACK ON CROFT CONSTABLE.
div.p: ATTACK ON CROFT CONSTABLE.
Six Months' Hard Labour for a Miner.

At the Manchester Assizes, on Thursday, James Hayes (37), and John Burrows (36) miners, were charged with wounding P.C. Mullen, with intent to do grievous bodily harm at Croft, on March 21st. The evidence showed that trouble arose amongst visitors to Croft on the night of March 21st, end Mullen was trying to restore order when Hayes hit him on the head with a heavy stick. The officer was rendered unconscious, and whilst in that condition others of the patty assaulted him, with the result that he was insensible for seven hours. _

The jury found Hayes guilty of unlawful wounding, but without intent. Burrows was found not guilty and discharged. Passing sentence on Thursday upon Hayes, Mr. Justice Bankes said the jury had not taken a very serious view of the case. If they had foutd prisoner guilty of attacking the policeman with intent, the sentence would have been one of penal servitude. If any evidence bad been given to show that Hayes bad been the person who attacked the officer when on the ground the sen- tence would have been a heavy one, but they had no evidence, and he had no right to assume that Hayes was the MaD. _ _ _ .
Hayes was sentenced to six months' impriEonmen with hard labour.
THURSDAY.

Before Mr. J. Upson (in the chair), Alderman James Evans, Dr. .Naden and Mr. A. J. Jolley. HORSE FOR 13s.—Harry Walker, 'Sankey Old-road, was summoned for cruelly working a horse in an unfit state and John Owen, 11, Lovely-lane, was summoned for causing the horse to be worked on the 18th April.— Inspector Dee said be saw the youth, Walker, hitting the horse with a whip and he said be could not get it to go. The horse was in a poor condition and not fit to work. Defeadant said "It is about done; it does not get enough to eat." The animal was weak, very low, end in a poor emaciated condition. Mr. Owen said "We have had difficulties several times in getting it out of the yard with an empty lurry. lam getting about sick of seeing it go about and I will not put it to work agair." He denied that Walker had said anything to him about his (the inspector's previous caution)—Mr. Owen said the horse which cost him 7s. to Bs. per week to keep, was sold on Monday morning.— Inspector Dee: He said he had sold it for 13s. to Tommy Connor. A shove would have knocked the horse down. Mr. Owen said that if Walker had told him he would not have worked the horse again. The Chairman said that Walker had acted under the influence of Owen and he would be dismissed with a caution.— Owen was fined 20s. and costs or one month's imprisonment.

div.head: JUVENILE COURT.
div.p: JUVENILE COURT.

At the Warrington juvenile r.;ourt on Thursday, before Mr. J..l3paon- (in the chair) and other magistrates. CRUELTY To A DONKEY.—John Walmsley (15) 72, Back Dallam-lane, and John Cartlidge (17), 21, Portland- street, were summonod for cruelly beating a donkey.— Inspector Dee said that on the 12th inst he saw the defendants in charge of donkeys on the Chester New- road. They were having a race. Walmsley was hitting his donkey with knotted rope reins, and Cartledge was striking and urging his animal with leather reins. They made the animals go as fast as they could for about three-quarters of a mile, when he (the Inspector) caught them up on his hiciele. Numerous complaints had been received of donkeys being cruelly treated.—The defendant Walmsleg prodded the donkey with an old saw.—The Chief Constable said there was more brutality to donkeys in the neighbourhood of the wholesale market place.—Toe magistrates, who were determined to put a stop to such cruelty, fined each defendact ss. including costs. SHOP THEFT.—William bowns (11), 31, Norris-street, and Harry Smith (9), 21, Norris-street, were aummoned for stealing from the shop 139, Marsh House-lane, 18 packets of chewing gum value 3s 9d., the property of William Beech, on the 19th April.—The boys went into the shop and ordered a halfpennyworth of sweets. Whilst Miss Beech was getting them she heard a noise, and on turning round saw one of the defendants pick the chewing gum box up. They ran away, dropping some of the gum as they ran. They climbed a railway fence and she lost sight of them. Seen at the Beamont School, the boys admitted the offence. Mr. Mason, headmaster at the school, made serious complaints about the boys, more particularly Downs who had been

pilfering from schoolboys. The lads had admitted stealing articles and money from their schoolmates. Mr. Meson bad characterised them as the worst boys in the school. The Chief Constable said the parents could not he blamed in this case.—Downs was ordered to receive six strokes of the birch and the other defendant was dismissed with a caution.

div.head: Borough Police Court.
div.p: Borough Police Court.
-AIONDA Y.

Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Bolton and Smethurst, Councillor Wilkiuson,Nlessrs. W Robe:ts, S. Wright and W. Furness. "A DRUNKEN, LAZY RASCAL."—Alphonsus Cullen and Samuel floyles, both of no fixed address, were charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Mersey-street.—The case having been proved, Cullen appealed to the Bench for leniencr. He said that he only came out of prison last Wednesday after" doing a mouth." It was very hard to be up again in so short a time. "I will sign the pledge," vowed Alphonsus, amidst laughter, " if you will deal leniently with me." —The Chief: He tells that tale always. It is a wonder he was not locked up before Saturday, seeing that he came out on Wednesday. He was a drunken, lazy rascal, and he made his Gsth appearance. if he came up again, he (the Chief Constable) would strongly advocate that he be sent to an inebriates' home, as he was absolutely beyond tedemption. The police had given him a chance to leave the borough, but he bad asked how could they expect a Warringtonian to leave his native shores ?—The Mayor: Hardly shores ; perhaps he meant the canal.—Cullen was sent to prison for one month, and Hoyle was fined 10s. and costs.

ATTEMPTED SUlClDE.—Frederick McCabe, 11, Leicester-street, appeared on remand on a charge of attempting to commit suicide by strangling himself with a stocking.—A month ago the prisoner was locked up on a charge of having been drunk and disorderly and whilst in the cells tried to take his life.—The Chief Constable said that since the adjournment priscner's conduct had been exemplary.—The charge was withdrawn

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.
Before Councillor H. Roberts (iii the chairs,, Colonel Edelsten, Messrs. C. Jackson Holmes and T. Locker.

TEMPORARY AITTIIORITY.—Tpmporary authotity was granted to Frederick Roper to sell at the Corporation Inn, Market-place. MISSING HALF SOVEREIGN.—Benjamin Webb, 21, Dixon-street, was summoned for assaulting ticket collector Edward Harrington employed on the C.L.C. Railway and living at 94, Harrington, .l. R. Lingard (Manchester), who prosecuted, said that defendant got off the 11.40 p.m. train at Warrington and gave his ticket to Harrington. Webb had got down the steps but turned back and said that he had given Harrington a half sovereign with the ticket. Harrington said he had not received the money. Webb wanted to search the collector and seized him by the shoulders. Harrington was searched by a police officer but the half sovereign was not in his possession.— Defendant then said Harrington had passed it on.— Defendant denied the assault end said he bad a sovereign and a half in his pocket along with his ticket. On going down the steps ha missed the smaller coin and thought he had given it up with his ticket.—He was fined in the costs.
'A WEDNESDAY. Before Mr. W. T. Williams (in the chair), Alderman
Smethurst and Mr. C. Jackson Holmes

"A HOPELESS CAsl...'4-I.lohn Higgins, of no fixed address, was charged with travelling on the London and North-Western Railway from Wigan to Warrington without having paid his fare, with intent to defraud. It was stated that prisoner alighted from the 9.10 train the previous night. He asked a railway official what time there was a train to Carlisle, but suspicions being aroused, he was asked for a ticket. He could not pro- duce one and an officer admitted that he could get nothing out of the prisoner, as to where he came from, where he was going, or his name and address. Prisoner had given the address as 128, Wallgate-street,Wigen,but be had an insurance card in his possession, bearing an address at Scarborough. When caked where he bad travelled from, prisoner said "Find eut." Be after- wards said "lam a hopeless case. I may as well be locked up :it will be better than sleeping out." Thu Chief Constable: There is not the least doubt about that ; he is a hopeless case.—Prisoner was fined 20s. and costs or one months' imprisonment.
FRIDAY. Before the Mayor (in the chair) Aldermen Pierpointy Smethurst and Bolton, Messrs. G. Pilling, S. Wright, T. Locker, A. J. Jolley and W. Furness.

DRANK AMMONIA FOR POP.—Bernard Reddican (20), 14 Melville-street, appeared on remand on a charge of attempting to commit suicide by drinking a quantity of liquid ammonia on March 23rd.—The Chief Constable said that on March 22nd. defendant came home the worse for drink and found that everyone had retired to bed. He drank the ammonia which was in a green bottle on the shelf. When the case was before the court a month ago,defendant's mother raid he shouted upstairs to ask where the pop was and she replied 'on the shelf." Defendant said he had taken the ammonia, tbinking it was pop. Prisoner had been drinking pretty freely and be (the chief constable), thought he took the ammonia in a sudden fit of temper, During the month he had been of good behaviour.—The charge was with- drawn on prisoner promising not to repeat the ofienca. CURIOUS ASSAULT CASE —Ellen Mills, 1, Dale- street, was summoned by Selina Manning, 103, Liver- pool-road, for assault.—Mr. E. A. Conner, who appeared for the complainant, said that about 9.30 on April 17th complainant had been to the Ship Inn for some beer which she carried in a jug. The defendant's husband passed by on his way home from work. On complainant coming out of the inn, Mrs. Mills, who had been stand- ing on the other side of the road,accused Mrs. Manning of waiting for her (defendant's) husband. Complainant said she was not waiting for Mr. Mills. Defendant followed her along the road shouting and calling her names. Complainant afterwards came out of her house and defendant brandished a stick which was part of the "dolly." She struck complainant on the forearm and in the struggle for the stick complainant received a kick on the leg.- -Defendant's story was that Mrs. Manning and her husband (Mills) had been drinking in public-houses together whilst she (defendant) was Ironing and wash- ing.—Complainant maid Mills was a friend of her husband, and they had both told him to keep away from the house. if there was any bother with his wife.— Defendant was bound over for six months and ordered to pay the costs of the case.

div.head: FORTUNES AND FEATHERS.
div.p: FORTUNES AND FEATHERS.

The wealth of South Africa is not solely derived from gold and diamond mines. An industry of scarcely less importance from the money-making standpoint is the modern,scientific breeding and rearing of ostriches on the irrigated areas of the vast Sundays River Valley in the Graaff Reinet Division of the Cape Province,where the birds are fed on lucerne (the queen of forage crops). This industry is nowadays highly specialised and a valuable monopoly; inasmuch as the ."South African Government penalises and prohibits to the utmost any attempt to export the rare " blood- strain " birds (never yet seen outside the Cape Mid- lands and South West) or any breed of ostriches or any ostrich eggs from Africa to oversea. Only the feathers may be marketed abroad. This South African ostrich- breeding industry is therefore the most highly pro- tected in the world, and is the most signal example of the preservation of rare and valuable types of plumage. Hitherto (since 1552) all resttalting mcsney-making and profit-earning benefits have accrued solely to breeders actually resident in South Africa and their brokers. But the demand in the world's markets for the best quality Cape prime feathers has now so far outdistanced, and promises to so much further out- strip, the available or calculable supply from Cape sources, that for the first time the investing public in the Mother Country is being invited to co-operate in an immediate expansion of this highly remunerative Cape industry. Attention is being called to thee facts and to the unique opportunities which they create by the Anglo-African Bureau Ltd., which has its head- quarters at 5, Southampton-street, Sp-and. London, and which represents the Graaff Reibet Ostrich and Lucerne Farms (Ltd.), who have issued a most interesting illustrated statement on the subject. Copies may be had from the Bureau above-named.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
NEWTON DISTRICT COUNCIL. ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of tbe Newton Cluncil was held at the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Monday. There were present Messrs. L. E. Pilkington, C. B. F. Borron, E. L, Bent, W. Latham, W. Davies, A. Tunstall, C. W. Emmett, I'. Ritchie, J. Sankey, Vs‘% Roughley, C. Cole (clerk), A. Bowes (surveyor), and R. T. Surtees (engineer). Mr. L E Pilkington was re-elected chair- man and Mr. E. L. Bent, vice-chairman. The committees were re-eppoiated en blots as last year. Mr. Collingwood was appointed the representa- tive on the West Lancashire Territorial Association. THE AIARCONI INQUIRY. LORD NEWTON AND THE POSITION OF

div.head: MINISTERS.
div.p: MINISTERS.

Lord Newton addressed the Newton-le-Willow Con- servatives on Saturday,tafter his re-election as prepident of the divisional association. Referring to the Marconi Inquiry, be said, nothing would induce him to believe that the Ministers concerned went into a business of this kind with the expectation of losing money. (Laughter and cheerF.) Nobody, Lord Newton added, ,hdd denounced these particular practices with such extreme fierceness as Mr. Lloyd George had done in the past. And yet we found this champion, who, for all he knew, figured in innumerable stained-glass windows in Welsh Nonconformist edifices with a ludo round his head, this maligred hero, actually consorting

with millionaires, indulging in the same tastes, and actually gambling on the Stock Exchange like an unregenerate Tory or Tariff Reformer. (Laughter.) "To my mind," continued Lord Newton "there are two profoundly unsatisfactory results which proceed from this inquiry. Hitherto English Ministers have always enjoyed a reputation throughout the world which I have no hesitation in saying was never enjoyed by the Ministers of any other country. I am not speaking ignorantly on this point, because I have had a great deal to do with foreign countries, and foreign politicians in particular, and I say emphatically that the distinction which English Ministers enjoyed above all others was that it was always supposed and believed that they held themselves entirely aloof from financial transactions of any kind or nature. (Cheers.) The other unsatisfactory feature was, he said, the new light in which we should henceforth be compelled to look', upon Parliamentary Committees. When it came to a 1 personal or political question a House of Commons Committee seemed to him a thoroughly unsatisfactory body.

Primitive Mcctolist Ministerial Change.

The Rev. W. Cooper has almost completed three Tears' work in charge of the Werrington Primitive Methodist circuit. He will leave Warrington in July to become superintendent of the Leigh circuit, whin!) embraces a wide and scattered area, extending as far as Platt Bridge in one direction nnd Cadishead in the other. Mr. Cooper, who has been in the ministry for thirteen years, has gained the affectionate regard of the local Primitive Methodist community, amongst whom he has laboured so devotedly and successfully, and he is also held in respect by Free Churchmen generally. His stalwart support of all that makes for progress and social uplifting is els, worthy of notice. Mr. Cooper will be succeeded by the Rev. J. S. Chessum, of Houghton-le-Springs, Durham.

• Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church. The Sunday school anniversary was celebrated at this church on Sunday when the Rev. J. H. Johnson, of Seacombe preached to large congregations. The school children rendered special hymns, under the conductor- ship of Mr. A. Spruce. In the afternoon they gave a musical and floral exercise entitled "A talk with the flowers." The scholars taking part represented various flowers and spoke of the mission of the flowers and of the lessons to be derived from them. Mrs. Hoyle and Miss Jones had charge of the exercise which proved to he a pleasant success. Mr. F. Banner was at the organ. Councillor J. T. Locker presided and spoke of his early connection with Legh-street Church. The collections for the day, which were in aid of the Sunday school funds, amounted to £lB, a considerable advance on the amounts received at recent anniversaries.
" Religion in the Home."

The Rey. H. Middlewood was the preacher at Bold- street Wesleyan Church on Sunday evening and the text chosen was Deuteronomy ii., 18-20. The text, he said, was a picture of an ideal Jewish home, and while full of suggestiveness to the present age, there was too much outward display in the conception to prevent its literal adoption. The suitability to the modern requirements was rather to be found in the commands to lay up the words in the heart, and to teach them to the children. The ideal home was ever characterized by its Christian temper and teaching, and religion which sprang from the heart of the parents was expressed in every phase of family life. The tenderest associations clustered round the idea of home, and the Bible was full of Hpictaites of home-life. There was nothing England needed so much as a revival of religion in itshome- life. Religion in the home was of more vital impartance than religion in the Church.
POOR SUBSTITUTE FOR HOME TEACHING.

It was far easier t 5 appear religious in a place of worship than it was to live the life of a Christian at home. The man who had learned to live rightly at home would manifest his Christianity in every depart- ment of his activities, commercial, social or political- The home should be the school of virtues, and to achieve its true purpose the primary rule should be " Recognition of God in all things." Home was the natural and appointed place in which children shousd learn about God. Whatever good might accrue from religious teaching in schools, it was a poor subsVtute for religious instruction in the home. There was no influence so vital as parental influence. Children were seldom moved by word,, but they were ever susceptible to the iLfluence ef a fragrant example.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A.

There was a good meeting on Sunday. The president Rev. T. 'l'. James, spoke on the ending up of another winter and the entrance of lovely spring. He urged the members to put forth their best efforts to put new life, new thoughts ead new inspiration in the work, and to show forth a newness of life and character. They should keep up the attendances during these summer months, so that when autumn came they might have a large increase in membership. Mr. Travis, of Widnes, gave the address on "influences of Christianity upon the life around us." They should not be for ever speaking and singing of the new Jerusalem, of the jasper walls and so on, but should labour for the uplifting of men around them, helping them to believe in love and the lovable teaching of Christ, His great love and compassion. Mr. William Cleave and Mr. A. Healey also took part in the meeting. Mr. James announced that be would give the address to the men about once a month. There are bright hopes for the future of Wycliffe P.S.A. Primitive Methodist Church, Legh-street. - The Sunday School anniversary services were held on Sunday, the preacher for the day being the Rev. .1. H. Johnson, of Seacombe. At the morning service the preacher gave an address to the scholars,based upon- Psalm i. verses 1 and 2. He appealed to the children to beware of the ungodly and the scornful but try to choose companions who would help them to keep in the true pathway of life; and to the adults be preached a sermon tossed upon Christ's words " Ca ye," with the life of David Livingstone as an example. The church was filled in the evening when the preacher took for his text the words of Paul to King Agrippa," I was not disobedient to the Heavenly fision; and appealed to the congregation to be willing to serve in answer to the heavenly vision which comes to all true and earnest Christians. In the afternoon Councillor J. T. Locker J.P. presided and spoke of the noble work of training the children in the sabbath schools. He mentioned that as a boy he often w orshipped on Sunday even- ing in the Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church. The scholars, led by Mrs. Hoyle and Miss Jones, gave a tnusicil and fl ‘` )ral exercise service entitled A talk with the flowers." The collections realised £IS.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Church. The Value of Home-Life.
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Church. The Value of Home-Life.
Preaching at this Church on Sunday morning, the Rev. W. Reid referred to the hour when Jesus was

found by His parents in the Temple as that in which He awoke to a new consciousness and as the mark of decision in His life. Tue pious home and the periods of His life upon which all reliable testimony is silent were the processes through which God prepared His soul for this hour and as He awoke to it He realised His Sonship to God. This, said the preacher,is the way by which the bulk of our children should reach the similar hour in their life.

In the evening Mr. Reid spoke of God's command to Abraham to offer his son Isaac as that which so far from clashing with the conscience of the Patriarch was actually conveyed through it, and represented to his soul the noblest form of worship. In order to manifest clearly his surrender to the Divine will, and at the same time to rid his mind of its wrong interpretation of God's command, He allowed His voice to be so heard. It was the sublime act of a gradually acquired faith, and in his perfect acquiesence to his father's conception of God's Will, substantiated by the fires of human sacrifice, Isaac entered into the spiritual inherit- ance of his Father's faith. When the sacrifice was made and the bitterness of death was already past, not only was manifested the common obedience and surrender of Isaac and his father, but they bad entered into the possession of the truth that God had been wanting to give, that His sacrifices are a broken and contrite heart.

div.head: " The Despair of Social Idealism.-
div.p: " The Despair of Social Idealism.-

_The Rev. Dr. Mellor preached at Cairo-street Chapel on Sunday evening, on "The despair of social idealism.' He said that the higher their aim, the nobler their endeavour, the more certainly was it doomed to failure in this world. It was possible that life here might give some sort of satisfaction to low aims, mean desires, paltry ambitions ; it could never satisfy the high and the heroic. he peaks of vision that the true man sought lay hidden in eternity,and no visible height of earth, though it seemed snow-capped and sublime, unspeakably pure and cold and cleanly good, could equal the majesty of the mountains of God. We climbed and climbed, and never reached the top, for over us, in all our earthly life, hung ever the vast human destiny of failure. And the truth of that destiny followed from the very dEitracter of the finite world in which we lived. That world in the end was only a perishing thing, doomed inevitably to change and decay, and a final passing into nothingness. Whether it seemed to us a hell or a para- dise, the world would surely pass away like a dream, or a cloud, or the track of a ship in the waters. Fleeting, evanescent, vain were all the things of time and the appearances of space ; they had in them no abiding, substance, no abiding reality. They could not there- fore satisfy the deep longing of the soul or. filling up the measure that was at every moment lacking, give to the wearied heart its need of successful rest and ample enjoyment in the bosom of God. "A NOBLE ILLUSION-A MAGNIFICENT BUBBLE."

It was not only the uensualist, the pleasure -seeker, the superficial liver, who in the end felt the dreadful nnsatisfactoriness of finite existence. It was also, and perhaps in afar greatAr degree and measure the inspired idealist, the strenuous tighter for good, the sweetest singer of sad thoughts, the soul that gave itself for future ends and aims. The moment came for him when footsore and weary, after many sturubliogs and haltings on his journey towards God, he at last sunk by the way disheartened. Not only was he beaten in his effort to realize what he falsely deemed his highest life and end, but the very ideat itself for which he seemed himself to be living, the earthly cause to which he had pledged his loyalty, palled upon him with its finitude, its relativity, when taken simply in and by itself. It, too, no less than the husks of the swine, proved vanity and vexation of spirit—a noble illusion, uo doubt, a magnificent bubble, but still a bubble, an illusion. Never, anywhere in the world of things that were seen, or of things that could he accomplished on earth, was there any final satisfaction.

div.head: NOT A HOPELESS GOSI'EL.
div.p: NOT A HOPELESS GOSI'EL.

"But," they would say, "This is the very gospel of hopelessness, the blackest night of pessimism." No, it was not. It was simply the gospel that demanded of us that we consider every valua- tion of our life and tesognize the det-per truth and mystery that surrounded us. Earth's failure .was heaven's high succees. The Cross of Jesus was the eternal victory of God. For humanity the truth was manifest in that it refused to be satisfied with any- thing less than God Himself; it would not rest in any finite achievement but, swayed and governed by the will to attain, it still went on, generation after genera- tion, century after century, spurning every past attain- ment, utterly dissatisfied with every present thing, building for an impossible future, saved from hopelesa- ness and inactivity all the time only because, along with the will to attain, went also the knowledge that already attainment was complete and victory assured. 1 The individual came to realize that all values were to be found not in the end he sought, but in the effort he made, not in the causes he served but in the loyalty with which he abandoned himself.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
DECEIVING A PAWNBROKER.

At St. Helens, on Monday, Thomas Macdonald, a fitter, of 125, Church-street, was dealt with on a charge of giving false information to a pawnbroker.—TheChief Constable said a number of articles of wearing apparel were stolen from 8, Sandfleld-crescent, last Sunday night week. The next morning the prisoner entered the articles in pledge at Mr. Moxon's shop, Claughton- street. He told the manager (Mr. Wilkinsorr) they were his own property. The prisoner had been accused of stealing the articles but they were not prepared to prove that was so. He told them when arrested that the pawnbroker would not have taken the things in if be had not said they belonged to him.—The defendant was fined 20s. and costs, or fourteen days' imprisonment.

Sr. HELENS HOSPITAL IN DEBT. The yearly report of the Providence Free Hospital a. St. Helens shows a deficiency on the year's working oi £3od. About £l5O had been spent on repairs and alterations. Having regard to the exceptional and try- ing circumbtances of the past year, the committee did not consider that a despondent view need be taken of the deficit. Nevertheless, it is manifest that in order to maintain the hospital in a state of efficiency greater efforts were required to increare permanently the annual subscriptions. During the year 880 cases were treated, 676 were discharged convalescent. 75 relieved, 16 transferred to other institutions, and 60 remained in the hospital. Since the hospital was opened in 1882, over 13,800 patients have been treated free. INQUIRY INTO MEASLES EPIDEMIC.

At the meeting of the St. Helens Health Committee on Wednesday, Alderman Green called attention to the fact that only one of the great towns of the country had a higher death-rate than St. Helens for the past four weeks ; and the medical officer i of health said it was true that they had bad one of the highest death- rates in recent years in the last quarter. He reported that there was a considerable diminution in the number of cases of measles reported, and also in the number of deaths from this disease. The chairman said a deputa- tion visited London and saw the chief medical officer of the Board of Education to lay before him their case with regard to measles. They produced sufficient evidence to convince him that it was in the interests of public health that an inquiry should be held ;.and this inquiry would be held and the result reported to them in due course.

div.head: HELP FOR THE SUBMERGED TENTH.
div.p: HELP FOR THE SUBMERGED TENTH.

How to help the helpless ! This has been the problem forced upon our attention of late; it is the question of the hour. With all the good will in the world, those who are untrained and inexperienced in social and philanthropic work, stand powerless to help the suffering poor around them. One solution to this problem is to be found in our advertising columns, where the Church Army offers free admission to their Central Training Home for Women Workers, with salaries guaranteed to successful candidates.

WORKHOUSE VISITORS.
Proposal to Abolish The Ladies Committee.
"A CRUEL THING."

There was a lively debate at the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday on the question of Workhouse visitation. As is usual at the annual meeting, it was nroposed that a Ladies' Visiting Committee and a Brabazon Ladies Committee be nominated by the House Com- mittee for appointment by the Board, with power to all members thereof to visit the Workhouse, Cottage Homes and schools at their discretion. "NO NEED FOR OUTSIDERS."

Mr. JOLLEY asked the Board to re-consider the whole position. He did not think he was misinterpreting the feeling of the Board when he said that a year ago a strong section was inclined to abandon the Ladies' Visiting Committee altogether. When first that com- mittee was formed it did an admirable and useful work. They had then no lady guardians, but at the present time there were four, and be ventured, to think they were quite competent to do the special work which women could do in connection wqh the Poor Law, without calling in any outsiders to assist. He proposed an amendment that no Ladies' Committee be appointed, other than the lady guardians. Mr. Cool( seconded. "ABSOLUTE HUMBUG."

Miss BROADBENT !said it would be a most cruel thing to do away with the Ladies' Visiting Committee. For Guardians to pretend that they were interested in the sick poor and to attempt to deprive them of the pleasure they derived from the ladies coming to see them, was absolute humbug. (" Oh " and laughter.) It was absolutely true. At any rate, the ladies could do no harm. _

Mr. JOLLY: Question. Miss BROADBENT : I don't think you have any idea of the pleasure which the ladies give to these people, many of whom will have to spend the rest of their lives in hospital. I earnesly beg of you not to do this wrong to them. Mrs. SIMPSON pointed out that the lady guardians had not always time to inquire into all cases end they were sometimes referred to the other ladies who took an interest in the sick poor. Through the agency of the committee, situations had been found for girls and they were looked after in various ways. The com- mittee was extremsly useful and it would be a pity to do away with it. Mr. COOK said he wished to withdraw his seconding of the amendment. _ _

Miss BROADBENT said that only a short titre ago when money was wanted to provide an inmate with a certain appliance, a member of the House Committee suggested that they should ask the Ladies' Committee to contribute towards it. Each member gave 4s, and it would be peculiarly ungracious, after having asked the committee to help in that way, to disband them. Mr. W. C. BROOKS asked how many members of the Ladies' Committee lived outside the Warrington Union? The CLERK : About four. Mr. BRoOKS : I think those ladies might find Scope to do useful work within their own Unions. Miss BROADBENT: There is no hospital in their own area.

div.head: AFRAID OF THE SUFFRAGETTES?
div.p: AFRAID OF THE SUFFRAGETTES?

The Rev. A. M. MITCHNLL said it would be a pity to shut the gates in the faces of the ladies. He did not know whether Mr. Jolley was alarmed because of the auffragette movement—(laughter)—but he (the speaker) thought that, while it was e•robably desirable that the ladies should be allowed to visit the institution some little restriction should be placed upon them. The resolution as it stood gave them too much liberty ni power, as they were authorised to isit t'ne Workhouse and Cottage Homes at their dis -

cretion. He suggested that certain days and hours of visitation should be specified. Other wise, they would) not quite know where they were. They were making the house a happy hunting field for ladies who lived outside th 9 district and who, when it suited them Or when they were in a particular mood, thought they' would like to see the sick and the old people in the' institution. The matter ought to be arranged on more businesslike lines. He would be sorry to see the ladiee excluded, but he thought Miss Broadbent would have strengthened her case if she had listened to his gentl& pleading some time ago when he asked her to make the committee more representative of the people and par- ticularly of the working classes. Miss BROADBENT : It IS not my place to put nevi members on. it has nothing to do with me. The CLERK: Mr. Mitchell has the right to name ani lady he thinks proper at the meeting of the House Com- mittee.
-I"...iSS BROADBENT : We are not ashamed of the ladiee visiting the house at any time. There is nothing ver3t shady._
The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: Nobody said anything about that
Mr. MATHER said his view was that if the Committee. were appointed at all, they ought to be given every freedom.

Miss BROADBENT : Or else it is no good at all. Mr. MATHER said he was somewhat inclined to• support Mr. Jolley's view that the Committee was' unnecessary, considering that there were four lady guardians. Miss BROADBENT : There is more work than we can, do. We cannot get to know all the people. There are. over 500 of them.

FRICTION IN THE WORKHOUSE. Mr. JOLLEY said that any attempt to make insinua- tions about his motives in the matter did not affect him at all. He fought very hard at the outset for the' appointment of a ladies' committee. In the early days that committee did a most honourable and useful work, but he ventured to suggest with some coufldence that recent years the character of the work and the reasons for the existence of the committee had changed. Personal considerations did not influence him in the matter. Several of the members were known to him and he had the highest regard for them. In the days when there were no lady guardians several useful reforms WOTO facilitated by the committee. Now, however, there was no' necessity for outside assistance. There bad occasionally been a great deal of friction in the house of recent. years and he believed that friction would be diminished by this abolition ol the ladies' committee. That wee• his sole reason for proposing that there should be no ladies' committee except the lady guardians. On a vote being taken, Mr. Jolley's amendment wag. lost and the cJmmittee will be appointed in the usual, way.

The facts were entirely different from what Councillor Pemberton had stated. The architects appointed sent in two sets of plans. The advertisement, in the first instance, was for plans, and not for plans and quantities, and both the plans of the selected architects were considered the best in the whole competition. The first of their plans complied strictly with the conditions of the advertisement and was for schools which should not cost more than ten guineas per head. fhe Sites and Buildings Committee, however, considered that the second plan was so very much superior to the first that, subject to a reference to the surveyor for his opinion, they preferred to accept it. All these matters had, in due course, b 'en brought before the Education Clmmittee, explained and con- firmed. Every member of the committee wss therefore responsible for the raising of the amount par head. It was not a change in the initial conditions, which were complied with to the letter by the selected architects. The present proposition was merely to pay the archi- tects, in the event of the scheme not teing proceeded with, 11 per ceot. for the qusutities,which were outside of and in addition to the duties implsed upon them by the advertisement. Under the cov3r of an amendment, Councillor Pemberton had raised the whole question from ato z. Such a discussion was entirely out of order.

div.head: ARCHITECTS' FEES.
div.p: ARCHITECTS' FEES.
Another Education Committee Debate.
COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON AND ALLEGED
SUSPICION

The vexed question of the conditions of competition for architectural work in connection with the erection of local Council schools again gave rise to discussion at the meeting of the Warrington Education Committee on Monday evening. Councillor 11. Roberts presided and there were also present :—Mr. A. J. Jolley (deputy- chairman), Aldermen Smethurst, James Evans and B Aton, Councillors Birtles, Jenkins, Pemberton, Archer, Lindley, Broadhcrst, Revs. Canon Stevenson, G. C. Briggs and Neville Wilson, Mrs. C. Jackson Holmes, Messrs. C. E. Parker, R. T. Fairclough, J. Jarman, E. Plinston, R. T. Fairclough, H. Kingdon, J. Upson, C. 11. Unsworth, J. Longland, G. Walker, J. Moore Murray (director of education) and R. B. Roberts (assistant director). "LOOKED UPON WITH SUSPICION." The Law Clerk and the Surveyor having reported to the Sites and Buildings Committee the result of their negotihtions with the architects for the Oakwo,d- avenue, 01:ver-street and Parr-street schools in accord- aLce with the instructions of the Committee at Ur:J.r last meeting. it eas resolved that the law clerk be instructed in preparing the agreement with the archi- tects to make provision so that, when the tenders for each school have been received, in the event of the Committee for any reason deciding not to proceed with the erection of any of the three schools named, the architects shall be paid for the preparation of the bills of quantities and all work connected therewith at the rate of 11 per cent. up to the limit of the cost origin- ally agreed upon in respect of the Oakwocd-avenue school, viz. r—Ell 126. per head of the accommodation to be provided. Councillor PEMBERTON moved an amendment that the minute be referred back.He said the last meeting but one of the Sites and Buildings Committee was the first occasion that he knew, as a member of that committee, that the conditions originally sanctioned for the com- petition of architects had beeu exceeded. It was clearly laid down in the conditions, that 10 guineas per head, with five per cent, should be the limit. The terms now submitted exceeded thit limit by 129. per head. That might not seem much, but when one considered that on the three schools it would amount to something approaching £I,OOO, it was a great dell. Those would rot be the last schools to be erected by the committee, and- the architectural world was looking on the work with greater interest than the members of the committee reAlized. At, the mooting of the Sites and Buildings Committee the members themselves seemed to be astonished at the extent to which the conditions had been exceeded—in fact one member was under the impression that they were to be 10s. less. In the past schools had been built at as low a price as £8 12s. per head, ao that the present amount was very high. It was obvious that if one firm of architects were to be allowed to spend 12s. per head more than the other corapetitors, they could evolve a very different design —as the great question which con- fronted the architects was how to keep within the limit laid down by the committee. Once before, in connection with that authority, matters went even further. Not only was the limit exceeded by the architects, but the builder actually gave a contract which was accepted by that committee and the Corporation. When the circumstances came to the knowledge of many members, a special meeting of the Council was called, with the result that the project was upset and the ratepayers were saved £l,OOO. He contended that this case was even worse, becaose in the fist case the architects had the authority of the com- mittee to alter the plans, whereas in the present instance they had not, as it, was the initial competition. Ile was staggered to find the present proposition advanced after all the controversy there had been about architectural work. One of the reasons why he was so keen on the question was that the architectural world was already looking upon the committee with suspicion. At first he did not think it was necessary to have an independent assessor, hut he had now come round to that view. The Society of Architects felt so strongly about it that they withdrew 73 of their most competent I men from the competition, and therefore the Committee had not, the best brains of England at their disposal. The average number of architects for schools was from 80 to 120, but in the case of the Warrington Committee, . it was only 20, for the reason he had stated. What would the contracting and architectural world say when these new conditions came out? The public life of the ' town and the work of any committee ought to be above - suspicion.
A I'OOTIIALL _FIELD ANALOGY.

If an attimpt were made to enact such unfair con- ditions on the football field, it would not be safe. (Laughter.) The lives of the people who tried it would be endangered, if the crowd were cognisant of it. It was now stated that the architects who won the com- petition sent in two sets of plans—one according to the printed conditions, and the other exceeding them. One of the most singular things about it was that bath sets of plans were considered serperior to all the others. The more the question was investigated, the more. unpleasmit it became. If the committee were deter- mined to spend .£ll 12s. per head on the schools, let all the architects have the opportunity of competing on that basis. It was because of this question, that he spoke so strongly about not having received notice of a certain r eeting,as be intended objocting to its going any further. The Town Clerk had advised the com- mittee that the printed conditions under which tha architects tendered, with regard to pricey, were in the melting pot, and new conditions had to be drawn up I All that proved that the origin''l conditions were not being adhered to. Alderman JAME'S EVANS sec )ndecl the amendment for the purpose of Ciscussion. CHAIRMAN'S DEFENCE OF THE COMMITTEE. The CHAIRMAN said that almost the entire speech of Councillor Pemberton was out of order, but he (the chairman) did not wish to curtail what he bad to say,

div.head: SANCTION OF THE COUNCIL.
div.p: THE SANCTION OF THE COUNCIL.

Alderman EvANs said the impression he got from Councillor Pemberton's remarks was ttat previous to the issuing of invitations to the architects for the plans referred to, there were conditions which fixed the price at ten guineas per heart, The CHAIRMAN : That is quite correct. Alderman EVANS : If that is the recognized figure that the Council has sanctioned, this propnsition is open to criticism and amendment by the Ceuncil. The CitAtrotAN : The Council has sanctioned the alteration, because this has all been submitted six months ago. The plans were explained and adopted and then submitted to the education authority end confirmed. Aldorman EVANS : I don't see how the Council could have done that, with all deference to you. The CRAIRMAN : It has done it, whether you see how it was done or not.

In reply to a further question by Alderman Evans, The CHAIRMAN said the Council had not 3et sanctioned the payment of a specific sum for quantities. Councillor PEMBERTON said that never in the minutes of the Council or of the Education Committee, did the amount £ll. 121. appear. Members had therefore voted for it without knowing it. Alderman BOLTON slid he did not know why Councillor Pemberton had raised the question now. They thrashed it out in committee and were practic- ally unanimow. Councillor Pemberton did nr.t then raise any objection. Councillor PEMBERTON : ElEcuse me.

- Alderman BOLTON : Your memory is sometimes defective. Continuing be said the plans had received the sanction of the Education Committee and the Town Council. Supposing, however, that the scheme were not c irried through and it transpired that the cost worked out at more than the agreed sum, the committee would not be liable to pay for quantities on a higher basis than £ll 12.. per head. That was the sole purpose of the present recommendation. The attempt to raise the general question was only like making a wind bag for someone to stick a pin into. (Laughter). Mr. JAR MAN took exception to Councillor Pemberton's statement that the whole of the conditions were in the melting pot. Printed conditions were laid down for these competitions but if, in order to safeguard the Council and the ratepayers, it was found necessary to , insert 3 special condition, he could not see any objec- tion to it. The amoant for qutntities-1} per cent— was teasonable—in (nut it was generally twice as much. The amendment was defeated and the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: IDEAL HOME-HEALER!
div.p: THE IDEAL HOME-HEALER!
Zam-Buk Heals Child's Ringworm, Mother's Cut Hand, & Father's Bad Foot.

More convincing evidence of Zam-Buk' all-round usefulness in the hctlie is given by Mrs. A. Tootle, of 51, Mill-street, Orrnskirk, Lancs. "Our Annie came home from school one day," Mrs. Tootle said to a reporter, " w ith nasty red blotches on her head. They spread as big as the palm of my hand, and destroyed Annie's hair, which came away in bunches, leaving her scalp as red as fire. The child suffered awfully from the irritation and smarting, and her head was such a sight with the ringworm that I felt ashamed for it to be seen. 'I tried ointments and other things recommended by friends, but they all failed to touch Annie's severe case. Then I wris persuadtd to get Zam-Buk from the chemist. This rare balm soothed Annie's itchy scalp beautifully and took out all the fiery inflamma- tion.

"Regular dressings with Zam-Buk killed the ring- worm and left the childs scalp quite clean. I never thought Alice's hair would grow any more, but it has come again splendidly. "While cutting bread the knife slipped and gashed my left hand badly near the thumb. I immediately got down my box of Zam-Buk, smeared the balm over the cut, and bandaged the hand up. A few dressings of Zam-Buk in this way soon healed the wound. "When my husband's boot rubbed the skin off his heel, Zam-Bub soothed the raw place and grew a new c„vering of skin over it. We have reason to feel very grateful to Zam-Buk in our home." It always pays to keep Zam-Buk handy. Beware of spurious imitations aug worthless aubstitutes.

MEDICAL TREATMENT.
WARRINGTON AUTHORITIES SECURE MAXIMUM GRANT.

Much gratification was expressed at the meeting of the Warrington Education Committee,on Monday even- ing,st the Board of Education's rec sguition of the way in which the committee is administering the Act fo! the medical inspection and treatment of school children Mr. HOLMAN KINGDON, chairman of the Medical Inspection Committee, drew attention to the following minutes of the Medical Inspection Committee : It was noted that a grant, amounting to £319 ss. 54., had been received from the Board of Education in respect of the expense incurred by this committee in car rying out the medical treatment of school children and that the grant represents the maximum assessment under th. Boar Vs regulations dealing with this matter. Mr. KINGDON said the minote marked a red-letter day for that committee. Med:ca! inspection and medical treatment were two very different things. Medical inspection was imposed upon them by law, but under the Act imposing that duty they were given powers to acquire rights to go in for medical treatment, ehich were more or less optional. War ing!-on took advantage of the opportunity thus given, and had done a certain amount of work in the direction of medical treatment. The Board of Education had now recognized the work by giving them a grant which would efford great satisfaction to the committee. The grant was in respect of medical treatment, and not of the medical inspection work. The grant to Warrington was the maximum scale given to any town. having rega:d to the population of the town they had got as large an amount of money as any town, in the country. Ile %cis not going to hAd out any hope th it the grant would effect a saving in the amount of money they spent. Further expenditure was absolu' ely necessary, and the grant received and the grants they hoped to receive in the future would go a fairly long way to wards meeting the extra expense which would otherwise be entailed.

div.head: DENTAL CLINIC.
div.p: THE DENTAL CLINIC.

The dental clinic was in its infancy. It was made quite clear when they commenced that work that it was only beginning in a very small way. The number of children they had been able to treat up to the present was very small. The money they were going to get in the way of grants for medical treatment work would h.tve to be set aside as a kind of reserve against any expense which the town would otherwise have to incur. (Hear, her.) Councillor BIRTLES seconded and the minutes were adopted.

div.head: OLD LIGHTHOUSE WOMAN. 20 Years* Watch.
div.p: OLD LIGHTHOUSE WOMAN. 20 Years* Watch.

To Warrington cyclists the lighthouse at Hale is a favourite place of pilgrimage. They will therefore hear with interest that Mrs. Joynson, who is the only woman lighthouse keeper in England, kept her last watch on Wednesday night at that pic:uresque spot. For twenty years Mrs. Johnson has lived at the lighthouse, and for the past four years, since the death of her husband, bas been the official keeper. "My life hai not been an unliApoy ote here," remarked Mrs. Joynson, who is a middle-aged woman of quick perception and remarkable intelligence, to a Daily Mai/ representative " and it is a wiench to go." "I am giving up the appointment for the sake of my children, who are desirous of iving at Stockport and so I have decided to leave %hat has been my home for the past twenty years. The Commissioner has tried several times to persuade me to continue. " He told me on iTitesday that he had never had even a repott concerning me. He said 'You are leaving with honour.' When my husband died at the lighthouse I took up the position on a three months' trial and have continued till now.

"I am on duty for three and a half hours before and after high tide, arid must keep the light burning at night time and the fog bell ringing if necessary. On several ccclsions I have rung the bell for the whole seven hours, and once I had nearly a fortnight of fog, but I got throught it all right. For the first two years I had some assistance from my son, but sine' then I have mat aged alone. I have never had an accident of any kind." The Hale light can be seen for six miles down the Mersey. It is a guide to vessels on their way to Widnes up the river. Most of the traffic consists of small coasting vessels and tugboats towing flats. Mrs. Joynson has been described as the "heroine" of the Mersey, and ir well known to mariners whose duties take them along the upper reaches of that waterway.

div.head: POOR LAW GUARDIANS' DIGNITY.
div.p: POOR LAW GUARDIANS' DIGNITY.

Whether workhouse inmates should be expected to stand upon the entry of guardians and officials as a sign of respect was warmly debated at Monday's meet- ir,g of the Grimsby Board of Guardian. Mr. Cordon, in moving that the practice be discon- tinued, said it was surprising that such a motion had to he moved in the twentieth century. The practice inflicted unnecasary humiliation upon the inmates of the house, many of whom we e there through no fault of their own. There was a good deal of interruption during the discussion, and it was brought to an end by the previous question beips moved and carried,

div.p: GUARDIANS' MEETING.

The nscvly-elected Warrington 13oard of Guardians held its first meeting on Wednesday when the business included the election of chairman and vice-chairman atd crummittees. Ou the initiative of the Rev. A. M. NI Rebell, some lively passages took place on the ques- tion of irregular attendance of members at the Board and committee meetings. Pend ng the e/ection of Chairman, the Clerk (Mr. A. Bo..tornley) presided. 1 here were present :—Mrs. Simpson, Miss Br,-ndbenr, Mrs. Hall, Revs. T. R. Nlattheu-s and A. M. Mitchell, Messrs. E. L. Bent. A. J. Jolley, J. Billinge, Philip C. Garnett, T. Dale, NV. C. Brooks, G. APen, J. A. Hughes, P. McKinley, G. Mather, J. Cook, .1. A. Hughes, T. It(1., won, .J. W. Knowles. .1. Cook, W. hli.nagan, J. Backhousr., M. W. Seton, T. Ritchie, R. Lee, W. Houghton, W. Furness, W. J. Brown (master), C. E. 14^_wrence (surerintendent of Cottage Howes).
THE CHAIRMAN. REV. A. M. MiTCHELL'S UNSUPPORTED PROTEST.

Mr. NIATIIER proposed the re-election to the chair- man. hip f Air. E. L. Bent whose rervices during the past twelve month, hid given complete satisfaction. Mr 111 ',INGE seconded and several members support, d. The RE v.A.M. MITCHELL said he took exception to M Bent's re-election for the same reasons that he stated Jest year and which he did not think it was necessary to enlarge upor. The CLERK : Have you any amendment to propose? 'I he Rev. A. M. MITCHELL : No, I don't propose an ameniment because I think opportunity should be given, before the resolution is voted npon, for full and tree discussion, apart from any amendment. The election of Mr. Bent was then put to the meet- ing and carried, the Rev. A. M. Mitchell being the only dissentient.

Mr. BENT, in returning thankr, said the little obstruc- tion which they bad just witnessed was the usual occurrence. It was nothing fresh to the Board. The Bev. A. M. MITCHELL : And it won't be either, Mr. Chairmen.

Mr. BENT said he believed he had the support of the Board generally in undertaking the position. He did not say he made an ideal chairman, but he tried to do his best, as far as his abilities would permit. He extended a hearty welcome to live new members of the Botird and mentioned that Mr. Robinson was Tenewing his association with the Board of %hich he was a a former member.

VICE-CHAIRMAN. Mr. BENT moved the re-election of Mr. Jolley as •ice-chairman, and aserved that his abilities were excelled by none. Mrs. SIMPSON seconded. Mr. MATHER said be thought all the members, with- out exception, would have pleasure in supporting Mr. Jolley's re-election.
The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. JOLLEY briefly returned thanks to the Board for that renewed mark of their confidence. IRREGULAR ATTENDERS.—A BREEZE.
The Board thcn proceeded with the appointment of committees.

Before the Assessment Committee was appointed, The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL said it would be well to know if those who were nominated for the work were willing to give the attendance which was expected of them. If they looked over the list of attendances for the past sear, they would find that about 33 per cent of the guardians had attended the Board meeting' less than twelve times. In his judgment, that was bad con. duct and it was most most, unnesirable that guardians should be elected to represent the people and to look after the poor if they did not, attend thk Board meetings The CHAIRMAN I think you ought to confine yourrelf to the appointment. _ _ _
The Rev. A. NI, .NIITCHELL : lam doing so. The CHAIRMAN: Then 30U must put that question to the individual members.
The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL : The same applies to ,he—
The CHAIRMAN : I c-innot allow you to proceed in that sort of way. The Rev. A M. MITCHELL attempted to continue his remarks but Ras assailed with cries of " Chair " and "Order."
The Rev. A. M. MrrcitELL : What is in order then ? The CHAIRMAN : I cannot allow ycu to proceed in that strain.
The Rev. A. M. MITatELL : What have I to do then ?

The CHAIRMAN : We are appointing members of the Assessment Committee. I want you to stick to that point. If you want any information from the members who constitute that committee, you must ask them The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: I don't want informw tion at all. What I ciant to insist upon is that those ho are put upon these committees shall attend to their duties.

Ths CHAIRMAN: I call upon Mr. Mather to move tte applintment of the Assessment Committee. The committee MU elected as follows :—Nlessts:E.L. Bent., A. J. Jolley, W. Furness, J, Billinge, W.C.Brooks, W. Houghton, G. Mather J. W. Knowles, R. Lee, J: A 4 Hitches, T. Robinson, and the Rev. I'. IL Mathews. When the appointment of the Cottage Homes Com, mittce was ccnsidered, Mr. MITCHELL again pressed his point as to regular attendance. Mr. BACKHOUSE : We are not all clergymen. We have not as much time as Mr. Mitchell. Mr. HUGHES said that those members who went to Padgste devoted about two hours to the work. They did not simply put in an appearance for two or three minutes.
The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: I give more time to the house than you do. It is not fair. BREAD AND CHEESE FOR VAGRANTS.

Mr. .IOLLEY moved that the Board express its approval of an inter-county schune for dealing with vagrants in Cumberland, Westmoreland, Lancashire and Cheshire. The proposals included the provision of a mid-day meal, consisting of half-a-pound of bread and two ounces of cheese, for vagrants, the money to be raised by a common fund from the Guardians hi the respective areas. Ile contended that the scheme would do much to check indiscrinfnate almsgiving and deal with a great social evil. The problem was a pressing one in Warrington, for owing to its situation on the main road from Manchester to Liverpool, the town attracted large numbers of vagrants. The expenditure n the scheme would be a small matter, as the number of vagrants in the entire area did not exceed 1,200 or 1,300 on nny given date. Mr. MATHER said the question was not what the bread and cheese would cost, but what it would cost to &Bulbar, it. If they were going to set up another body of officialz all over the country, it would mean a considerable sum.

Mr. liriowLEs : You are quite right. We are killed with officials to-day. Mr. NIATHER : Well, lam beginning to feel sickly. (Laughter.) Continuing, be said they would always have vagrancy, but if anything could be done to mitiga'e the evil, it would have his support. In reply to Mr. Mather, the WORKIIOI.JbE MASTER stated that the number of tramps passing through the Workhouse was about 30n per week. Mr. NIATHER : That is very low indeed. _ _ _

Mr. BACKIIOUSE said the fact that 300 vagrants wet° passing through the house weekly at the present time, %hen there was work for all, was nothing less than a public sc Mr. KNOWLES said the relief proposed was a step in the right direction, but be did not think it vras sufficient to give to the poor man on the road. the Rev. A. M. Mt rCHEI.r. said they should do every- thing in their power to help the poor vagrant, but they must not think that, beo tuse they had adopted a scheme, they must shut up their hearts end thereby attempt to get rid of indiscriminate almsgiving. The Board approved the scheme and appointed Mr. Jolley and the Clerk to attend a conference on the subject.

div.head: DORIC SIMPLICITY.
div.p: DORIC SIMPLICITY.

The Dorians in anc'ent Greece were of simple habits one of which was the partaking of common meals. This custom was know'. as Syssitia or Pheiditia, and prevailed also in Sparta. The men did not dine with the rest of the family, but with other males who formed small parties, each individual contributing a share towards the meal. The contributions were mostly in kind, the varius items supplied by the diners being pre-arranged. Whenever obtainable, the Greek grape was on the table. They knew its wonderful food value arid savoury properties and so do we. That is why Currant Recipes are always acceptable. Try this one.
CURRANT PATTIES.

loz cornfl ur, 4)zs. currants, 1 lemon, 4oz. castor sugar, !,(,z. butter, short-crust paste. Method.—Line some patty pans with thinly rolled out short-crust paste, providing paste covers for each. Mix the con flour with a gill of cold water, stir in the grated rind and juice f lemon, the currants and the sugar, cook hll together for five minutes, stirring all the time, and add the butter; mix well, fill the paste- lined patty pans with the preparation, wet the edges of tie paste, put on the covers, brush over with sweet milk and bake 20 minutes.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, April 26, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, April 26, 1913.
COMPLETE 'EXAMINER' STORY.
rALL RIGHTS RESERVED.

If you will allow .me, I will tell you my errand, and leave you to judge whether. Mr. Aiwa should be communicated with at once. or what steps it will be best to take. Pardon me, are yon Miss Averil?" "Yes. I declare, you make me quits curt. WSJ " she exclaimed. "Pray come this way." She led the wag across-the hail, and as she passed for a momr,At under a broad band of light that streamed from an open door, I caught a glimpse of a petite figurej rather plump, with crinkly black hair. " Now, what is it?" she said, when she had shewn me into a large, unlighted room, and closed the door behind her. .

I thought I would startle her out of her- self-complacency. "The bank underneath us,'" I said, "is to be entered by burglars to- niot—burglars in collusion with some people living on the premises." " Impossible ! " "So I should have said—only I overheard the conspirators talking in their room at the hotel. There can't be a doubt about it."'

There was some light in the room from the street; and I thought the young lady—she did not look more than twenty—had turned very pale. There was little wonder. For perhaps a minute she stood silent, her eyes fixed on the floor. "Have you mentioned this to anyone else,

"Neville is my name," I replied. "No, have not. I thought your father was the pro- per person-" "You were quite right, and I am sure he will be extremely obliged to you," Miss Averil interrupted: "I will send for him at once, and tell him all you say. You are stay- ing at the Royal George, I understand?" Yes, for the present." "And you are quite sure that some of the inmates of this house- It seems incred- ible ! "

"No doubt it does to you. But I am quite cure. I heard one rc 3n—who seemed, by his voice, to be a gentleman—asking whether the police would not be able to spot it—meaning, I suppose, detect that the burglary was no burglary at all. He promised the other man one hundred pounds. The other, man strongly objected to waiting for his money till the thing was over. I suppose he thought that if he were not paid in advance he would not be paid at all." "No doubt. Well; Mr. Neville, I am suro my father will be .infinitely obliged to you. I will send for him at once, and, of course, he will put the matter into the hands of the police. But there is one thing. As my father's honour and credit are concerned, may I ask you to tell no one else?" Oh, certainly," I exclaimed. "I should not dream of doing such a thing." "And you will come to dinner to-morrow and let my father thank you himself? Dot!" "You forget that I am quite a. stranger, Miss Averill," I said, laughing. " I won't say yes or no to your kind invitation in the meantime; but I hope all will go well to-night." "There is no fear of that, I think; but how can we ever thank you enough?" "Please don't say anything more," I re- turned. "Indeed, you have thanked me quite enough." I left her, went back to the hotel, .and had a meal which they called dinner. I then dressed for the ball.

When I entered the ballroom I knew, be- fore I had had time to search for her, that Lettice was not there. But I waited patiently, and when the evening was half over she came. With her coming everything was changed. The lights shone more brilliantly; the dancers moved more rapidly; the music, in an instant, became gay and bright. I sought for and obtained an introduction, and in another minute I was in Paradise. My step suited hers admirably; we seemed to be floating together on a sea of melody. "We need not go back to your mother just yet?" I asked when the dance was over. I was forced to say "your mother" because the stupid fellow who had introduced us had so mumbled her name that I could not catch it.

"I have no mother," said the girl, her •face changing as she spoke. "The lady who brought me is Mrs. Gilbert." The hours that night sped like so many minutes; and I imagine I must have made good use of my time, for as the ball was breaking up I managed to get Lettice in a quiet corner, and began to speak of the days when I had seen her every day without being able to speak to her—of my reason for coming to Astonbury—of the delight I felt at meeting her. I was going on to confess that I loved her when she gently stopped me. "I think ypti had better say no more, Mr. Neville. It is perhaps only fair to tell you that lam engaged." . • Engaged! Fool that I was, I had never dreamt of this! Yet what was more likely? Did I fancy that no men in the world had eyes in their heads but myself? I was silent—dumb from misery and the bitterness of my disappointment. "Come, Mr. Neville," said Lettice, so gently that I felt sure she was sorry for me, Mrs. Gilbert is waiting for me. Will you take me to her?"
As we passed through a deserted corridor I startled my companion by saying to her, "Do you know, I have had the impudence to speak to you as I did without even knowing your name."
"My name is Lettice," she said, 'blushing. "That I did know, and I shall never forget that dear name as long as I live. It was the other name-"
"My surname, you mean? It is Averil." "Averil? You are related to .Mr. Averil, the banker?"

"I am his daughter." "Well—pardon me, but I am surprised. You don't in the least resemble your sister." "My sister? I have no sister." "Not even a step-sister?" "Of course not! How ridiculous you are!"

"Miss Averil, listen to me for -a minute, please. I called on your, father this evening. He was dining out-" "Now you are really talking nonsense. He dined at home at two o'clock, and I know he had no engagement for to-night." I was dumb with astonishment, but I soon recovered myself, and went on: "I called on business of the utmost import- ance, and saw a young tidy of about your own height, but stouter, with black wavy hair--" Oh' I see now. You have made a very natural mistake. You took her for my father's daughter, and she is only his secretary. But here is Mrs. Gilbert. I really must go." Having put the two ladies into the carriage that was waiting for them I went down to the courtyard of the hotel for a quiet smoke. My brain was quite bewildered. Did not the young lady I had seen at Mr. Averil's say that she was his daughter? She certainly did. Of that I was ready to take my oath. What did it all mean? Had my message over reached Mr. Averil? Not likely, if the false Miss Averil were the person upon whom the burglars were depending for help. Anyhow, I thought, it could do no harm to stroll past the bank and see what precautions had been taken. It was dawn when I reached the bank. To my surprise a small motor-car, painted yel- low, was standing before the door. No one seemed to be in charge of it. As I stood looking on the street-door of the bank opened, and a girl in full motoring cos- tume came out. She paused on the top-most step to embrace someone in the doorway in- visible to me, then ran lightly down the steps, and jumped into the motor-car. In another instant it was half-way down the street. It stopped, and a man jumped into it; but it started again immediately, and in a few seconds it was out of sight. All this seemed to me so strange that I went straight to the nearest police-station and told them all I knew. They assured me that if the burglar's accomplice had escaped in the motor-car she could not go far, for messages would be sent to all the police. stations within a fifty-mile radius. So 1 went back to the hotel and tumbled into bed.

I was awakened by a loud knock at my door. Mr. Averil wanted to see me. I told him to come in, and he came in and sat on the edge of my bed and cried—a gentle, pink- faced old man with snow-white hair.
He was ruined, he told me. His foolish con- fidence in his secretary, Miss Healy, had re- sulted in her borrowing his keys and sterainst
Our forefathers neglected their eyes, the present generation
now suffers.
Don't neglect yours, CONSULT
JOHNSTON WATSON, SIGHT TESTING OPTICIAN, 84, BRIDGE STREET, WARRINGTON.
