div.head: FRE YELLOW MOTOR-CAR.
div.p: FRE YELLOW MOTOR-CAR.
BY JOHN K. LEYS
Aufkor of "The Fateful Ring," "By Traitor's Gate," "A Blind Man's Vengeance," "The Lawyer's Secret," "The Broken Fetter," 4c.

I met her regularly every morning, and I was convinced she knew me by sight, for she zould not help doing so; yet we had never spoken, never even exchanged a smile. I felt i.nstinctively that she was not a girl with whom an acquaintance could be struck up in that way; and, alas! I could think of no way of getting an introduction to her. I had caught a rather earlier train-to town than usual, and glancing up from my paper I found myself looking straight into the love- liest brown eyes I had ever seen. lam not going to expatiate upon her beauty or the charm of her personality. I hungered for the privilege of speaking to her; but- it was denied me. Once—l may as well confess it—once I fol- lowed her, and discovered by that ignoble means that she was an art student at South Kensington. But that was all I could learn about her—and then, one morning, the train started without her. I looked out for her anxiously the next day. She did not come. She never travelled by that train again. But we were fated to meet again. One day at Waterloo I saw a young girl run up to a girl friend who had her back to me, calling out: "Lettice! Who would have thought of see- ing you here? Are you going home?' Yes; I only ran up for the day," said the other; and before I saw her face I knew it was she. They continued to talk for a while, and then made their way to one of the platforms. I hung about in the vague hope that chance would throw some little scrap of information in my way. And I was lucky. The two girls made their way to the left- luggage office, and I followed at a respectful distance. To one of them—my friend—a large brown-paper parcel was handed. A perter came up to relieve her of it, and I hurried up, searching my pockets for an imaginary counterfoil ticket. "Will you label this for Astonbury?" I heard her say to the man; and I retired jubilant. Not that I had any definite plan in my head; but I had learnt something, and I felt that my lucky star was rising. I took my holidays as early as possible that year—in June. And when the fellows asked me where I was going I did not say "To Astoubury" ; but I _went there all the same, arriving early in the afternoon. I noticed an unusual bustle in the Royal George (the only good hotel in the place), and was told that there was to be a ball that night in the Assembly Rooms attached to the hotel, on behalf of some charity. As 80011 as I heard this I rushed to the telegraph office and wired to my landlady to pack my dress suit and send it by cob to Waterloo and on to Aston- bury. For I made sure she would attend the ball that night. If not, I would have to de- pend on a chance meeting in the street, from which nothing could be hoped. Obviously, I could not go about the- town inquiring for "Lettice." To calm my excitement and poss away the time I took a walk in the country, and when I returned I went up to my room for a wash. Being rather tired I threw myself-on the top of my bed, and, as I might have expected, fell fast asleep. I was awakened by the sound of voices, and for a few moments I could not imagine where they came from. But in a little I un- derstood. - -

V.,. • AB there was a great demand for rooms at the hotel that night owing to the ball, some rough attic chambers had been utilised. Mine was one of these. The voices came from another. They were not loud, but a word or two was plainly audible now and then, and I thought it would be only decent to knock upon the plank partition and tell my neigh- bours not to talk so loud. I actually had my fist raised for this pur- pose, when a word that reached my ears arrested it in mid-air. "Sure the police won't be able to spot it?" said one of the men.
"Certain," responded the other. I paused in some uncertainty. The next word I heard banished it entirely. "What will be the best time? There's so little dark now."_

"True—curse it! Better say two." "Very good. I'll be there, and hand over the hundred when you've done the job." "No, by—!" "Speak lower, can't you? These are only wooden partitions. How do you know there isn't somebody listening behind that?" And the speaker struck the beards within an inch of my head. "We'll soon settle that!" cried his com- panion. He jumped up, and I heard him cress the room to open his door. As he did so I disappeared under the bed, so that when he opened my door and glanced within, the room was apparently empty. When he returned I crawled out; but after that I heard but little. That little, however, told me something. "Doesn't old Averil keep a gun?" " "Yee, but I'll see that it's not leaded. Be- sides, he sleeps very sound." "And the dog?" "I'll see to him."
"What about the door of the strong- room?"
"I'll see that Ws left unlocked when r go to bed."

There was an interval of silence, and then the conspirators left the room together. • As far as I could see, some house was to be robbed—or, rather, there Woe an appearance of a burglary to be made up, the crime being really committed from within. That was how I interpreted the bits of conversation I had overheard.

My first thought, naturally, was to go straight to the police-station. But I reflected that if in this case a man's foes were they of his own household—if the burglary was (as I suspected) a "put-up job," to cover the crime of some son or nephew or servant—it might possibly be a cruel kindness to the victim to make the affair public. Why not. ascertain who this Mr. Averil might be and deliver my warning to him? Making my way to the bar through a crowd of loafers who surrounded it, I got hold of a local directory, and there I soon discovered that the only person of that name in the town was George M. Averil, manager of the Aston- bury Branch of Sinclair's Bank. A few steps brought me to the substantial stone building known to the inhabitants of Astonbury as "Si n clair'6." The ground 'floor was evidently used as the bank offices; the manager's residence was on the first and second floors. The strong-room was probably in the basement.
I rang the house-bell, for, of course, the bank had been, closed several hours before, and asked for Mr. Averil.

He was out, the maid said; and as T was hesitating whether to vc ait for his return or go. at once to the police, a gentle feminine voice fell on my ear. There was a caressing note in it that made it peculiarly attractive. "Who is it?" said the lady, out of the .darkness of the hall. "Oh, a gentleman to see Mr. Averil? I am so sorry, but he is not in at present. If it is anything I can do-" "I am not sure," I answered. "I am anxi- ous to see Mr. Averil himself. It is a matter of great importance." "Really?" said the Ind, and I could not decide whether she as speaking ironically or not.

"Yes," I returned, thinking that she little Imagined how important it was. "If you care to confide your business -to me," said she, "I will see that your message is delivered to my father as soon as he eome3 in, which will be about ten—not before." " Can't you tell me where he is?"
"Dining- with some friends." "I mill come back at ten," I said; then, rememberipa the ball. I added boAtily. "No:
thirty thousand pounds in notes and gold !tom the safe. No doubt she had gone on on the motor-car I had seen.

it had not been traced, and he was sure it never would be traced. He would go down to his grave a ruined and dishonoured man. if his daughter Lettice had not, from her rib- curd lovo of art. eons un to study at South tiensington, he would never have been led to confide so much in Miss Healy.

it was really Lettice's fault that the whole thing had happened, and he should not won- dor if one result was that her engagement would be broken off. Engaged? Oh, yes; she had been engaged for the last twelve months to Arthur Locke, one of the clerks in the bank, a second cousin of the senior partner:

I devoutly hoped that the engagement would be broken off, though I did not utter the wish aloud. And when the old gentleman had satisfied himself that I could tell him nothing that I had not told the police already, he left me.

For the next week I lingered still at Aston- bury, without any definite object. Only once did I get a glimpse of Lettice, and then she was accompanied by a tall, fair, good-looking young man whom I rightly conjectured to be Arthur Locke. She gave me a constrained little bow as she passed me. And this was all that remained to me after my taste of Paradise! My time during that week was mostly spent in taking long country walks; and on the last day of my stay—for I had decided to leave Astonbury—l found myself about eight in the evening a dozen miles from home. There was evidently a storm coming on, and no house was near.

I had neither overcoat nor umbrella—if I had had either, perhaps this story would have had a different ending. I had barely covered three miles of my jour- ney home when the thunder broke over my head, and the rain came down in torrents. The Only shelter near me was a farmhouse, not far from the road. I ran for it, but as I drew near I saw that it was empty and deserted. "No matter," thought I. "I can take shel- ter in one of the sheds." _ _

As I was standing in one of them watching the downpour I heard a light footstep, and peering through the gathering twilight I saw a plump, yet alert, figure that I thought I recognised. She was walking away from me, yet I knew her. It was Miss Healy. And she carried in one hand a heavy black bag. I waited till she was out of sight, and then I proceeded to investigate. And in one of the sheds I found, screened by a large tarpaulin, a yellow motor-car! The rain detained me no longer after that. I went straight to the bank, and as I stood dripping on the door-step I heard a voice in the hall—the voice of one of the men I lad overheard planning the robbery. Acting on the impulse of the moment, I stepped into the hall and found, as I half expected, that the voice was that of Mr. Arthur Locke.

So I said nothing to Mr. Averil of my dis- covery, but made some excuse for calling at that late hour, and went to the police-station. Miss Healy, it transpired, had taken rooms in a cottage near the deserted farmhouse. Aided by the actual burglar, who was an old friend of hers, she had hidden the motor-car in the forsaken buildings, and was engaged in sending the gold with which it was laden to London in small quantities. She and her companion were captured, and most of the money was recovered. Arthur Locke loudly expressed his satisfaction at this conclusion—somewhat too loudly, for echoes of what he said reached the prisoners' ears, and they promptly denounced him as their accom- plice, though in reality they had fooled him and left him in the lurch. Locke did not make any protestation of in- nocence. He laid hands on a few hundred pounds that happened to be in the till, and bolted. _ _ .

It was not long before I discovered that Lettice's engagement had been her father's doing; and anyone could see that, although it had been a shock to her to discover that she had promised to mrry a scoundrel, yet she was relieved and glad that the engagement was broken. - -

I stayed at Astonbury as long as I could, but at last I had to go. I had scarcely seen Lettice since the finding of the yellow motor-car, for I had an instinc- tive feeling that she would want to be left alone for a time • and yet I shrank from the idea of going back to my lonely London lodg- ings without something of hope to gild my dreams of days to come. Fortune favoured me in one respect when I paid my farewell visit to the Averils. The banker was too busy to do more than shake hands with me. He did not offer to accom- pany me into the garden at the back of the bank premises where his daughter was sitting under a glory of clustering roses. "Please don't rise ! " I called out as I hup- ried up to her. "You make such a pretty picture—the roses and you together—thc,i I can't bear the idea of disturbing you." _ _ _ _ _ _

She blushed and looked confiised for 6. mo. ment, but laughed as she gave me her hand. " I'm afraid that is a compliment," she said, with mock gravity. "Please forgive me this time," said I. " I will this time, but please don't do it again." "You shouldn't tempt me so, then," I said, with an aggrieved air, seating myself beside her on the rustic seat.

" Again—already " she . cried, holding up an accusing forefinger. " I will be more careful, really," I said; mad then for awhile neither of us cared to speak. "I must go back to London to-morrow," I said at last. " So soon? " she breathed, and, though she did not lift her eyes from the gauzy stuff be- tween her fingers, I Auld see that her breath came faster. _

" Yes ; my holiday has come to an end." "What a good thing it is you happened to come here! " she cried. "If you had not been here the yellow motor-car might never have been found, and—and—l shudder to think of what might have happened then." I knew she was thinking of Locke and her engagement to him, and I had nothing to say in answer. "You were a year studying in South Ken- sington, weren't you? " I asked. "Oh, more than -that."
" Is there any chance of your coming up to town next winter to go on with your work there? " She shook her head.
"After the narrow escape we have had I dare not leave my father exposed to the wiles of some other Miss Healy," said she ; and for my life I could not tell whether she was in earnest or not. _
"But you must leave your father some day," I urged. Again she shook her head, but I could not make her look up. I had to bend low to see into her face.

"You must leave him some day," I re- peated, "and I want you to come and live with me in London. Do you know that I longed to tell you how I love you that night at the ball? I meant it all then—l mean it all now. Dearest Lettiee, will you marry me?" I offered her my hand as I spoke, and she put hers into it. As my fingers closed over hers she looked up at me as though she would read my very soul, and then, without r: word, I took her in my arms., . • . •
I (lid not take Lettlce to London, after all. I bought a small practice that fell vacant in Astonbury, and settled down. And in the second year of my residence there we were married,
[THE END.]

div.head: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS.
div.p: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS.
Foreign Dictation in the Matter of Fasnion.
GIRLS' TRIUMPH OVER CONVENTION.

THE MILITANT LEADER. Mrs. Pankhurst, who is due to surrender herself at Holloway en April 23b, to undergo the remainder of her Bente 0 comes of a family long oast ciated with the spirit of rebdlion, and her grandfather nearly lost his life at Peterloo, in the agitation in Lancashire in 1819. Her fathf r was a well-to-do Manchester calico printer named Goulden, who sent her to Paris to com- plete her edccAtion. There her great school companion ai a d :tighter of Henri lloChefo:t, that well-known firebrand in French politics, and as a girl Mrs. Pankhurst rein ned from Frat C 3 with strongly developed Republican tastes. Her husband, whom she married in 1879, was a barrister. She was left a widow in 1898 with three daughters and a sou to bring up on a small income. Sbe obtained an appointment as registrar of births and deaths in a Mat caester disttict, but had to resign on account of objectioa being tak n to her political activities. Since she founded the Wottea's Social and Political Union, which first brought her into public prominence, she has been seotenced to five terms of imprisonmeot, the first, for Eix weeks, being the only one she served throughout.

CHANGING WOMEN. It has been prophesied that at the end of the century all the Western nations of Europe ciii talk, eat and dress alike. It may be so but present indications do not point tbs.!, way. Germany is particularly active in pro- teAs agi inst foreign innovations and importations. She has raised strong cbjections to the popular use of "kitchen French ". in the menus of the lending hotels and restaurants. That was merely an agitation against words and plusses, but there is now a fresh campaign spinst foreign dictation in the matter of women's fashions,tind it Is asked mhy Germany cannot dress her daughters as she pleases. /Another prediction is to the effect that as the natural tendency for human beings is to dress in accordance with their occupations, so women with more freedom and fuller lives, will tend m ire and more to the masculine style of dress. Women, however, will Dever become purely utilitarian in this matter. They may desire the freedom of n a:culine dress, but they will never lose sight of the charm that clings essentially to the feminipe. Their more vigorous mode of life may be expressed in changing fashions,but no at le that is without, womanly grace will ever find favour with any appreciable number of the gentle sex. WOMEN AND THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION.

Although shut out from the law, women rre steadily making headway in medicine and the sciences, and it is noteworthy that for the first time since its foundation a section of the meeting of the Briti h Association which will be held this year at B rrningham is to be presided over by a lady—Miss Ethel Sargent, who has been chosen to fill the presidential chair in the sessions devoted to botany. She has done valuable research work in connection with vegetable life and well deserves the honour accorded be r. Mrs Sargent was OLO Of the first half dozen ladies to be adnart•ed to Fellowship of the Lennean Society in 1895 when that learned body opened its doors to women. •Another lady Mrs. Howard, has received the only Kaiser-o-Hind medal of India awarded this year, this being for her valuable aFsistance in the Government department of Botany. THE; YOUNG GIRL'S TRIUMPH. This is not only the children's century, tut that of the young girl also. Men and women of middle age pronounce the position of the young girl to-Cay one of the most remarkable of the changes wrought in late years by Fatter Time. Ste has waited for centuries to accomplish her deliverance from the thraldom of con- vention, but has now come into her kingdom, although twenty years ago such a change would hsve been con- sidered impossible. During the last decade even the young married woman carried all before her, and unmarried daughters had not much chance of sharing her good time until they themselves became matrons. The office of chaperon to-day is a mere aim cure, the young girl shops by herself, journeys and pays week end visits accompanied only by a maid, and instead of returning as formerly to the shelter of her chaperons wing when a dance ended, may be seen at public bars chatting and mixing freely with her young friends and partners. Hostesses give boy and girl dinners and arrange dancsa solely for their entertainment. The girl of to-day compares most favourably with her demure prototype of the last century. She has a full sense of the responsibilities that devolve upon her in her changed position, and may be trusted to take good care of herself and to rate her privileges at their true value without abusing them.
THE NINON SLEEVE ON THE AFTERNOON

FROCK. Pith afternoon dresses of simplo kind slew, of ninon are used with a kimono bodice. They are let in a little below the shoulder and reach to the wrist. For frocks of five serge or cloth this sleeve gives a note of lightness as it is cool ard comfortable it will doubt- ss be used on net or lace with linen or cotton dresses later on. The cottons of this season are so fascinating and charming that to no small extent they will take the place of richer materials for this summer's mart afternoon frocks. Navy serge and black charmeuse are two materials that cannot be banished from the realm •of fashion and a new note in connection with both has been struck this year by the introduction of Oriental and Bulgarian embroideries The barbaric blending of the most vivid and brilliant hues in these trimmings prove particularly suitable when used in either of those materials.ln some instances the collar, cuffs, and waist- coat are of these embroideries and they are not very expensive as quite a small length suffices to trim a dress A sash in the same colour, or in the leading tores gives relief to a black or envy blue frock. SLEEVES FOR EVENING DRESSES. Sleeves on many of this season's evening dresses have no right to the appellation for they consist of a mere band of embroidery, jetted tulle or jewelled trimming veiled with some diaphanous fabric lace as also employed en this connection. 'I he fashion is a pretty one for young girls who possess well-shaped rounded t rms and :atit.-like sit in.Sorne evening corseiges have a fichu-like arrangement of drapery over the ' shoulder which does duty for a sleeve and this is especially becoming to slender figuree. The vogue for traniparint fabrics shows no sign of waning, on the contrary the majority of ball and reception dresses for young girls are of net, lace, or ninon over shimmering satin as a rule, of contrasting colour. Flounces of old lace may be more advantageously used as trimmings for these charming dresses and share these are not forth- coming the really beautiful and almost perfect imita- tions may take their place since so cleverly are the old designs copied that even coneoisseurs are sometimes deceived. CLOSER FITTING COATS.

_ The blouse of extremely thin materials is alai med by the prophets as another indication of a change in coats which are to cling mush more closely to the figure than they have done of late years. Already some models are cut to fall away from the shoulders to give this effect. The one-piece frock has renewed its youth this season and, as even more popular than last year. It is of a simplicity bordering on extreme severity and both skill and experience are required on the modelling to the figure of the closely clinging bodices when made of transparencies as they usually are. Until the weather permits of cottons being warm, Shantung of a chic variety is a favourite miterial for those simple frocks, and when contrasted with black is particularly striking and effective.
DEATH OF "LITTLE DORRIT."

Mrs. Mary Ann Cooper, of Southgate, the original of Dickens's" Little Dorritt," died on Wednesday in her 100th , ear. She and Dickens were boy and girl together when they lived in the same street in Somers Town, London, N.W. "At first," Mrs. Cooper used to relate "Charles called me his little girl, but afterwards he called me Little Dorrit because be did not like the name of Mary Ann." When the novelist came to write his story of the Marshalssa, the little friend and play- mate of his youth was utilised as the heroine, although, of course, the adventures of the child of the Marshalsea had no foundation in fact as regards the original of Little Dorrit. Airs. Cooper used to recall the frequent visits of Dickens to her father's farm at Sunbury, and she retained at her Sinthgate home the bedstead on which he used to sleep. On one Of his visits she said Dickens, for a jlke, dressed himself in corduroys and applied to her father for work. The request was refused, but the applicant was offered a bed of straw in the barn for the night.

div.head: RED CROSS SOCIETY.
div.p: RED CROSS SOCIETY.
PREPARING FOR WAR OR INVASION.

Although the in ternational peace movement is steadily gaining ground, few would deny the wisdom of being prepared for all eventualities, and with that object in view the British Red Cross Society was formed. A meeting of the Daresbury Division of the Cheshire Branch was held on Wednesday evening in the Parish Room, Latchford. The Rev. G. C. Briggs presided over a large attendance and, in addition to speeches being made as to the utility of the society, a demonstration of practical work was given by a women's voluntary aid detachment, Cheshire 22. The Chairman was supported by Major Appleton, Captain Waring, Mrs. F. A. Frost, Miss Sylvia Broadbent, Nurse Callender and Miss Sparshott (matron of the Royal Infirmary Manchester), who gave an interesting address on the work of the society. In his opening remarks, the CHAIWIAN referred to the appropriateness of holding a meeting of the Red Cross Society on St. George's Day. The lestival of St. George ought to be calling Englishmen to a truer anti nobler sense of nationalism and patriotism. One of the things most needed to-day was the building up again of true nationalists. By that, he did not mean toe blatant aggressive insolence of a nation conscious merely of brutal strength for the cheap, pitiful jingoism of the street. He meant the ideal of true kcightliness typified by St. George, each conscious of strength, disciptined and patient, arid which was ready to sacrifice much in order to serve. To those who in olden days placed themselves under bt. George's patronage, and especi- ally to those in the various orders of knighthood, called Guilds, which bore St. George's name, a noble ideal of life and service was 51w53s present. That ideal should be ours to-day, and would that we could restore it. True nationalism implied honour and courage, service and self-sacriflce, and we all had a measure of responsibility for the spirit of true nationalism. Amongst others, the British Red Cross Society helped to remind us of our duties in this respect. What was the Society ? Much misconception prevailed ; some people thought it was a society which was run in opposition to St. John Ambulance Brigade. Nothing could be further from the truth, for its aims , and objects were different from the Ambulance Brigade. Those who gave their time and thought to the work of the society had no motive but that of true nationalism and patriutism.After reading the objects of the society, the Chairman said that whatever their opinions might be on such a subject as National Service, there could be no two opinions on the subject of the Red Cross Society. They must all admit that war was always possible and that invasion was always a possibility. 'The British Red Cross Society asked them, in the event of war and invasion, to be ready. English people hated being prepared; they preferred to mudule througb.They always had ruuddlea through, why bother? in these days that was a policy which we could not, aflord to tolerate. A conflict of the future if we were not prepared
May leave our England a sinking land Some third-rate isle half lost among her seas."

That, concluded the speaker, is a contingency which we must at. all costs avoid. (Applause). Miss SPA RsHoTT prefaced an interesting address with the remark that the more prepared we were for war the less likely it was that people would attack lie. Cotinuing, she said the Red Cross Society was chosen in War time because it was the only society recognised all over the civilised world which could offer gifts ond distribute them amongst the sick and wounded. The society was most perfect in Austria, Germany and Japan, England being the furthest behind of all. On the battlefield there was no fighting in the direction of the Red Cross if g,where willing nurses were attend- ing to the sick and wounded soldiers. It behoved women to join this society, whose aims and objects were so noble. The county was divided into twenty- three divisions. Miss spa' shott then gave a description of the methods which would be adopted in Manchester in time of war. She had on her list in Manchester 128 nurses and a list of doctors and places whica would be commandeered for hospitals. The men would be in charge of the stretchers and the women would do the nursing work. flaying described what the nurses would do in time of war, she continued to urge that they should have places in'their naidst,instancing Latch- ford,whieti they could use as hospitals. The room they were assembled in that night was a suitable one for the purpose. A record could be kept from where they could borrow articles,for they wanted to do things as cheaply as possible. (Hear, hear). They wanted beds, couches, &c. There were plenty of opportunities for men to show their patriotism but here was a chance for women to show their patriotism by joining the Red Cross Society and she asked the women to join the detach- ment—either the comfort section or the voluntary aid detachment, in conclusion she appealed to the men and worueu of Latchford to show their patriotism by working actively for the Society. (Applause.) On the proposition of Major Appleton a hearty vote of thanks was accorded Miss Sparshott who, Major Appleton said, was the matron of one or the most efficient and finest infirmaries in the world. (Hear,hear.) It was an honour to Latchford to have her come amongst them and give such an able address. He seconaed her appeal to the men of Latchford to do their utmost for the Society. They knew what an able body of the St. John's Ambulance Brigade they had,but the two societies did not over-lap and he hoped that before long they would have a men's Red Cross Society. Dr. 11. Bower had written regretting his inability to be present and the Major read tne letter. Miss Sylvia Broadbent seconded and commented upon the good work the doctor had done for the society in giving lectures &c. From the address by Miss Spar- ebott they had gathered a great deal of information which would be most helpful to them in the future. The cause was a patriotic one and deserved their greatest efforts and etipport. That day was the wedding day anuiversary Rev. G. C. and Mrs. Briggs to whom they extended their best wishes that they would have many years of happiness and continued helpful influence in the parish. It was also the golden wedding day of Mr. and Mrs. Banning to whom they were pleased to accord their heartiest congratulations. Mr. Banning had been a most active and useful member of the St. John Ambulance Brigade for many years. (Hear, hear.) 'lhe following were the townships in the divisiou with their I respective leaders :—Latchford, Mrs. G. Dakin ; Grappenhall Miss Ethel Appleton ; Stockton Heath, Mrs. Gordon Roberts; Stratton and Appleton. Mrs. Bower; and Daresbury and Moore, Mrs. E. Davies. Shc also thanked the Latchford Company of the C.L.B. for the services they had rendered. Miss Sparshott briefly replied and skilful demon- strations in first aid treatmsnt were given by the follow- ing vadets of the Voluntaly Aid Detachment :—Mrs. Clarke, Miss Ellison, Miss D. Evans, Mi-s Fairclough, Miss J. Fairolough, Miss Horrabin, Miss Hutton, Miss , Stone, Miss Ronald and Mrs. Turner, with Miss M. Broadbent (commandant) Nurse Callender (lady superintendent) and Mrs. F. A. Frost (quartermaster). ' Nurse Calender thanked the members of the detach- ment for the trouble they had taken at all the classes and the interest they manifested at all times. Mr. F. A. Frost proposed a hearty vots of thanks to the detachment for their excellent demonstrations and for the trouble they were taking in preparing to succour the sick and wounded in case of an invasion or war. The women were engaged in a noble and patriotic work and deserved the hearty support of all. At first people were inclined to scoff at the idea but it was not all "Tommy nonsense" but a serious matter. (Hear, hear.) Nurse Callender was also deserving of their warmest thanks.

Captain Gordon Roberts seconded and said, as a Territorial,that it was gratifying to know that they had such an excellent detachment of qualified nurses so new their headquarters. The Chairman said that Major Green, who was in charge of the depot should have spoken but ho had been detained. Apologies for non-attendance had also been received from Captain Beeman, Major Crosfield, and Mr. B. S. Townroe.

Mrs. F. A. Frost replied on behalf of the detachment. They were proud to think they were ready to resist an enemy, but they had yet a great deal to accomplish. They hoped many more detachments would be formed and that they would be prepared for all emergencies. (Aeplause).

div.head: ACID STOMACHS ARE DANGEROUS.
div.p: ACID STOMACHS ARE DANGEROUS.
COMMON SENSE ADVICE BY A DISTINGUISHED SPECIALIST.

" Acid " stomachs are dangerous because acid irritates and inflames the delicate lining of the stomach thus hindering and preventing the proper action of the stomach, and leading to nine-tenths of the cases of stomach trouble from which people suffer. Medicines and medicinal treatments are useless in such cases, for they leave the source of the trouble, the acid in the stoniarh, as dangerous as ever. The acid must be neutralised, and its formation prevented, and the best thing for this purpose is half a teaspoonful of bisurated magnesia, a simple antacid, taken in a little warm or cold water after eating, which not only neutralises the acid, but also prevents the fermenta- tion f:otn which acidity is developed. Foods which ordinarily cause greatest distress can he eaten with impunity if the meal is followed with a little bisurated magnesia, which can be obtained by any chemist, and should always be kept handy.

div.head: DR. MANSON AND A TRUE CHRISTIAN SCIENCE.
div.p: DR. MANSON AND A TRUE CHRISTIAN SCIENCE.

Sir,—ln your report of Dr. Manson's lecture, before the Bewsey Adult school, he is quoted as saying, that "a true Christian Science could be evolved by giving the full force of religious authority to the practice of the truths garnered by modern science." In the first place, it must be evident to every think- ing person, that there can only he one Christian Science, and that it must necessarily be true, to be science.

Dr. Manson, like many others, has now arrived st the point where he can see far enough to recognise such a thing as the Science of Christ to be a possibil- ity. He still seems anxious, however, not to recognise that very Christian Science which has been demon- strated and proved to be a science for the last fifty yew s, in the healing of thousands of cases of sin and disease, but he is even anxious to invent, or see invented, a new form of Christian Science, which would be nothing more nor less than a mixture of spiritual law and material so-called science. ./ And, by the by, it would be interesting to know what truths modern science has garnered ? To-day modern science is busy rushing to and fro, from inanimate chugs to hypnotism and suagestion, and back again to inanimate drugs, with indifferent results. Its efforts to explain material conditions are just about as futile as ever. and Dr. Manson's address itself, is an admission that this so-called science is in no way meeting the needs of mankind. The mainstay of modern science has been the atomic theory, but this has now ceased to exist, and the devotees of this science are at present wandering in a maze of specula- tion, trying to explain what is the foundation or basis of matter. _ _

According to the latest theories, matter is supposed to be a vacuum or knot in the ether, and the ether itself is only a theory, so that according to present day t-cience, which Dr. Manson says, is making wonderful discoveries of truth, matter, which is the foundation of all these discoveries, is a vacuum or knot in a theory, and this is just about as far as this science has arrived after centuries of experimentation. Moses was, as Dr. Manson says, in a good many ways, a sanitarian, but Jesus Christ was a better sanitarian, for He healed all manner of disease, and His methods excel those of Moses, because they were more spiritual. The attempt to ir ix matter and spirit, of which we hear so much to-day, is one which the Saviour exposed once arm for all, when he declared that "it is the Spirit that quickeneth, the flesh profiteth nothing." Christian Scientists thoroughly agree with, and use all wholesome sanitary methods, and the man who becomes a Christian Scientist, will naturally become a cleaner man, but they recognize that the salvation of mankind from sin and disease, must be accomplished wholly through spiritual means, and that any attempt to mix the Science of Spirit or Christian Science,with material means, must inevitably end in failure, for" that which is born of the Spirit, is Spirit, and that which is born of the flesh, is flesh." If Dr. Manson wants a true Christian Science, he can find it in the Christian Science text-book, "Science and Health," with the Key to the Scriptures, by Mary Baker Eddy, and he will have the satisfaction of knowing that this Science has been proved to ha a Science, and in fact, if he understands it, he can prove it for himself.

As everyone knows, it was not Christianity but the lack of Christianity and fanaticism and ignorance, which caused the friehtful conditions of the 14th century of which Dr. Manson speaks. Christian Science is to-day bringing men out of awful conditions of sin and disease, and of plagues of every kind, and is leading them to bright and clean lives through spiritual means alone, that is, through teaching them what man really is, and what his relation to God is, and there is no other by which man can be saved either physically or mentally. If Dr. Manson really desires to help humanity to overcome the sins and diseases of the carnal mind, he must find a remedy outside of that carnal mind which claims to cause these effects, and that remedy, if Jesus Christ's teaching is worth a button,is wholly spiritual. "The Law of the Spirit of life in Christ makes free from the law of sin and death," and nothing else can. —Yours faithfully,
JOHN W. DOORLY. :;1, Corporation-street, Manchester.

div.head: PLUNGING ON TARIFF " REFORM."
div.p: PLUNGING ON TARIFF " REFORM."
Lord W6lmer's Version and President Wilson's Declaration of American Intentions.

Sir,—After reading in Saturday's issue of your contemporary the report of the Women's Tariff Reform annual meeting, extending over two columns which contained nothing about either Tariffs or Reform, it was refreshing to turn to something definite in a speech at Sankey by a local M.P. Lord Wolmer speaking of the proposed alteration of the American Tariff says" If the Bill is carried a duty of 30 per cent. will be imposed. The Conservative Party of this country proposed a duty of 10 per cent. The reason that a 10 per cent. was imposed was that the system, must be made gradually. In striking contrast with these words are those of President Woodrow Wilson, who says : "We have to deal with our economic system as it is and as it may be modified, not as it might he if we had a clean sheet of paper to write upon, and step by step we shall make it what it shoald be." In the first place Lord Wolmer is incorrect, and conveys a wrong impression when be say that "a tariff of 30 per cent. will be imposed." What may be the average of the new American Tariff it is difficult to tell. No-one can arrive at a figure without weighing the separate factors by quantities. But an indication of the tendency of the fariff can be gathered from the following : All Food Products (except a few minor articles) are put on the Free List. The following Manufactured Articles also appear on the Free List :—Boots and shoes, harness, agricul- tural implements, leather, printing paper, typewriters, sewing machines, sheet rail, fence wire, nails, and hoop and band iron. Amongst the raw products free are :—Wool, wood pulp, tanning materials, soda, borax and lumber products. The reductions are very considerable as the follow- ing examples show : Cotton cloth, from 42 74 to 26.69. Cotton underwear, from 60 27 to 25. Women's dress goods, from 99.70 to 35. Woollen Yarns, from 79.31 to 20 Woollen goods, from 79 56 to 35. One Schedule carries a general provision decreas- ing the duty on manufactured articles, not specifically provided, 15 per cent. to 20 per cent. and that on unspecified manufactured articles remaining at 10 per cent. It will therefore be seen how mis leading is Lord Wolmer's description. But the principal point is the contrast shown by the above quotations. The intention of the American president "is step by step to make the Tariff what it should be." The above figures show that the first step is a very big one, and like the further steps in prospect, it is downwards. On the other hand, Lord Wolluer's words convey the opposite movement. He says :—" The reason that a 10 per cent. was pro- posed was that the system must be made gradually." In other words the American Tariff is being reformed downwards, while, according to Lord Wollner, the proposed British Tariff is gradually to be reformed upwards, and 10 per cent. is "the beginning—"the first step. I suppose the 2s. on corn when it arrives will also be "the beginning," the first step in the bread tax. But I would counsel local Tariff Reformers not to be nervous about the American Tariff, it may never become law. I would recall the fact that President Cleveland disappointed the Democrats of his day in regard to a substantial downward revision. President 'Taft also came in on a promise to revise downwards ; the result was on the whole upwards. The Canadian Premier Laurier, returned by the Liberals to revise the Tariff downwards, also proved too weak for the task. In all these cases the poner of the manufac- turers and agriculturists to hold their monoplv proved ' too strong for the spirit of reform springing 'from the people. Who knows but that the American Trust i will not prove too strong for President Woodrow Wilson?
I would—if it be not considered an impertinence—

counsel the local Tariff " Reformers" to buck up, not to meet trouble half way, to have confidence that the era of Protection, dear food, and dear everything, is not yet ended in America. Let them never lose heart until the Bill signed by a Free Trade President is on the Statute book.—Yours &c. CHARLES E. PARKER. Penketb, April 21st, 1913.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

The Hippodrome fully maintains its reputation for providing most acceptable variety entertainments. This week, patrons are highly satisfied with a pro- gramme of more than average attractiveness and large houses have assembled twice nightly. There is really a touch of novelty, not usually found, in the ' clever trick and comedy cycling turn provided by the Newhouse and Ward Trio. We refer to the " scratch race "at which even the Sphinx might laugh. Granted it is absurd, ludicrous to the extreme, but we laugh at and enjoy smart absurdities nowadays, and this trio of entertainers and inirth merchants ate deserv- of congratulation for introducing something unor- thodox in a cycling act. The Gascoignes are past masters of the art of entertaining and in their comedy juggling turn brought the house down on Monday evening. Minnie Paget is more successful in song than as the concertina Queen." Although the audience were delighted with her imitations of the bag pipes and a church organ on the concertina, their more vociferous applause was reserved for her rendition of her latest success "Denis Darlin." Victor and Louis " The golfer and the caddy," indulge in a great deal of cross talking and gag splitting which keeps the audience rolling with humour. There is a notable absence of " chestnuts ' and the turn is a very bright one. Florrie Elliston scores a decided success with her vocal items, for she possesses a splendid voice, which she uses to distinct advantage. The Fimans are as successful as ever, as laughter pro- vokers in the original comedy scena "The Fire Station." They introduce with success, singing, dancing and dialogue. A pleasing turn is provided by the Three Owens, who appear in " Dollies deforming themselves." The two ladies dance remarkably well and act the part of dolls very cleverly, whilst the male member of the trio keeps the ball of humour rolling. Jack Sheridan (son of Mark) is a popular " turn" at ;Varrington. He has an abundance of clever stories and witty gags. Kathleen O'Hanlon and Earl Rivkin appear as musicians, vocalists and dancers, and are well received. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

An attractive programme will be submitted next week, for it includes Ernest Edelsteins Co. in new and original morality sketch " Evexybody " ; Robb Wilton, the confidential comedian; Smarts Bros. acrobatic eccentrics; Norton and Doon, in a comedy act, "The Wrong Wright " ; Katie, entertainer assisted by Miss Dorothy Hughes, at the piano; Harry Halsey, laugh manufacturer in " Curtains " ; and The Aza trio, vocalists and dancers.

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
" A Butterfly on the Wheel."

Large audiences at the Royal Court Theatre this week have attested the interest taken in the first pro- duction in Warrington of that much talked of play "A butterfly on the wheel" and the judgments passed, both on the drama and the method of its presentation, have been uniformly favourable. We have no hesita- tion in pronouncing" A Butterfly on the wheel " one of the finest attractions ever offered at the Court Theatre. The fact that it is the collaborated work of two members of Parliament —Mr. Edward G. Ileminerde, K.C. and Mr. Francis Neilson—is suffi- cient to claim special attention, but merit is the supreme test and in this respect the play satisfies the most exacting standards It is a play with a purpose, but that purpose is not ridden to death and the audience is not—as is so often the case when play- wrights set before themselves a definite mission— being incess mtly preached at. The dialogue is remarkably clever, and the dramatic situations are worked up in 'a powerful way evidencing that sure command of stagecraft which does not always accom- pany the abilily to write brilliant and biting things. The play shows how harshly our Divorce Court system may be made to operate in the case of a perfectly innocent person. The web of suspicion and inference is so closely drawn around the victim that escape is difficult, even at the price of that ruthless cross-examination which, to a sensitive person, must be a terrible ordeal. Incidentally, the advocates of woman suffrage will find points in the play to support their protest against man-made laws. The story is simple, but it grips one from the com- mencement. There is the rising M.P. so absorbed in political ambitions that,with no idea of selfishness, he neglects his wife— a young, vivacious, impulsive creature who is trustful of everyone. She is naturally disposed to accept the attentions of an old friend,with- out appreciating the sinister side of his motives, and the voice of rumour and scandal is soon busy. her desire is simply for congenial companionship but it is easy for the husband, warned by a so-called friend, to discover the couple under compromising circum- stances. Notwithstanding his wife's protestations of innocence, he at once institutes divorce pro- ceedings and we then have the Court scene —the great feature of the play. Its remarkable realism bolds the audience as by k spell, and it is a revelation of the machinery which can be set in motion to weave a chain of damning evidence. In the end, the whole case hangs upon an anonymous letter, but the establishment of its authorship I exonerates the wife and the suit is withdrawn.

Mr. Arthur Hardy's company give a first-class performance. Miss Frances Titheradge, as Peggy, achieves a notable success in a difficult part. In the opening stages she has all the brightness and irres- ponsibility of the society butterfly, but she rises to fine dramatic heights in the Court scene, her passion- ate protests against the merciless procedure creating a powerful impression. Mr. T. A. Shannon imperson- ates Roderick Collingwood, the co-respondent, in most convincing style, his acting being marked by great earnestness without exaggeration. A parti- cularly clever study is that of Lord Ellerdine, by Mr. Douglas Greet who, as the awkward, blundering, yet true-hearted friend, is one of the popular favourites of the play. He is so thoroughly at home in the part that there is not the slightest suspicion of artificality. Mr. 0. Powis Griffiths is admirable as the Right Hon. George Admaston, M.P., Peggy's husband, and in the one incident in which be has the opportunity for dis- tinction—the denunciation cf his wife's supposed deceitfulness—he fully rises to the occasion. Mr. Herbert Greville, as Sir Robert Pyffe, XC., is the barrister to the life and his keen cross-examination is

div.head: "FROM MANGER TO GROSS."
div.p: "FROM MANGER TO GROSS."

Thanks to the enterprise of Messrs. Andrews' Pictures Ltd., Warrington people have this week had the opportunity of seeing that remarkable and much- discussed film "From manger to Cross," which has been presented twice daily at the Parr Hall. The scenes in the life of the Saviour were actually re-enacted in the Holy Land and every care was taken to ensure not only historical accuracy but impressive and devotional treatment. The result is seen in pictures (.1 remarkable beauty which make the incidents of the Gospel narrative really live before the eyes of the audience.
Tb-e final performances will be given to-day at 2.30 and 7.30.

div.head: GORGEOUS TULIP.
div.p: A GORGEOUS TULIP.

One of the most interesting flowers in our garden Just now is Tulips fosteriaua, a beautiful species from Bokhara that deserves to be grown wherever Tulips are appreciated. The immense goblet-shaped flowers are rich scarlet, glowing as a furnace, with a rich yellow centre, in which are delicately poised slate blue anthers, We have given it a warm corner in deep, loamy soil, and there it seems quite happy. The largest flower measures 6ins. from the bare to the tips of the petals, the largest of which is 2ins. wide. The foliage is large and pale, almost glaucous, green in colour, and the flower-stems attain a height of about eighteen inches.— " The Garden."

div.head: AUSTRALIAN CAPITAL CITY.
div.p: THE AUSTRALIAN CAPITAL CITY.

There was great enthusiasm in Australia lasi month when the foundation-stone of a column to mark the commencement of Canberra capital city was laid by the wife of the Governor-General. As regards the meaning of the name Canberra, an Australian gentleman who has made a study of native names has written to the Minister for Home Affairs an interesting suggestion. "Places were named by the natives," he says," from the prevalence of particular trees, plants, or animals, stones or coloured earth, or from the contour of hills or creeks. lam disposed to think that Canberra is a• form of Caberra, meaning head.' In which case itt, would probably be a name of a hill in the neighbour- hood of the new capital." It is interesting to note that Professor E. E. Morris, in his " Austral English," gives the spelling as" cobbra." Variations are kabura or kabbera, with such modifications as kobra, kobbera, kappara, and kopul, from the Malay kapala, meaning head.
I.
The Examiner, Saturday, April 26, 1913.

div.head: On Local and General Topics.
div.p: On Local and General Topics.
GOOD LUCK TO WARRINGTON!

The Warrington Football Club again enter the final struggle for the Northern Union Cup to-day and the best wishes of all will be with the team as they go forth against their great antagonists, Huddersfield, called by some competent critics the finest com- bination that ever played together. Our representatives go full of confidence and if they do not bring the Cup home we shall know that they, at all events, deserve all the honours that are going. Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., and Mr. Crosfield regret their inability to attend the final; but the Mayor will be present and Warrington will send a goodly company of supporters to Leeds in the full expectation of seeing a crowning and famous victory. Rylands Recreation have shown the Manchester League authorities that War- rington men play for the top place always; and the Athletic Club have taken such a prominent place in this year's running that the Northern Counties A.A. have allocated the ten miles championship to their ground, and an enterprising programme is being arranged for next month.

WALKING DAY AND THE KING'S VISIT. The question raised by a correspondent as to the convenience that would flow from an arrangement whereby this year's , Walking Day could be made to be the Friday preceding the Monday on which their Majesties visit Warrington is of vital import- ance. As a matter of fact, Friday July 4th is Walking Day, being the Friday nearest the first of July. But a doubt having sprung up as to the advisability of having a recep- tion of Royalty at the end of a holiday, ' which usually exhausts the resources of many, there is a suggestion in influential quarters to the effect that Friday, June 27th should be Walking Day. The fixing ,of this festival is, of course, a matter that rests with the Sunday school authorities who would do well to get to work upon a 'scheme that would cast all doubt aside. The question is, Would it be better to, have Walking Day well over so that we could come to the enjoyment of the Royal visit fresh, or would it be more convenient to continue the holidays and the visit and so make one break? As it at present stands the latter arrangement, asked for by our oorrespondent, holds the field. that is Walk- ing Day,Friday, July 4; King's Visit Monday July 7. For our part, we think that time honoured custom weighs heavily on the side of keeping the two events together.

div.head: WORTHY SON OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: A WORTHY SON OF WARRINGTON.

Mr. George Edgar, whose article published in last week's " Examiner " was read with pleasure and not a little pride by all loyal Warringtonians, was born herein 1877, and his earliest associations were with the town as a boy and youth. He served successively the "Liverpool Post" (in Warrington), the "Sandbach Guardian," and the "Runcorn Examiner." He was afterwards with the "Blackpool Gazette" for two periods, between which he went first to Wigan for the "Liverpool Courier" a paper he afterwards represented in Warrington. From Blackpool he went to the "Dewsbury Distiict News," and left that town for London, where he has been ever since. Mostly he has been a free-lance, contributing widely to a variety of daily newspaper,weekly and monthly publications. He now writes fiction exclusively for the enterprises of Messrs. E. Hulton. His best- known books are "Martin Harvey," published by Grant Richards; "The Blue Bird's Eye," published by Mills and Boin, and "Swift Nick," a new novel, out this summer, from the same publishing house.' He has edited "Modern Business," for the Caxton Publishing Co. and produced "Careers," a work on employments, for George Newnes Ltd. He has just completed a new story, "The Red Colonel," to be pub- lished in the autumn and now running serially in "Ideas," while a successful serial "The Rose Girl," ended in " Answers" two weeks ago.

div.head: PRICES AND PROSPERITY.
div.p: PRICES AND PROSPERITY.

"High prices and plenty mean prosper- ity; lo Kr prices and scarcity mean misery."— Adam Smith. " It's no use to tell me that eggs are a penny a dozen in the Highlands. That does not prove that eggs are cheap. That only shows that pence are scarce."—Dr. Samuel Johnson.

div.head: BOOKS THAT HAVE MADE HISTORY.
div.p: BOOKS THAT HAVE MADE HISTORY.

In many instances it is quite as correct to say !hat books have made history, as it is to say that history has made books. Very often such books are the indirect outcome of some social evil which they denounce. If the state of society is bad or corrupt, if any class groans under in- jnstice, soontr or later there is bound to be a protest. One of the most feasible ways of find- ing expression for a grievance, of endeavouring to right a wrong, is to publish a book, and in proportion as the writer's message is a popular or a just one, so will he have an effect on thi opinions of his fellows and the policy of the nation, so will his book have helped to make history. TIIE POWER OF RE:LIGIOUS BOOKS.

Of course, on the face of it, it will be at once apparent that the books which have had the most profound influence on the world's history have been those of a religious significance. The Bible cannot be considered as a book in the or- dinary acceptance of the term, but a whole series of volumes could be written of its effect on the history of mankind: how its acceptance has altered the destiny of nations, and how the adoption of one version rather than another has plunged countries into bloody and internecine warfare. The Koran, too—the Moslem's Bible-- seems to have made history in the most mar- vellous fashion by inspiring its Mahommedan readers with a burning zeal and an all-conquer- ing martial spirit, which enabled them to blazon the name of Mahomet on the annals of two continents.

Even apart from the Scriptures, books of a religious character or tendency, and more espe. cially those of a controversial character— which at times of religious unrest like that of the Reformation are espoused by one party and execrated by the others—have a most decided effect on the coarse of events.

div.head: LLOYD GEORGE STORY.
div.p: A LLOYD GEORGE STORY.

Professor Currie Martin added another to the stock of Lloyd George stories in a lecture at the Adult School last week. When lecturing recently in London on the Book of Revelation he had referred to the mystery of the Beast who was described under the Symbol 666. After describing the attempts of expositors to identify the Beast with the Pope, Napoleon, Boulanger and others, he added, jocularly, "And I should'nt wonder if someone made out the Awful Beast to be Mr. Lloyd George." At the close a man with a grave and earnest look tracked down the lecturer and announced with marked emphasis, "No. 666 is Lloyd George. Our Vicar has proved it."

div.head: CARDINAL 7gEWMAN'S STORY. _
div.p: CARDINAL 7gEWMAN'S STORY. _

In the "Memories of the Hon. Stephen Coleridge" just published by John Lane a good story is quoted from Cardinal Newman. The Cardinal when dining with Judge Coleridge told him of a certain High Church Anglican who travelled in Italy and when he got to Rome attended service at the earliest moment in one of the Churches. This advanced churchman followed the service as diligently and conscientiously as he could, participating in the ceremonial to the utmost, standing when the priest stood and kneeling when the priest knelt. He had taken a front place and at the conclusion he 'noted on looking round that he was the only man in the congregation. All the rest were woman. Then he made a discovery. It was a service for the " Churching of women." The zealous, famous and dignified English- man had been " churched."

div.head: " IFS " AND "Burrs."
div.p: " IFS " AND "Burrs."

We present the following extract from the "Brewers and Wine Merchant" for April. It is taken from an editorial article entitled 'Tariff Reform," which opens with the state- ment that "it is quite possible that foreign hops and barley will be taxed." We quite appreciate the fact that brewers must have foreign hops and barley, and they would probably have to pay the tax to a certain extent, but it must not be overlooked that beer is the national drink of the working population, and if Tariff Reform brings about more employment, which it should do, the working classes would have more money to spend, and trade must , necessarily be improved; therefore we think, on the whole, that Tariff Reform would benefit the trade. ; Comment is almost needless. The extract I recalls the surprise of the Tariff Reform League's Tripper to Germany, who recorded, as a sign of the superior prosperity of the German workman, that "we watched a brick-layer's labourer go up a ladder three times with bricks, and each time became down again with a hod full of empty lager beer bottles!"

div.head: SHEFFIELD • AND TARIFF REFORM.
div.p: SHEFFIELD • AND TARIFF REFORM.
Nett to Birmingham, the city of Sheffield among provincial cities is the one most closely associated with active Protectionist propaganda. Yet we read in the local Pro- tectionist journal:

"Sir John E Bingnam, Bart., presiding at the annual meeting of the Sheffield Branch of tke Tariff Reform League, held at the Cutlers' Hall, yesterday, regarded the smallness of the attend- no%ce as a proof that the boom in trade had aff.cted the enthusiasm of Tariff Reformers, but when hard times returned they would regret that they had not supported the movement. Yet he felt sure that despite the comparat:vely small interest shown, the League was advancing, and notwithstanding statements to the contrary, they were cnnvincing a large ntmaher of the working classes."—"Sheffield Daily Telegraph." This same prosperous baronet, head of one of the most progressive firms in Sheffield, declared in the same speech that: " In her cities and villages, and in London itself, England is decadent." If that is the way Tariff Reform is taught in Sheffield, we do not wonder at the small attendance at the meeting. Even the treasurer of the branch, we observe, " thought there was room for more generous support on the part of those whom its propaganda benefited." How can they expect support from a decadent people like Sheffield manufacturers, who are too busy even to attend a meeting of the Tariff Reform League?. The "Sheffield Daily Independent" of the same date says that, including the chairman, there were six people present at the meeting.

div.head: MORNING PRAYER
div.p: MORNING PRAYER
From every rural cot a wreath of smoke; Sunbeams soft on wood and mere and lawn; From mavis, merle and lark sweet canticles; Clear and calm the air, this vernal morn.
Vouchsafe, Most High, this day our steps to guide. Grant us raiment, bread and all things meet. Infuse our hearts with truth, with zeal, with love. Confirm us, Father, in Thy service sweet. J. C.

.Nt. Isidore's. During the Moorish wars most bf the other missals had been destroyed, but after the Moors were expelled from Spain, Alfonso VI. ordered the Roman missal to be used. The people of Toledo preferred their own ancient version as revised by St. Isidore, and refused to comply. Both parties being equally deter- mined, it was at length agreed that the matter should be decided by single combat The cham- pion of Toledo felled at one blow the champion of the Roman missal. But Alfonso was not yet satisfied, he ordered both books to be thrown into the fire. Again the elect of Toledo triumphed, and the T'oledan missal survived the ordeal. At length the king gave way and the missal of St. Isidore was pronounced orthodox, and was allowed to be used in Toledo. Strange to say, the copies of this missal became very scarce. It seemed as if, when none opposed the reading of the missal, no one care to use it. Cardinal Xime-nes found it so difficult to obtain a copy that he had a large impression printed himself.

div.head: SOCIAL BOMBSHELLS.
div.p: SOCIAL BOMBSHELLS.

On the part which the writings of Voltaire, Pou*ssean, the Encyclopmdists generally plated in the formation of the iconoclastic type of public opinion which found its culmination and its expression in the French Revolution, space does not permit us to enlarge. Whole Libraries have been written on the subject, and still it is not exhausted. But it cannot but be admitted that the writers we have mentioned sowed the seed, or—to change the metaphor— kindled the flame which only flickered out in he blood and ashes of the Revolution. At no )ther period of history is the connection be- :ween precept and practice, between the book and the event, so clear; at no other time can ve find so easily books that have made history. No less than 14 of Voltaire's works were con- lemned—six being publicly burnt. But their ,nfluenct- remained, as also did that of such woks as Rousseau's "Du Contrat Social," which lirectly or indirectly affected the destinies of 'France and of the whole civilised world.

div.head: FREE TRADE FINANCE TRIUMPH.
div.p: FREE TRADE FINANCE TRIUMPH.

Mr. LLOYD GEORGE has confounded the Opposition by proving, in his Budget speech this week, that Free Trade Finance has not by any means, run its full course. It there was one thing the Tories hoped for more fondly than that the country would accept the quack remedy for a disease that never existed, by applying Tariff " Reform" tdour supposed declining trade, it was that , the public might be deluded into the idea that the country:was exhausted as a revenue- producing machine. Free Trade finance, they said, had run itself dry and MR. LLOYD GEORGE'S failure was taken for granted. Then came the quack nostrum to the fore again. Let us have Tariff "Reform," and the public needs of the Exchequer would be met. True, the attempt was never made to prove how the thing was to be done, but allow- ances have to be made for the des- perate ;plight of the Party that dared to champion such a heresy. It is not easy to see how the growing burden of the State could be better met by admini- stering a shock to its trade, the like of which would be unprecedented, but it was argued, with becoming gravity, that taxes, could be levied under a system of Tariff " Reform " that would meet our needs. That tax down trade and supply a stunting operation to our industries and—from some- where—would come the revenue that Free Trade could not produce. The question of solvency or bankruptcy, political or commercial, is one of these matters which time unerringly'proves and time has brought triumph, complete and uncontrovertible, as the reward of the labours of the CHANCELLOR OF' TrtE EXCHEQUER.

Our expenditure is going up and up, thanks to the demands of the legislation of the present Government for the amelioration of the lot of the people, and thanks also to the less satisfactory cause, the increasing cost of armaments. But the country is so prosperous and the taxes arranged by the CHANCELLOR have been so productive that no new impositions have been found necessary this year. In other words, Free Trade finance not only shows how the money may be raised but has set about raising it in a manner that will not do the foolish trick that Tariff Reformers would do, the foolishness of killing the goose that lays the the golden egg. We want £195,640,000, an appalling sum viewed in the light of the requirements of other years, not so far behind, and we are going to raise it without any apparent effort, because good as trade is it is to be better next year. "Judged by any test," said Mr. LLOYD GEORGE when he was speaking of last year's trade which was handicapped by the great strike, a bad harvest, and the shadow of the European War, "the volume of trade, profits, employment and business was thoroughly sound and healthy. Our over- seas trade was at its highest and our home trade never reached such dimensions." That "most prosperous year that British trade has ever known," is, says the confident CHANCELLOR, to be followed by "the most glowing year yet seen in the trade of this country" Besides meeting all current require- ments, the present Government will have reduced the National Debt by '£102,000,000 since their brilliant term of office began. In the light of all these established facts there appearsito be but little chance for the success of Protectionist fables.
