Mr. and Mrs Panning, of Bridge Mont, Gvappen- hall-road, celebrated their golden wedding on Wednes. day and received numerous congratulatory message.- Mr. Banning has been a most active member of go St. John Ambulance brigade for a number of years, and prior to a recogni.ed branch being framed in Warrington, he was a member of the Warrington Ambulance Society. Laet year be received the service medal for 15 years' service with the brigade.

div.head: Sequel to a Collision.
div.p: Sequel to a Collision.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Stanger, Messrs. G. and J. Weaver, cabinet makers, &c.. Bridge-street, claimed ;C:,17 13s. 33. from the Road Transport Co., London, in respect of loss and damage sustained by them as a result of a collision at Rixton on November let between a motor waggon belonging to defendants and one of plaintiff's furniture vane.—His Honour awarded plaintiffs £l7 13. and costs.—Mr. W. B. Forehaw appeared for the plaintiffs, but the defendants did not appear.

The Property Market. Messrs. Thomas Sutton Sz Sons offered for sale I.y auction at the Blue Bell Inn on Wednesday, five lots, consisting of freehold and leasehold properties in Warrington, Poulton and Great Sankey. There was a good attendance hut, as the bidding 3 were not satis- factory the whole of the lots were withdrawn. We understand that lots 1 and 2, consisting respectively of the dwelling-house, 23. Mill-lane, and the three dwelling-houses, 156, 158 and NO, Forster-street, will probably he disposed of by privets treaty. Mr. J. Longland was the solicitor to the vendors. Messrs. J. Atkinson & Sons' New Premises.

Messrs. J. Atkinson & Sons, drapers, who have for many years carried on business at 7, 11,13, Bridge Street, open their handsome new premises at 128, Bridge Street, to-day. A new stock of general drapery good.. blouses, &c., has been purchased, and customers have the usual wide range of gocds to choose from. The new frontage looks exceedingly smart, and the interior of the shop, which will he lighted by electricity, has been newly painted and decorated in an artistic manner. The fittings are all new and up-to-date, and, the establishment is fully in keeping with the firm's high reputation. Inspection is cordially invited. Old English Bazaar. The Wesleyans of the Warrington Circuit are hold- ing an Old English Bazaar in the Parr Hal! next week in aid of Norris-street building scheme. It will be opened on Tuesday at 2-30 by Mrs. Parker and will continue until Friday evening. The school-chapel, which is to be erected at the corner of Norris-street and O'Leary-street, will he designed to cope with the need, of the rapidly growing population in the Orford district. The site contains about 2,000 square yards, so that it will allow of ample development for the purposes of Church. s'thonls, lecture rooms, etc. It is hoped to raise at least £l,OOO by the bazaar. An admirable series of side-shows and special Attractions have been arranged, including concerts by the various church choirs in the circuit, tableaux vivants, pierrot and marionette entertainments, performing dog, etc. Mr. T. J. Down's orchestra and military band will play selections each evening. Warrington Photographic Society.

The first of a long series of summer outings was taken on Saturday, the weather favouring on the whole. Six members travelled to Preston Brook by the 1.15 train, and tbence walked and snap-shotted through the village" o'-th'-flill, Dutton and Pickering Bridge to Crowton. The Workhou.e. gates at Dutton were happily chosen as the scene of the official group, some evidently trying to obtain admission. At Pickering Bridge the party was ferried across, as the Swing Bridge has for some time been closed. Tea was served at the Hare and Hounds, Crowton, and the party left Acton Bridge Station for home at 7.30 p.m. The walk was made still more interesting by the sight of distant heavy rain storms which seemed to specially favour the photographers by circling round them about a mile distant.

Health of the Borough, The Medical Officer cf Health (Dr. J. Coote Hibbert) in his report on the health of the borough for the week ending April 19th. states that the births totalled 50 (24 males and 26 females), as compared with 38 (14 males and 24 females) in the corresponding week of 1912. The deaths numbered 29 (18 males and 11 females) as against 22 (11 males and 11 females). The death rate was 20.3, as against 17.9 the average for the previous six weeks, and 15.8 for the corresponding week last year. The birth rate was 35.1, as against 31.0, the average for the previous six weeks, and 27.3 for the corresponding week last year. The deaths included :-1 from enteric, 1 from enteritis, 2 from plithisis, 1 from other tubercular diseases, 2 from cancer, 3 from bronchitis, 2 from pneumonia, 1 from alcoholism, 3 premature births, 1 from heart disease, 3 from accidents, 0 front all other causes. The following cases of infectious diseases have been reported : Scarlet fever, 1 ; tuberculosis 8; cerebro spinal fever, 1. The number of patients in hospital was 43, The mean temperature was 45 degrees and therefore 3 degrees higher than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 54 degrees was reeorded on the 14th and 15th inst and ths minimum tempera- ture, 34 degrees, on the 13th inst. The rainfall measured '72 inch.

div.head: GOOD BAKING POWDER.
div.p: A GOOD BAKING POWDER.

Another noteworthy success has been a chieved by Borwick's Baking Powder, the prize in the " A " section of the recent " Evening News" Cake Competition having been awarded to a lady who used one of Borwick's well-known recipes, the winning cake being made with Borwick's Baking Powder. To give some idea of the extent of this competition, it may be men- tioned that no fewer than 260 cakes were sent in, com- prising fully three dozen'different varieties. Housewives can, with every confidence, rely upon this excellent preparation for making the lightest and most digestible cakesmuddings and pastry,and any ladies who anticipate entering for similar competitions to that above- mentioned, should not fail to use Borwick's Baking Powder, as this will do much in helping them to attain success.
The bx arniaer. saturday, April 26, 1913.

div.head: SHAKESPEAREAN REVIVAL IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: SHAKESPEAREAN REVIVAL IN WARRINGTON.

On Saturday night the Warrington Shakespearean Commemoration Company played " Macbeth " before a large and fashionable audience at the Royal Court Theatre, and brought their short but brilliant run to a successful conclusion.

Nothing appeared to have been omitted that could lend lustre to the general effect. The credit for the complete success of the production is mainly due to the mag- nanimous and untiring efforts put forth by Mr. Charles Law in preparing and perfecting the members of the company through rehearsals extending over several months, besides undertaking the superintendence of all the arrangements relating to the productions.
BRILLIANT CONCLUSION TO A SUCCESSFUL • COMMEMORATION WEEK.
Daintith, had been unable to take part in the perform- ance or in that night's proceedings. (Bear, hear-) Mr. LAW concluded by proposing " the Memory of Immortal Bard of Avon, William Shakespeare.'"

div.head: COMMEMORATION DINNER.
div.p: COMMEMORATION DINNER.
Mr. Law and the Elevatng Effect of Shakespeare.
CONGRATULATIONS AND PRESENTATIONS.

The members of the Shakespearean Commemoration Company, who last week presented "The Merchant of Venice" and " Macbeth" so successfully at the Royal Court Theatre, under the leadership of Mr. Charles D. Law assembled at dinner at the King's Cafe, Bridge-street, on Monday evening, under the genial chairmanship of the President, Mr. Oswald Lofthouse. The proceedings were lightened by con- tributions of various kinds by several of the talented ladies and gentlemen of the company, and a pleasing feature of the evening's enjoyment was the presenta- tion to Mr. Law, followed by other similar recognitions of valuable services rendered, recognitions that had been reserved so as to partake of the nature of a surprise.

div.head: SILVER SALVER FOR MR. LAW.
div.p: SILVER SALVER FOR MR. LAW.

The CitAmmix having propostd the health of the King, which was most enthusiastically drunk,expressed the heartiest thanks of the Committee to all the members of the company from Mr. Law down to the humblest member, for the excelleut service they had rendered to this year's commemoration. He felt convinced that in expressing the appreciation of the committee he was also expressing the opinion of the community upon the performances they had given, for after having heard them discussed in many quarters he could say that he had heard nothing but eulogy of their really artistic work. This applied not only to the principals but to the "crowd." (Laughter and applause.) They had, of course, seen the criticism in the newspaper—(laughter)--but his advice was that whatever was favourable in a newspaper might he accepted as "Gospel truth," but that whatever was unfavourable was the result of error arising from the fact that the writer was labouring under the impres- sion that he could have acted the part very much better. (Laughter.) Women, they knew' were now ,coming forward to occupy positions men bad hitherto occupied—with lamentable results. (Laughter.) They had shown them how to act at the theatre—(applause) —and he had pleasure in calling upon Miss Gladys Adams to show them how a presentation ought to be made. (Applause.) Miss GLADYS ADAMS said, amid cheers, how happy she was in having the privilege of making a presenta- io Mr. Law. This was the third occasion upon which they had had a happy little gathering after a very successful show—and she thought that each time the happiness of the occasion grew. (Applause.) Their gratitude to Mr. Law also grew with time for the splendid work he did in the way of coaching and training them. (Applause.) She had the greatest pleasure in asking him to accept a little token of their Increasing gratitude. Miss Adams then handed to Mr. Law. a splendid silver salver inscribed Presented to Dr. C. D. Law by the members of the Warrington Shakespearean Co., Merchant of Venice, Macbeth, April 1649, 1913. HOW SHAKESPEARE PAYS.

Mr. LAW, when the strains of "For he's a jolly good fellow" had died down, said that last week he was in many trying situations—notably when Mr. Harold Smith was feeling for his dagger—(laughter)—but he was always hopeful of extricating himself, and those situations were not to be compared with the one in which at that moment he found himself. He had not even a spring dagger to assist him—(laughter)—but only words with which to express his deep gratitude far the really magnificent presentation which Miss Adams, acting for the company, had made to him. He felt the credit of their productions, which he honestly thought had been very successful, was really due to them and not to Lim. They had sacrificed their time and given up their amusements in order to attend rehearsals and he felt they were treating him in a, manner absolutely beyond his deserts. He was, how- ever, none the less appreciative; he would look back upon the last three seasons with nothing but pleasant memories. He thought by acting and reading the works of the greatest man from a literary point of view who ever lived, they were doing good in their humble way not only for themselves but for their acquaintances and their country. (Hear, hear.) It used to be said, but he thought the fable was dying out, that Shakespeare spelt ruin. lt might not spell a great success from a financial point of view, but it did something far better than the gaining of money and the improving of a banking account. It had nothing but a good and elevating effect upon those who played it, and those who witnessed it,a good which was derived from the know- ledge of nature and human feeliug.He hoped they would able to play Shakespeare together at least for another year. (Applause.) He had no doubt that they would score another success. They could not, however, succeed without the assistance which had been given so liberally and effectively by those who did not enjoy tbe glare of the footlights. The committee had been of inestimable service headed by their worthy chairman, Mr. Lofthouse. Mr. James Henry Smethurst had as usual been a tower of strength; Mr. Edwin Bradshavv's financial knowledge had been a tremendous help; Mr. Henry Collin, as treasurer, could not have been bettered; and Mr. Eric Fair- clough had been most encouraging in everything he had done. Mr. Walter Ashton and Mr. Hodgson had been worthy representatives of the players on the committee. Mr. Lewis Rowson combined the duties of prompter with those of general factotum—(laughter)-- along with those of a most excellent committee man. Mr_liarvey 0. Adams,the possessor of enormous enthu- siasm and strength to carry it into effect, had made a splendid secretary to whom no labour had been too great and if the commemoration went on he hoped Mr. Harvey Adams would continue to be associated with it. (Applause). Mr. A. C. Hodgson had done a great and useful service in summoning people to rehearsals. He thanked all the ladies and gentlemen who had formed the committee. REPUTATIONS MAINTAINED AND IMPROVED.'

It gave him great happiness when he induced Mrs. Garnett to come back to play with them; her return to the fold had been one of the reasons why they had been so successful. (Applause). Mrs. Garnett had certainly eclipsed her great success of 1911, she had 'acted better than ever before and they were all immensely proud of her. (Cheers.) With regard to Miss G 1 idys Adams what astonished him was that two years ago she was a child—a crimson child - (laughter)—who came out of a cauldron and had developed, in that short space of time, into an actress of great charm and ability. So :rapidly indeed had been the development of her talent that she astonished the Duke of Venice and he evidently could not believe his eyes, but mistook her for a young Jew. " (Loud laughter.) This year Miss Adams had played the part associated with the names of the greatest English actresses ; and he could say, without adulation, that, though she had not eclipsed Miss Ellen Terry, she certainly trod just on the edge of her train. (Cheers). It was certainly a great feat and that Society were very proud of having brought such a Portia forward. (Hear, hear.) They were exceedingly sorry that three zealous members of the Company, the Misses Truslove and Mr. Leonard
PREMIER CYCLES. Excelsior Cycles, Lea Francis Cycles, Di 10/-to .£l6 16/-.---Sole Agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 35, 13ridge st., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: WONDERFUL SECRETARY.
div.p: A WONDERFUL SECRETARY.

The CHAIRMAN spoke of the wonderful work Mr. Harvey 0. Adams had done as secretary, and called upon Mrs. Garnett (who was accorded musical orders) to make a presentation to him. Mrs. GABNETT said it had given her the greatest pleasure to come back" —(cheers)—and she was grateful to Mr. Law for the opportunity and the help he gave her to enable her to play Lady Macbeth. She had great pleasure in asking Mr. Adams to accept a silver ink sta.lid from her colleagues, "Those Christians with varnished faces." (Laughter.) He might have been severe upon them and even bullied them in the wings— (laughter)—but they forgave him. (Laughter). Mr. BARVEY 0. ADAMS, who was warmly cheered, thanked them for the present, which he would always treasure, and for the courtesy and assistance which he had received frcm everyone connected with the com- mittee. As assistant stage-manager he apologised to all for the things said during last week. (Loud laughter).

div.head: COMPANVS WHIP.
div.p: THE COMPANVS WHIP.

The CHAIIIM iN next called upon their excellent Nerissa to present Mr. Hodgson with a silver cigarette case for sending them the post cards they received so regularly. This duty was charmingly performed by Mrs. Garton Stone and Mr. Hodgson, who was loudly applauded, acknowledged the gift. Mr. Lofthouse vacated the chair at this point and Mr. J. H. SMETHURST, who took his place, expressed his 'regret that Mr. Harold Smith was not present. (Hear, hear.) They had been delighted to see him leave the burly burly of the House of Commons to come to Warrington to play the part he did in their performance. (Applause). Mr. HENRY COLLINS (treasurer) intimated that ,:,200 would not pay the accounts but a balance sheet would be published as soon as the figures were complete. Mr. LAW proposed the health of Mr. Rowson (prompter) and Mr. Edwin Bradshaw; and in respond- ing, Mr. Rowson mentioned their indebtedness to the theatre staff—Mr. Warburton, Mr. Boothroyd, Mr. Slater, not forgetting their little call boy. (Hear, hear). Mr. SMETHURST proposed "The Press" and Mr. T. WESTON responded. During the evening Miss Gladys Adams sang " Martha ; " Mr. Leslie Longford recited " East and West" (Kipling) ; Miss Royston recited "How be saved St. Michael's " ; Mr. Hodgson sang "Young Tom of Devon ; " Mr. 11. M. Ashton recited "The Optimist " ; and Mr. H. G. Marston gave a humorous reading. "Auld Lang Syne " wound up a most enjoyable evening.

div.head: MR. CHAS. LAW'S INTERPRETATION OF SHYLOCK,
div.p: MR. CHAS. LAW'S INTERPRETATION OF SHYLOCK,
DR. MELLOWS UNQUALIFIED PRAISE.
170 TIIE EDITOR OF THE " EXAMINER.".I

Sir,—l have read, with interest, the criticism, in your to-day's issue, by my friend, Mr. Alfred Perris, of the performance of " The Merchant of Venice" in connection with the Warrington Shakespeare commem- oration, and I cannot feel myself quite in agreement with some of the things said by Mr. Perris, especially in regard to Mr. Law's acting in the part of Shylock. Let me say first that, on the whole, the acting of Mr. Law struck me as being on a decidedly high level, very seldom attained by amateurs. Further, Mr. Law's conception of the character of Shylock, if I grasped it rightly, appealed to me, in general, as eminently sincere to the play and faithful to Shakespeare, and as showing, also, that Mr. Law had made a great, and successful endeavour to think the part out thoroughly and to reach its deep inner significance. Hardly any other of Shakespeare's creations can compare with Shylock in intricacy and difficulty, a fact sufficiently proved by the variety of interpretations the part has received from different actors at different times. It seems likely that Shakes- peare borrowed the plot of "The Merchant of Venice " from Italian sources, some story in which the Jew, Shylock,was drawn after the conventional model, as an object, a proper object, of hatred and contempt, mean, low, avaricious, cringing and servile. Shakespeare's genius played on this stock character to such an extent that, in the poet's mind,the cringing, mercenary Jew becomes cot an object for contempt, beside whom the upright Antonio stands admired, but an object for pity, a wholly tragic creature, whose long- ing for revenge seems largely justified and is foiled simply by a forensic trick. Shakespeare began with the conventional notion of the Jew as a despicable outcast, fitted only for the lending of money to profli- gate Christians, to be spat upon and passed by in scorn ; he ends on the tragic thought of the desperately human representative of an heroic but evilly entreated race. In Shakespeare's day, even less than in our own, there was little sympathy for the Jew, little respect and little mercy : there was plenty of contempt and hatred, prejudice and persecution. Shakespeare realized that, after all, even a Jew is also a man, capable of love and hate, of tears and curses, of kisses and revenge, like any other man. So his genius masters his subject, the play becomes a tragedy, and the poet demands our sympathy for Shylock. As one of Shakespeare's best critics truly says: "The Jew of the story," that is, of the story whence the poet took his plot, "is the monster of the mediaeval imagination, and the story almost requires such a monster, if it is to go with ringing effect on the stage. Shylock is a man, and a man more sinned against than sinning." And just in this lies the intricacy and difficulty of the part. Mr. Perris says that Mr. Law's acting gave him a sense of "incongruity in the Jew's proceedings." The incongruity is actually in the play, and Shakespeare knew it. The actor who displays it is faithful to the author. Shylock has" two soul sides, one to face the world with, one to show a woman when he loves her." The genius of Shakespeare recognised this fact, and, in the play, both soul sides have to appear, and the clash between the two, in the circumstances of the play, makes the tragedy. Mr. Perris talks about " Eastern dignity." Shylock is a man positively torn by eternal conflict, and, moreover, the representative of a race nearly broken by conflict. Shylock's passion is real, fierce, human indignation, clothed not in" Eastern" colour, but in the dignity of pure human nature, biting savagely at its chains! A Christian spits upon him, and then borrows money; a Christian robs him of his daughter and thinks it laudable. Of course, Shylock is infuri- ated ; of course, he raves and storms; he has the pride of his race, and he loves his daughter, yes, even more than he does his ducat, a point which Mr. Law's acting decidedly emphasised. Mr. Law's frantic grief did not seem to me much exaggerated, whilst his rapid changes from grief to the open desire for revenge were eminently real and human. Mr. Perris suggests that Mr. Law's exit did not evoke , sympathy; I simply cannot agree. He departed as one broken, but still a man, though a Jew, and in the fine way in which Mr Law drew himself up to his full height, and scanned the court and the crowd, before leaving, followed immediately by the sense of wretchedness and a broken life, was peculiarly impressive. There was dignity there, not " Eastern " but human, and there was tragedy also, tragedy so acute that Gratiano's jibes seemed impertinent, and Portia's eloquence a clever ruse. The question Shakespeare asked was : What has Heaven or God to say to all this? And I, personally, found that question in my mind as I watched Mr. Law leave the stage. Considering,then, the intricacy of the part, I should myself bestow on Mr. Law's acting almost unqualified praise, and I should like to thank him for giving such a challenging and faithful present- ment. I shall remember his acting for a long time to COEIO.—YOII To &c•
STANLEY A. MELLOR. April 10th, 1913. [Further correspondence on this question appears in Letters to the Editor.]

div.head: JAunb AULDIUn.
div.p: JAunb AULDIUn.

Whilst the Committee of the Warrington Football Club have been very much occupied in cup ties, and incidentally, the pla:ters have been mystif3ing the pessimists and electrifying their enthusiastic suppor,ers, they have also been alive to the tact that the back division of the team will need strengthening for next season. With that ohject in view, they have been successful in securing the services of James Ruddick, the clever little half-back who has played for Coventry during the season.

Ruddick first played for Egremont, Cumberland, afterwards for two seasons he was with Hunslet, and we understand that they have been most anxious to have him back. The Warrington' Committee have beaten them for possession. He is reputed to be a very clever half—either " scrum" or "stand-off "—is very speedy and a great tackler. He knows bow to make openings for his hacks and also the shortest way to the line. He is young and ought to be of much service to the team. We wish him luck.
With Nicholas, Daintith and Ruddick, the half-back pcsition should now be strong.

div.head: BOY'S ESCAPADE.
div.p: A BOY'S ESCAPADE.
DAMAGE IN CHURCH AND SCHOOL.

A seven year old boy named Thomas Oakes, 35, Crossley-street, was summoned at the Warrington Juvenile Court on Thursday, before Mr. J. Upson and other magistrates, for having committed wilful damage to the extent of 255. 61 to a window and atlas, the property of the Warrington Education Committee, at St. Marv's school. Buttermarket, on April 16th. The Chief C•bostable said that the defendant, along with a boy named Cairns, aged six years, went to the school and climbed a drain pipe over six feet high, smashed the window with a lid from a drain and entered the schools. They attempted to set fire to two large maps which were very badly charred, and after- wards went into the Roman Catholic Clauroh and set fire to sacred things. Having regard to a conversation with the headmaster of the school and Father Primavesi it was thonght highly desirable that the boy should be sent to an industrial school. The Edncationl authorities had found a suitable school. Mr. Houghton, the caretaker at the schools, said the boys had opened the piano and pulled things out of the rostrum. lie found matches near a door which the boys apparently could not open as the bolt was tight. To get out they climbed on top of the teacher's rostrum. • and went through the window. In the chapel they had tried to burn open an offertory box by applying a' light to the bottom. Fatherr Primavesi said the box was charred consider- ably An old clogger's knife was left. in the baptistry. A charwoman heard a noise awl saw the lads attempt to set fire to the altar cloth. They ran away on seeing the woman. Mr. R. B. Roberts (assistant director of eduction) said they advocated sending the boy away very reluctantly,and it was ouly after conferring with school teachers and clergy that they decided on that course. The father of the lad said the other boy had tempted his lad and was responsible for his wrong- doing. • The Chairman: It is not Cairns, but a man named Oakes (meaning the father), who is responsible. If you had done your duty by your boy he would not have been:here. The defendant said they had intended buying caps (for toy guns) and chocolates. Mr. Roberts s This young man has been in trouble by himself. The boy was sent to St. Thomas's Industrial School Preston, and the father was ,ordered to contribute 2s. per week to his maintenance. The Chairman said it would cost the State Ns. per week to look after the boy. Mr. Roberts said that within the laft seven days he had been concerned in bringing before the court no fewer than seven children uuder school age,for offences auch as breaking in, sleeping out, and theft. He suggested that the ningistrates should make an appeal to parents to take greater interest in their children and exercise greater control over them during the hours when they were out of school. There was some- thing wrong somewhere, end he thought the fault lay more with the parents than with the children. They would have fewer cases like the previous one,if parents would look after their children better. -

The Chairman (Mr. Lipson) said the Bench agreed that parental neglect had been the cause of bringing many children into court. They were convinced, from the evidence which came before them at various times,that children appeared as defendants, owing to parental neglect and not to the causes whichweere generally said to bring them there. They would not allow the parents to escape paying maintenance for the children who were sent to the sQhools.

div.head: MESSRS. F. W. WOOLWORTH'S STORES.
div.p: MESSRS. F. W. WOOLWORTH'S STORES.

A notable and, in some respects unique, addition to Warrington's retail trading enterprises is marked by the opening to-day (Saturday) of the extensive stores of Messrs. K W. Woolworth and Co., Ltd., 21, Sankey- street. This firm, which has branches all over the country and in Canada, makes "cheapness and good quality" its watchwords. Not one of the thousands of articles stocked exceeds sixpence in price and the range and variety of the goods is something to marvel at. Domestic and fancy wares, jewellery, haber dashery, cellulord goods, mirrors, pictures. and a host of special lines too numerous to mention are on sale at prices ranging from one penny to sixpence. An umbrella for the nimble sixpence is certainly a novelty, but we have it at this up-to-date establishment. There is also an admirable assortment of incandescent gas-fittings, nickle-plated trays and overmantels. Over 80 per cent. of the goods are British made. The manager of the branch is a Lancashire man and he has engaged a local staff. The arrangements of the shop are on the brightest and most convenient lines, and the well- stocked windows have been a centre of attraction during the week. Yesterday, thousands of the townspeople tock the opportunity of inspect- ing the premises which had been tastefully decorated with plants. supplied by the Parka Committee. Mr. R. H. Pep.rson's orchestra played selections and the scene, as the constant stream of visitors passed round the stores, was one of great animation.

div.head: STRIKE SPIRIT,
div.p: THE STRIKE SPIRIT,
MESSRS. WALKER'S ACTION.
Bonus and Increased Wages for 200 Employes.

We have received the following communication : The directors of Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, Warrington and Burton, Ltd., have decided to recog- nise in a practical manner the loyalty of some two hundred of their employees who remained loyal in their service during a recent attempt to stop the working of the brewery. In August 1911, iu conse- quence of the large increase in the price of food supplies, the directors raised the wages of every working man in their employ by a shilling a week. An official notice issued on Tuesday states : " These prices having further increased, the Directors have pleasure in giving notice that they will now give to the 200 employes who remained loyal in their service during the recent endeavour to stop the working of their brewery, a further rise of is. a week and a bonus of 10s. to each man and ss, to each boy and girl for the honourable and loyal way in which they supported them when 64 strikers left the brewery premises and their work unfinished, without notice. The Directors would also like to state that in spite of all state- ments to the contrary, no man in their service has been dismissed without adequate cause."

div.head: Trade Unionists Support Brewery Workers.
div.p: Trade Unionists Support Brewery Workers.

The cause of the strikers was supported at an open- air meeting held near the old mill, Biidge Foot, on. Sunday afternoon. Prior to the meeting, which attracted a large crowd, there was a procession Leaded by a brass _band.

A resolution was passed, condemning the action of Messrs. Walker in dismissing eleven men, supporting the Gasworkers' and General Labourers' Union in their right to submit a wages scheme on behalf of the workers concerned, and pledging those present to support the strikers by whatever means seemed likely to be most effective. THE DEMAND FOR RECOGNITION.

Mr. S. H. SMITIf, president of the Trades and Labour Council, under whose auspices the meeting was held, said the brewery officials had definitely stated, in the local Papers, that they refused to meet the officials of the Claim When one set of officials declined to meet another set, it was an illogical position and it was high time that the Trades Council organized demonstrations in order that their fellow-workers might obtain recognition from their employers. HISTORY OF THE DISPUTE. - - -

- - --- Mr. CHARLES DUKES, secretary of the Trade 3 and Labour Council, outlined the circumstances of the dis- pute. He stated that on March lit:. the Gasworkers and General Labourers' Union submitted a claim for increased wages on behalf of the men. The replies received from the firm were to the effect that they were capable of dealing with their men without any outside interference. beeing that the Union officials had organized the rnen and had been deputed to act in their interests, they did not relish the designation of Messrs. Walker's employes as" belonging " to the firm. The term "ours " was misapplied when speaking of a body of men, despite the fact that they obtained their livelihood by working for the company. A further letter was sent to tne firm, pressing the men's claims and asking for an interview.Follovring that communica- tion, eleven men were dismissed without explana- tion and nothing beyond a mere inference on behalf of the firm, in the terms "We will have none of your Union tricks here " was offered as a reason. The Union again communicated with the firm on behalf of the men who had been stopped, but they were told that the firm had always treated their employes with every consideration. They got nor definite answer stating clearly why tilt men had been dismissed. Further attempts to communicate with the firm resulted in failure. Tbe only alternative left to, the Union was to submit notices on behalf of the labourers.

ACCEPTING TIIE GAUNTLET. Immediately those notices were received the firm began to supplement the number of their employes, obviously with the object of demonstrating to the men inside that they woula be able to fill their places if they left on the expiration of the notices. The firm threw down the gauntlet. The men had tendered notices and were prepared honourably to abide by them, provided they had been met with like action on the part of the firm. But when the firm threw down the gauntlet the men wisely took it up and ceased work,in a fair number at any rate. Unfortunately the Union had not got. them all out,but that was not their fault. Every indoce- merit had been offered to bring the whole of the men out, and he wanted to say that the assertions made, through the Press, by representatives of the firm, were not true, neither did they reflect credit upon those responsible for their insertion. They had been told seventy men had ceased work and that the firm had been able to obtain others to take tneir places without any difficulty. (Cries of " Blacklegs" and" Scabs.") At least 130 men had left the employ of the firm and the Union would use every means in its power to win a victory for them. Messrs. Walker had always posed as ideal employers of labour. For a considerable period they had 'tilled themselves into mental intoxication by their ability to keep their employes subdued and subjected by throb, - ing out to them doles of beef and other things at Chris- was time. (Laughter.) The Union did not want the men to get so much per week and so much beef. They wanted them to obtain wages which should be the equivalent of the maintenance of decency and comfort. They held that the wages claims submitted on behalf of the men were legitimate and that they were put forward honourably and straightforwardly. They had not, however, been met in a like spirit. It was too late in the day for any firm to say to a body of men : 6' We claim the exclusive right to deal with you as we think fit, and we deny you the tight to appoint repre- sentatives to support your claims." (Applause). If Messrs. Walker persisted in their statements that they would continue their industry with the assistance of non-union labour, it was time the organised workers declared that they would stand loyally by tbelemployes to enforce their claims. When he pointed out. that the workers in question were above the average in physique and that they were compelled to work tor a miserable wage of a guinea per week, it did not redound to the credit of those people who waved the Union Jack and appealed to the people to support this glorious Empire.

"LIBERTY AND HONESTY." When the Licensing Bill was introduced, the firm sent employes to a Hyde Park demonstration, weariog badges incribed "Liberty and honesty." The men claimed the right to demonstrate their liberty in other spheres and not merely to clamour for that kind of liberty which the employers desired. Mr. DUKES concluded by predicting that if the workers remained staunch, the result of the strike would be even more 'successful than that of the carters. (Applause).

NO DESIRE FOR DISPUTES. Mr. FLEM MING ECCLES (organising secretary, Oldham) read correspondence which had passed between the firm and the Union with reference to the dispute. The brewery workers passed a resolution requesting the representatives of their union to press the claims sub- mitted, and calling upon Messrs. Walker to reinstate at once the eleven men recently discharged. As the matter was urgent the officials intimated that they proposed to wait upon the firm on a given date. The firmn replied that it would be useless for the officials to call, as they declined to see them. Even when the notices were tendered, the men intimated that in the hope of a peaceful settlement, they had arranged for a few of the men, with the representatives of their society, to attend for discussion of the points at issue. Trade unions, continued !idr. Eccles, were not formed for the purpose of creating disputes. They existed for the better defence of the workmen's interests, so that. they might stand on more equitable lines, as compared with the employers. He claimed that the men's demands were moderate and just. A trade union like theirs, having something like 500 branches and a mem- bership of over 100,000, was not going to be limited by one firm. (Applause.) They had done all they could to avoid friction and they now asked with confidence for the co-operation of all organised labourers in the battle they had to fight. (Applause.) COME TO STAY. Mr. ALBE LIT LEES (organiser to the Gasworkers' and General Labourers' Union) said much bigger firms than Messrs. Walker had recognized the right of workmen to combine. He instanced the great concern of Vicars, Son and Maxim, who employed between 15,000 and 16,000 workmen, and did not hesitate to confer with trade union officials on the wages question. Whether Messrs. Walker liked it or not, the principle of industrial organisation had come to stay. (Applause).

div.head: FREE TRADE CONSERVATIVE.
div.p: A FREE TRADE CONSERVATIVE.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. No Co-opted Members.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. No Co-opted Members.

The annual meeting of the Runcorn Bard of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday. The Clerk occupied the chair pro kin. Mr. Spruce proposed that Mr. Linaker, jun.' be appointed chairman. For the past three years he had been his (the speaker's) right hand man, and he would hold the office of chairman with every credit to himself and to the Board. Mr. Roylance seconded the proposition which was unanimously carried. Mr. Linaker, in reply, said he had been a member of the Board for the past nine years and had climbed very rapidly to the office of chairman, owing to the kindness of the Board. Mr. Spruce had been a most exemplary chairman and had conducted the work of the Board in a thoroughly business-like manner. He (the speaker) believed that the workhouse had been in existence for .55 years and it only came to his knowledge the other day that the second Chairman to be elected was the present Lord Cross who was still a guardian of the Derbyshire Board as a co-opted member. He (the chairman) would endeavour to conduct the business of the Board in the best possible manner. If he could follow the lead of their most estimable Mr. Spruce, he would satisfy himself. vICE-CHAIRMAN. Mr. Woodward said that in looking for a vice- chairman, there were several considerations which ought to be in their minds, but perhaps the most important was that the honour should be given to those who had served the district well for a number of years and whose services had never previously been recognised by the granting of an honorary position. With that outlook in view, he knew of no-one more fully entitled to the honour than Mr. John L. Jones, of Moore. He hoped that there would be a unanimous vote in appointing that gentleman to the vice-chair. Mr. G. Pilling seconded. He said that if Any man was deserving of the honour, it was Mr. Jones. Mr. Collins moved, as an amendment, the appoint- ment of Mr. Morris, who had rendered valuable service for the past ten years and bad worked most assiduously as chairman of the House Committee. (Hear, hear.) He had worked hard in every branch of pour law work in which be had been engaged. Mr. J. Horton seconded and said they would be doing the right thing in appointing Mr. Morris. Mr. B. Gibbs supported the amendment. They, in the -Urban District of Runcorn thought it was high time they had a look-in, with regard to the appointment of vice-chairman. They sent a man regularly from Runcorn and his appointment was approved by the public. On a vote being taken eleven voted for the amend- ment, and twenty for the proposition. Mr. Jones, took the vice-chair, and, in returning thanks, said he bad not sought the honour but was proud of the appointment and would do his best during his term of office. Mr. Morris said he would like to assure the Board that he would try to do as much as he had done in the past and give his loyal support to the chairman and Mr. Jones. (Applause). THE LATE MR. JOSEPH STOKES. Mr. Linaker, jun., proposed a vote of condolence with Mrs. Stokes and her family in the bereavement they had sustained by the death of Mr. Stokes, who had worked hard and well for many years as a member of -the Board until failing health prevented him attending the meetings. Even in the present year he had been elected a member of the Board, and they could only express their regret at his decease. He was a good, kind Christian man, and he never bad a harsh word for anyone. Be had been associated with the Board since 1878 and was the oldest member. Mr. Wright said he had known Mr. Stokes for 50 years as a kind-hearted man. He was a friend of all, and an enemy of none. He never knew a man with a finer character than that of Mr. Stokes. The sick and poor of Clifton and Frodsham would lose one of their best friends. Mr. Hallows spoke highly of the good work Mr. Stokes did for his fellow men in a private capacity. Mr. Woodward said the deceased was a man of broad charity and gripped the very essence of Christian teaching inasmuch as he was a lover of all men. (Hear, bear.) The vote was passed, all the members standing. NO Co-OPTED MEMBERS. Mr. Morris proposed that Mr. Thomas Baxter, sen., and Mr. J. H. Davies be co-opted members of the Board. This was seconded. . Mr. Linaker seri., said he had previously proposed the co-option of Mr. Baxter but he did not agree with the resolution now advanced. He was very jealous_ of making co-opted members. Mr. Davies had had the opportunity of contesting his seat and he had allowed another gentleman to take it.He(the speaker) objected to membersbeing co-opted simply because they did not fight for their seats.lf Mr. Davies bad been a member for 25 years he (Mr. Linaker) would perhaps have less to say on the matter. It would be a great mistake if they began to co-opt members simply because they did not put themselves into opposition to someone nominated in their place. It would be giving some townships double representation on Boards of Guardians, which ought not to be. He was sorry Mr. Morris had made

MEDICAL OFFICER'S SALARY.

Dr. T. J. Selby, medical officer at the 'Workhouse, wrote asking for an increase of salary on the ground that there was a large increase of pAtients in hospital. He thought the question of attendance at Dutton Lodge should be a separate arrangement. It was decided to refer the matter to the Finance Committee for consideration.

div.head: NEW HOME.
div.p: THE NEW HOME.

The Chiliren's Home Committee recommended that an outside fire escape staircase be erected on the girls' side of the home and that a door communicating there- with be constructed on the first floor landing ; that a canvas chute be obtained for the dormitories over the boys' day room and that it be an instruction to the superintendent that the boys be frequently practised in its use; that one dozen fire buckets be purchased and placed in convenient places througout the home ; that all the children attend the religious services at the workhouse; that choir practices be held at the home and that Miss Cunnah attend at the home for the purpose An application having been made by the Superinten- dent for an addition to the staff, it was resolved that the superintendent lay before the clerk full particulars of the duties as at. present carried out by the existing staff and of the work being done or which may be done by those children in the home who have left school. It was recommended that, as a general rule, both boys and girls be retained in the Home for training purposes for one year sfter they have left school. The minutes were confirmed. THANKS.
On the proposition of Mr. Morris a hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mrs. Darwall of Frodsham for her gift of cups 8:c. to the House.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
Annual Meeting.
The annual meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday. At the outset, Mr. Woodward proposed and Mr. Harrison seconded the re-election of Mr. Linaker as chairman.

Mr. Linaker briefly replied and hoped they would get through the business of the Council as well and as pleasantly as they had done during his first year of office. They heartily welcomed all the new members of the Council that day. (Hear, hear.) They might have little breezes in the meetings now and then, but they were like April showers and soon passed over. A vote of condolence was passed with the bereaved family of Mr. Stokes. The Chairman said Mr. Stokes had been a member of the Council since 1894 and had taken a keen interest in the work of the Guardians and Council. He was fearless in what he did and was upright in every way.
VICE-CHAIRMAN. On the proposition of Mr. Pilling seconded by the Chairman, Mr. Antwiss was re-elected vice-chairman. _ _ _ _
Mr. Aniwiss thanked the Council for the honour had.conferred upon him.
The various committees were then appointed with their respective chairmen.

div.head: PREMIER OF QUEBEC ON THE
div.p: THE PREMIER OF QUEBEC ON THE
NEEDS OF CANADA.

Sir Lomer Gouiu, Premier of Quebec, who has been spending some time in Europe end London, recently discussed with a newspaper representative the future of the province of Qnebec and its present opportunities as a field for the English settler. Sir Lomer expressed regretful surprise at the want of knowledge on the part of the average Englishman concerning the nearest part of our great Dominion, _

" Peciple do not realise," he said," that Quebec is a very near neighbour of this country, and with the present excellent travelling facilities the journey is neither long nor tedious. There are endless oppor- tunities for those who find that they cannot make a living out of the land here, and to all agricultural labourers and mechanics I declare most emphatically that they will de well to come and settle with us. I can guarantee annual, not monthly, work for all the farm labourers who come to us. They will begin with an average wage of £5 a month and living, and at the end of a couple of years they should have a thorough knowledge of the possibilities of the province, be acquainted with methods of farming, and be in a position to take up land of their own."

LECTURES ON NURSING.—In connection with the Higher Education Committee of the Cheshire County Council, Miss Hawkes,a former nurse at the Manchtster Royal Infirmary, and a well-known lecturer on Sick Nursing, commenced a series of lectures in the Girls' Schoolroom, Pepper-street, on Tuesday afternoon. The lectures which are for women only, are to be held every Tuesday afternoon, with the exception of Whit-Tuesday The subject this week was " Bandaging, sick-room diet, and the feeding of invalids. DEATH OF MR. E. BEDELL.—Lymm Congrega- tionalists will learn with deep regret of the passing away of Mr. James Edward Bedell, who died at his residence, Springfield," The Downs, Bowdon, on Tuesday. The deceased gentleman was the eldest SOD of the late Rev. James Bedell who held a successful pastorate of the Lymm Congregational Church from 1878 to 1884, when failing health compelled him to retire, though he continued his residence in L 5 mm up to the time of his death. Mr. J. E. Bedell was thus brought into prominent association with the Congre- gational Church where he became an ardent worker in the Sunday school. Though he removed to Bowdon,his interest in the Lymm Sunday school was maintained until his decease. Each Christmas he sent a supply of toys to be given to the infants on the occasion of their annual party, and his monetary assistance has I,een on a most generous scale. His death, will, there- fore bee great loss to the Lymm Church. He was a familiar figure on the Manchester Royal Exchange where he was highly respected. The interment took place at the Bowdon Church, on Thursday, when several Lymm gfntlemen went to represent the local Con gregational Churcb. A RARE VISITOR.—In Tuesday's edition of one of our contemporaries it was reported that an otter 3 feet 6 inches long had been electrocuted on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Co.'s. line at Churchtown, near Southport. This reminds one of the great interest that has been raised in Lymm zeological circles through the shooting of a dog otter in Lvnam a little over a fort- night ago. As Mr. William Gould was shooting over his father's (Mr. James Gould's) preserves along the upper reaches of the lake, he noticed on a bank about forty yards away, near the "Private Lake," a dark uncommon looking animal. Firing at it he wounded the stranger which, becoming infuriated,rushed at him, only to receive the contents of Mr. W. Gould's second barrel, which proved fatal. The animal turned out to be a large dark brown otter, about four feet long. Mr. Gould sent the dead animal to a taxidermist in Man- chester, and is, we understand, going to present it to the museum of that city. Mr. Gould informs us that he has seen five young otters and other witnesses aver to having caught sight of the female. The otter is a rare visitor to Lymm waters, though the late John Plant recorded two killed at Oughtrhigton in 1850, and reters to their former abundance on the river Bollin. Otters have also been killed at Arley, Rostherne Mere' and Dunham. It is one of the most persecuted of British mammals, and though its predatory habits supply something in the way of an excuse for the harsh treat- ment to which it is subjected, we should be sorry to hear of its extinction.

• LYMM LADS' CLUB: GYMNASTIC DISPLAY.—On Wednesday night the Drill Hall was visited by a large number of people to witness the third annual gymnastic display of the Lyrnm Lads' Club team. Memt.ers of the club's committee present were Messrs. J.G. Lister Farrar, F. (E. Evans, G. W. C. Hartley, R. 011iver, and Thompson. The programme, which consisted of eight members, was carried through in a very satisfactory manner and afforded clear evidence of the patience of the team, and of the able tuition received from the instructor, Mr. S. Hinde, an old member of the club, and winner of this year's second prize at the Warring- ton Gymnasium. At the conclusion of the marching exercises, the audience were given a clever exhibition on the horrizontal bar by six members, whilst the succeeding item, bar bells, was even better, uniformity and precision heing most marked. Some excellent work on the parallel bars was received with hearty applause, the efforts of the two junior members of the team. G. Goffin and H. Fogg, and the solos by Messrs. S. Hinds (instructor), and H. Barber (leader), being specially prominent. A series of four pyramids was also presented and a diversion caused through their being photographed by flishlight. Exercises with the clubs and on the horse were also given, and a couple of good wrestling , matches were provided by F. Hewitt, G. Knott, S. Hinde and J. Woodhead. Pianoforte accompaniments and interludes were contributed by Miss E. Callender. Another feature of the evening was the presentation of the following prizes by IVlrs. J. G. Lister-Farrar : Second year bars to F. Hewitt, James Woodhead, Geo. Woodhead ; first year badges to J. Broadey; H. Fogg, G. Coffin, I'. Kirkpatrick, G. Knott, F. Moss and A. Reid; challenge cup, given by Mr. Lecomber, and medal for the best senior gymnast, won by F. Hewitt ; medal for the beat junior gymnast, C. Coffin; a challenge cup given by Mr. J. G. Lister Farrar for the best billiard player was won by H. Barber, a second prize being secured by T, Kirkpatrick ; shooting prizes, presented to the club by Lieut. G, W. C, Hartley were won by J. Antrobus (Ist) ; and G Woodhead (2nd).—Mr. R. Oliver, in the course of a pithy speech, expressed his appreciation of the team's efforts, and of • the unstinted labours of Mr. Farrar to make the club a success. He said the committee were delighted to see so many friends present and that it was to them they looked for financial support. Lieutenant G. W. C. Hartley, in speaking about the great. improvement in the members' marksmanship, said that the recent com- petition had been very keenly contested and that he was looking forward to an increased number of com- petitors next year.

div.head: HONOUR FOR SURVEYOR.
div.p: HONOUR FOR SURVEYOR.

Mr. De Jong, proposed a vote of congratulation to Mr. Mort who he was pleased to say, had been elected a member of the Borough and County Surveyors' Institute He (the doctor), knew that that was practically the blue ribbon of such an office. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Warburton seconded. He bad always had a high opinion of Mr. Mort. He bad a lot to contend with but he did so in a thorough and appreciable manner. They were glad to see him elected to such a bigh office. Mr. Smith supported and said Mr. Mort bad done credit to himself and also to the Council. Mr. Groves : Is it a financial increase, Mr. Mort? The proposition was carried and Mr. Mort in reply, said the qualification was not as high as the doctor had made out. Many of the surveyors in the country were members--
Dr. de Jong: And proud to be members. Mr. Mort said he was very much obliged to the Council for their congratulations.

div.head: ISOLATION HOSPITAL.
div.p: ISOLATION HOSPITAL.
Improving the Equipment.

Public interest in the Local Government Board inquiry held at the Connell offices on Tuesday morning into the proposal to improve the Equipment of the isolation hospital, arousel no public interest and apart from members and officials of the Couuoil, not a solitary rateps3er put. in an appearance. Dr. J. R. Hukhinson c .nduutr-d the inquiry, which concereei the application of the Urban District Council for sanction to borrow £5OO for the provision of steam disinfector and laundry at the Isolation Hospital. There were present : Mr R H. Gotobed (vice-chairman of the Council), Mr Wu-. Mullard (clerk and collector of tbe Council), Dr De Jong (me Beal officer), Mr. D. Mort (surveyor), and 130,-. Young (medical officer for Cheshire), The Clerk stated that the need for the disinfector and laundry was pointed out by the Local Government Board. The Council, directly the Board said the additions were required, instructed the Surveyor to prepare plans and estimates, which had been before the Board for 12 months. All their inttructions had been carried out by the Council. Further questioned, he said the rateable value of the district was £24,103, the population 5,025, and the acreage 4,375. The outstanding debt under the Public Health Act was £8,941 19s. 4d. in respect mainly of sewerage, the building ef the Council offices, and the new sewerage scheme. There were no other districts involved in the present application.

The Inspectoi Whai: is the length of time you require for repayment ? The Clerk : As long as we can get; 50 years if we cm!). (Laughter). The I ospector : I suppose that no part of the work has been commenced

The Clerk replied in the negative. Dr. De Jong said that, in his opkion, the disinfector and laundry were absolutely necessary. The hospital was situated in the best p .aiticn in Lymrn. They bad disinfected as thoroughly as possible by spraying and saturation (formalin 'pray) Mr. Mort said be had prepared plans in accordance with the dio ectinns of the Local Government Board, and estimates had been approved by the Council as to the structural p rt of the huildine. The total cost of toe building was £252 and the machinery £230. There were incider,tal expenses, and the total cost of the work w.,uld he £5OO. The population within a quarter of a mile of the hospital .as 20 and within half a mile from 80 to 100. There were no barracks, publio buildings school or workhouse in the vicinity of the hospital. Dr. Young said he cool substantiate all that Dr. De Jong had said as to the necessity for the disinfector. Mr. Gotobed said the Council did not wish to spend more money than was necessary, hut it was felt that the provision of the disinfector and laundry was necessary. He believed in efficiency before economy. The Inspector: Is there plenty of room for extension ?

The Clerk replied that there was. The water supply, he said in answer to the Inspector, was the towa supply. Dr. De Jong said it was not proposed to use the hospital for smallpox cases. If smallpox broke out it would be necessary to erect woooen shelters or tents. The district in question was the least populated, and that was why the site had been chosen. This was the wile evidence.

Mr. Gotobed, in proposing a vote of thanks to Dr Hutchinson, said it was hoped the sanction asked for would be given, although the Council did not wish to spend more money than was necessary. On the face of the evidence which had been given by the Medical Officer he thought the additions to the hospital were absolutely necessary. The Clerk seconded the motion which was carried. The Inspector then visited the hospital.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.

SANKEY FOOTBALL CLUB WHIST DRIVE AND DANCE. —Last Friday the above club held a successful whist and dance in the Sankey Sunday Schools. The arrange- ments were in the hands of the football committee, with the energetic Secretary, Mr. Edwin Clarke. The catering was carried out by Mrs. Clarke in her usual satisfactory style. The Bros. Hall supplied the music for dancing. The M.C.'s for the whist drive were Messrs. F. Davies and E. Dnmbill and for dancing Messrs. T. Whitfield and H. Plumpton. Mrs. Cook very kindly presented the prizes to the winners of the whist drive, who were as follows : —Ladies: 1, J. Ainsworth: 2,1-1. tendon ; consolation. Gentlemen : 1, T. Lightfoot; 9, T. CJok, sen. ; consolation, J. Chatterton. About 150 were present.

div.head: SANKEY PARISH COUNCIL.
div.p: SANKEY PARISH COUNCIL.
Mr. W. Furness Appointed as Chairman.

The annual meeting of the Sankey Parish Council was held in the Council schoolroom on Monday evening. There were present :—Messrs. W H. Ireland (retiring chairman), Wm. I aylor, J. G. Pownall, It. Long, W. Furness, S. Fair and J. Smith clerk).

div.head: NOT A MUTUAL ADMIRATION SOCIETY.
div.p: NOT A MUTUAL ADMIRATION SOCIETY.

The declarations having been signed, Mr. Taylor pro- posed and Mr. Long seconded, that Mr, W. Furness be appointed chairman. This was carried unanimously and Mr. Furness. in reply, said he accepted the office on the understanding that it was for 12 months only. He fully appreciated the honour they h.d conferred upon him, but he endorsed the views expressed by the retiring chairman that the office of chairman ought to go round. It would give their co-workers an opportun!ty of getting into officer. They, as a council, were not overworked, nor were they a mutual admiration society. They all tried to do their best for the benefit of the ratepapers. He hoped that during the next 12 months their record would be as good as it had been in the past. (Hear, hear).

div.head: VICE-CHAIRMAN.
div.p: VICE-CHAIRMAN.
On the proposition of Mr. Ireland seconded by Mr. Long, Mr. Taylor was elected vice-chairman.

div.head: OVERSEERS.
div.p: OVERSEERS.

The following gentlemen were elected overseers : Mr. Richard William Wright (senior overseer) and Mr. W. Ireland (junior overseer). The Clerk said that the ratepayers had not had the opportunity of appreciating the "work done by the overseers, because they had had no calls on their pockets recently.

div.head: -EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: -EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
The Rev. J. R. Jones was appointed representative on the district Education Committee at Earlestown.
SANKEY SCHOOL MANAGERS.

Mr. Pownall propoced and Mr. Fair seconded that Mr. Long be appointed a representative manager of the Sankey Council schools. Mr. Ireland proposed and Mr. Fair seconded that Mr. Smith (clerk) be the other manager.
Boih propositions were heartily carried and the Clerk said that the Parilih Council were prepared to rcommend your members on the Lancashire Education Committee ahould they be requested to do so.
TAR SPRAYING OF ROADS.
The question of tar spraying the roads was raised by Mr. Pownall.

Mr. Ireland : The apparatus is already in the district but I understand some of the machinery is cut of order. Mr. Pownall : There is always some trouble over the tar-spraying. Mr. Long asked if the Council could have the use of a watering cart in the meantime? Mr. Pownall : That is a very good suggestion. It was eventually decided to leave the matter in the hands of the rural district councillor, Mr. W. Furness.

div.head: GAS RATS TOO HIGH.
div.p: GAS RATS TOO HIGH.
Mr. Long moved that a lamp be erected between Penketh-lane-end and Mr. Kelsall's farm.
Mr. Keleall_said a lamp was needed in Park-road. _

Mr. Pownall considered that the district was being charged too high a rate for gas. The Corporation Gas Department were making large profits, and instead of reducing the price of gas they were assisting in relieving their rates at the expense of outsiders. The Corporation might make a concession by giving them an extra lamp or two. It was resolved that the whole matter of lighting be brought up again in July.

div.head: MOORE.
div.p: MOORE.

WESLEYAN CHURCIL—A service of song entitled "Jessica's first prayer" was very creditably rendered by the choir on Sunday. Mr. Warburton presided, and the connective readings were given by Miss B. Dutton. The collection, which amounted to £2 4s. 7d., was in aid of the National Children's Home and Orphanage.- -On Monday evening, in the school, an entertainment was given by a party of friends from Ellesmere-street, who had generously offered tbeir services. The pro- gramme consisted of songs by Miss Scarisbrick and Mr. Taylor, and a musical sketch by the children fwhich proved to be the feature of the evening) entitled 'The Silver Penny.' Much praise is due to Mr. Lee and Mr. Wareham for the training of the childrezr, and to the children themselves for their clever and most interest- ing performance.—A vote of thanks was proposed by Mr. Lawton and seoonded by Miss Dutton to all who bad helped to make the evening a success.—The pro- ceeds are to go to the Circuit Bazaar fund.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.
HOSPITAL SUNDA.Y.—Services on behalf of the Wartington Infirmary were held in Christ Church on Sunday. The Rector was the preacher. The offertories amounted t) 93. 9d.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

WESLEY GUILD.—The gene,al meeting of the guild was held on Monday evening, presided over by the Rev. E. Morgan. The accounts were p•esented laft Mr. J. E. Richardson, and past officers thanked, and new ones elected for the coming year. PRIMROSE LEAGUE.—In connection with the above a tea followed by a concert and dance etas held in the Church Room. on Thursday evening. At en interval in the concert lin address on the objects of the League was ably delivered by Miss Pilkington. At the close of the concert a beautiful dinner service was presented by Miss Pilkington, on behalf of the members, to Mr. and Mrs. Faulkes on the occasion of their marriage. The winners in the whist drive were : Ladies : 1, Mrs. Walsh ;2, Miss Berry Gentlemen : 1, Mr. Cousins ; 2, Mr. J. Antrobus. The tea was ca'ered for,by Mrs. Fryer and the whole evening's entertainment was a marked success and thoroughly enjo3 ed. CONCERT AT THE WESLEY HALL.—On Saturday evening the last of a series of five concerts was given in the Wesley Hall, Padgate. Considering the fine talent, one might reasonably have expected a larger attendance. Two violin solos given by Miss Lockerbie were listened to with appreciation, and an encore in each case was accorded. Miss Emily Taylor's songs " A May morning" and "Love the Pedlar," were well received, and an encore for the latter was responded to. Mr. McArthur sang in his usual pleasing style "When I think of the happy days absent" and " The Trumpeter." Mr. Clayton was heard to advantage in his solos, "Nirvana " and the" Sailor's grave." Toe humorous element was ably represented by Mr. and Mrs. Wilson Holt, the latter being enthusiastically received in her recitals 6` Love in a balloon " and "Santa Claus," and in cash case the artiste received a hearty recall. Mr. Wilson Holt greatly amused the audience by his renditions of two humorous sketches, and the character study "Rather too old." For each item an eucare was demanded and responded to. Mr. Proffit, who has been mainly responsible for this series of concerts deserves great credit for his untiring energy. SCHOLAR'S CONCEttT.—Ou Thursday evening a concert was given in the Wesley Hall, by the scholars of the Sunday school and friends. 'lbis effort was made with the laudable object of raising money to clear off a debt on the Sunday scuool working expenses. The first part of the programme was miscellaneous in character. Ile song " John Peel " was given by all the children. In the musical sketch" Wno stole the rabbit" the boss were in their element, and their appearance in wigs and police.uen's uniform caused no little merriment. The girls were enthusiastically applauded for their dances, the" Scotch reel" and tLe " Irish Jig" and also for the musical sketch "Christmas Stocking." Miss A. Tomlin 's recitation was heartily applauded. Mr. W. earrar,a budding comedian, furnished the comic element in a very efficient manner, and for his song "Don't take me home " received a very emphatic re-call. The non- appearance of Mr. Bates, who was announced to give a violin sole, was much regretted, especially as it was understood that his absence was due to au injury to his band. The second part of the programme consisted of an operetta "The madcap months," and this was a very pleasing and unique feature. rhe children were in costume, and the varied effects of the groupings were most picturesque. Twelve girls representing the months, sang the songs" The twelve little months" and " Higgledy piggledy "after which they gracetully danced. After this they were joined by their mothers—the four seasons—represented by tour of the elder girls, arid together they sang the song "The weather." Then a number of little buys dressed as harvesters, appeared on the scene, and gave the action song " 6ee the harvesters at work" and the march entitled" The harvesters march." A number of little girls in fairie's c3Btuntes sweetly sang " We're Christmas fairies." Miss A. Ball (summer), gave a sweet rendering of "When the skies are blue." Miss M. Taylor (the Queen of May), attended by her maids and two little page bays also sang very sweetly " I'm Queen of the May." The dialogue interspersed between the songs and choruses was well recited by the res- pective characters. Mr. W. Bate (clerk of the weather) amused the audience with his doleful " Oh dears," and his song " 0 what's the world a' coming to" was well sung. The final, " [he season's greeting " and the song" Good-night all "sung by all the characters,gave the finishing touch to a m at successful concert. Mr. Jarman presided and thanked the workers and children on behalf of the audience for the strenuous effort which they must have made in preparing such a delight- ful entertainment. Mrs. J. Dakin (conductress) assisted by the Misses London end Wright, and all who have helped in any way, must be heartily congratulated on the success of their enterprise. Toe accompaniments to the various songs and dances were executed by several teachers and scholars.

div.head: PROGRESS AT THE COTTAGE HONES.
div.p: PROGRESS AT THE COTTAGE HONES.

At the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardian on Wednesday a gratifying report on the work of the Cottage Homes, Padgate, was read by the Clerk. Mr. Young, H.M. Inspector of Schools, reported as follows on the Cottages :—Many changes have taken place in the staff of the institution during the past year, and improvementu have been instituted which bid fair to increase the happiness and raise the level of education of the children. Signs are already evident that the school is undergoing a change, the children are gradually sho sing response to the sympathy and disinterested care that are expended upon their education both in and out of school hours. The starting of a small school library is particularly worthy of encouragement. The scheme of instruction is framed to make the lessons less mechanical in character and both teachers and scholars are profiting by this. The instruction of the elder children in the various trades is wider in scope and more experimental. The Guardians are recommended to adopt the two unused class rooms for the teaching of woodwork and cookery. -
--The--reporl--wa; referred to the Cottage Homes Committee.

div.head: STOCKTON HE ATM
div.p: STOCKTON HE ATM

STOCKTON HEATH STREETS.—At a meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council on Tuesday, it was decided, on the proposition of Mr. Mclntrye, to make application to the Local Government Board with respect to the making of Alexandra-road, Stockton Heath, under the provisions of the Private Street Works Act, 1892. CYCLISTS' SOCIAL.—St. Thomas's Men's Bible Class "B" Cycling Club, Stockton Heath, after a run to Arley held a successful social evening in the Parish Room on Saturday evening. Songs were well rendered by Messrs. F. Moon, H. Holmes, S. Spencer. Miss A. Scott gave a recitation. Mr. Stannard presented a brooch to Mrs. Cleaton for best attendance last season. Mr. Cleaton and Mr. Bridgewater acted as M.C.'s. ST. THOMAS' BAND OF HOPE.—The last of a series of entertainments in connection with the above was held in the Parish Room, on Monday evening. There was a good attendance and a very interesting pro- gramme was gone through, consisting of action and other songs, recitations, sketches, and part songs by the choir. Mr. Hallows said the season bad been a very successful one, thanks to Mr. vChiternan and a band of willing helpers. The following took an active part in the entertainment :—Mrs. Whiteman. Mrs. Altman, the Misses Hallows, Acton, Bagulev, Vernon, Douglas and Perks and Messrs. Whiteman. Baguley, Hough, Hatton, Perks, Clayton, Kolly, and Livingstone. On the motion of Mr. Stannard,seconded by Mr. C. Hallows. a very hearty vote of thanks was passed to all who had taken part.

HILL CLIFFE AND STOCKTON HEATH UNITED BAND OF HOPE.—The members of this society held their final concert of the season iu the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Monday evening, Mr. Joseph Moss presiding in the absence of the Rev. G. Curtis (president). A capital programme was given by the members and friends. The pupils of Miss Lloyd Williams's, Lorne House School contributed an historic sketch "Lady Catherine" and " rho Waxwork Show," which were much enjoyed. and the members of Penketh Band of Hope contributed a Dutch action song in character, which was deservedly encored. Songs were given by Bertha Stringer, Eva Phillips and Mr. H. Elliott. Miss Dorothy Hill con- tributed a selection on the mandoline, and Miss Evelyn Fraser a pianoforte solo. Recitations were given by Sarah Gamble, Lucy Gerrard, Edith Travis and Hilda Taylor, and the dialogue "Like Mother" by L. Sandford, E. Rustage, E. Travis, E. Williams and H. Adamson,and "The Stores" by A. Phillips and B. Clarke. The humonr of the evening was supplied by Mr.J. H. Bibby. Mr. G. Whitfield (secretary) presented a number of medals to those who had been members over three years and had attained 13 years of age. Miss Bell,Miss Kirkland, and Mr. J. A. Fairclough were the accompanists.

div.head: TWENTY-SEVEN YEARS AGO,
div.p: TWENTY-SEVEN YEARS AGO,

It is all very well for Protectionists and Fair Traders to say that they do not propose a tax on food. What they mean is that they dare not propose such a tax. It is so unpopular, as the elections of 1985 show,that thsy would be hissed out of court if they suggested it. But it is nevertheless the inevitable logical result of those principles. There is not an argument for protecting the manufacture of goods, which does not equally apply to the manufacture of bread ; and if we once go back to protecting manufactures, we shall be forced. as a matter of the simplest justice to the agriculturist, to re-impose a corn law. "—The late Lord Farrer in "Free Taade versus Fair Trade," published 1886.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD
JOURNALIST.

THE EDITOR. With eager interest, as will be readily - understood, I devoured every wore. that was written respecting the advent of Mr. T. a eston to the editorship of the "Examiner" Ind local journalism, past and present. As 0 read, ough was repeatedly reminded of certain ..utstanding events in my own career— though , sooth to say, although I also have been editor of three weekly newspapers, no „11,.s ch honour was ever done me as fell to Mr. ston's lot last week. I strongly suspect, that if he might have had his way —but one 1,1,1ay not pursue the subject. Certain I am ttat the new chief of staff is heartily glad that the preliminaries are over, and now he s at liberty to settle quietly down to his Work. LITTLE WORRIES. h Quietly," quotha Well, I trust he may re more fortunate in certain relations than -1- have ever been. I have previously had eecasion to mention in this column how I °nee declined to reveal the name of a poor pus stoker whose letter I had published iring a strike, with the result that A had to defend an action at the thssizes, and, of course, lost it—for ° average juryman seems to have lie latter grudge against the press, and le latter seldom meets with justice, to say 1111°t,!-Iing of mercy, at his hands. Moreover, e 's generally a Tory, and if the paper pro- ceeded against happen to be a Liberal organ, Much the worse for the defendants. Dur- lug one reasonable period, I was threatened °with seven actions of libel in as many weeks. vile Case was singularly like the above men- C°lled, though the letter complained of was 4,.°111 the employer's side in a trade dispute. . de secretary of the workers organisation Instructed a solicitor to demand disclosure of the Writer's name, with the alternative of an action for damages. Having accepted the responsibility of publication, I followed the I,l,mnwritten law and refused information as to e co-respondent's identity. As I had sup- Pcised, the object was simply to get at him, anYhow, I heard no more of the matter. AN UNCONSCIOUS HUMORIST.

tol:here's another kind of joker who thinks whl.ntimidate, by dark allusions to the law, 11 as I think and have found in tieirsonal experience, is consistently " agin " the newspaper. This individual once entered tillY den with a complaint that a member of the staff had taken a note of an application to e County Court Judge, although, as he I,4B.isted, it was a private matter. I ascer- teained that it had reference to a compensation pase, and told the indignant protestant that would be reported in the usual way. With Pite a violent outburst, he avowed his ,Intention of going forthwith to a neighbour- town' to set his solicitor to work. I ,elnarked that his train was well nigh due, '1.11!1 urged him not to miss it. When all is t;tld and clone this kind of person has a better onc,irle of it than the fellow who comes to the ,wee with a bribe in his hand, thinking that rneY will suppress whatever happens to be nrnin his point of view undesirable. He still 'lists, but is gradually learning better. lI"TDIVIDUAL COMMUNION CUPS. I note with greater satisfaction than sur- Drise that these are to be used at Burton- -1:°0d Church on and from Whit Sunday. One ti3clPects the Rev. A. M. Mitchell to show in hils as in all else that he has the courage of d.s Convictions. One day this very week I eussed the question with another church- who, while disposed to sympathise (17" n Mr. Mitchell,himself continues to let "I Aare not" wait upon "I would." Said he: ssuredly— the Lord will not let any harm eome to his people through the use of the obnion cup. Against this was set the Jection that it is not sound morality on the eDart of the lazy, or the indifferent, or the °wardly to expect the Almighty to do what °lle can easily do for oneself.
