div.head: CARTER, Jeweller; CARTER, Breadmaker ; and SHAW, Butcher.
div.p: CARTER, Jeweller; CARTER, Breadmaker ; and SHAW, Butcher.

The still more picturesque shop adorned by the central clock was that of Mr Carter Jeweller and Clock maker. a name which was with us until recently and which we were all sorry to lose. The other shop was that of Mr. James Cartel, baker, the founder of the. firm of Carter and Son. It would have been interest- ing had the old shop lingered to see the lordly premises of the firm upon the other side of Bridge-street. The contrast would have been delightfully typical. We are glad to be able to present the picture, "Carter jeweller, " "Carter bread baker" and "Shaw butcher" were household phrases in Warrington and it is pleasant to see the quaint premises in which these three old firms did business elbow by elbow in the leisurely days of long ago. The date of the picture, we ought to have said is 1854. As we have begun to write about Bridge- street we may extend our article to say a little about some other old buildings which adjoined. YOUNG HERCULES IN STONE. A few doors higher, two doors from Market Gate we believe, was an old brick building three storeys high, from the topmost of which on a projecting stone platform stood ' the massive stone stature of a boy holding up aloft a large stone ball. The ball was held in both hands as though the boy was about to throw it down upon the passers by, It was not an image that was calculated to inspire the passers-by with comfort, and we have not been able to discover anything about its meaning or its fate. Possibly it was some sculptor's effort to depict young Hercules or a youthful Ajax defying the lightning. But old Warrington was not famous for classical learning, and the only information that enquiring childhood obtained was that when the stone boy heard the town clock chime the curfew at eight o'clock at night he threw the stone ball at any boy or girl he saw, in the street, the inference being that every good boy or girl would at that hour be in bed. It is a pity that this watchful, though rather strenuous image was not preserved. As a centre piece for a park rockery it would have been splendid. And what a text for a parent's homily on those other different days when there werelno picture palaces or children's evening parties and when all good bairns were safe in bed before the curfew bell at eight!

PATTEN'S LANE AND P.ATTEN HOUSE. Immedia'ely opposite to the scene of our illustration were the yards of the Green Dragon and the Eagle and Child taverns which like many others in old Warrington hid themselves from the public gaze in quiet recesses. This second mentioned opening was, as we indicated last week, anciently known as Patten's Lane. It was a narrow and inconvenient road only just wide enough to admit the passage of a coach,and indeed a roadway more familiar with the Sedan chair than the coach. Hemmed in by dull buildings it was quite unworthy of the fine little Square and finer old house to which it led. Here lived, previous to the building of Bank Hall, the Patten family. Upon their removal the house became the home of the Boyer family and the small road- way lost its title of Pattens-lane. MISS BOVER, WIT AND BEAUTY. Miss Boyer, as all the world knew, was famous for her beauty, and if Opie did not flatter her in the picture he painted her fame was well merited. She drew around her a circle of brilliant company, and inspired the poets to their best effprts as they attempted

in the days of the Fattens for in the Parish Church Register under date 1664 it is mentioned as being then kept by William Pe itou. There is a thread of interest in the fact that the poet Byrom made it his resting place lin 1738. We noticed in his collected works a letter written thence on Valentine's day of that year. He thus addressed his wife: Warrington, February 14th, 1738, Dear Valentine, All happines to thee and thine. We canoe bete just now irom Mr. Egert Legh's, where we lay last night, Eitel are going to Mr. Hadden's now we have lefreshed ourselves at the Eagle and Child here, where we lie to night. It snowed in the morning, and that occasioned cur staying longer in Lymm. I have just writ to Mr. Leycester by a fo)t mst that was in the house here, and the other half sheet I sent thee to wish thee a go( d Lent, Easter, Whitsuntide and all good tides and tiding, with my dear and cordial love to thee, praying for thy health, to me ino,t dear and desirable, and my blessing to my beloved little ' flock. Service to all Enquirers etc. Thine ever, J. 13. That is a good letter and belongs to a period when people took pride and patience in their writing. Its reference to the foot post is interesting, and the dividing of the sheet of notepaper to make it sufficient for two letters (it would be a double quarto sheet) is a reminder that the price of paper made care- fulness a virtue. The quiei ness of the Inn yards would make them restful places for the traveller, and many of Britain's famous sons have slept within the sound of the old courthouse bell which still rings the Curfew from Trinity Tower. Many letters among the collected ones of prominent men are dated from War- rington, written at the inns by travellers who, in the old phrase, "lay there" for a night and arose to join the coach next morn- ing at the blast of the horn. Some day we must devote some special chapters to Warrington's Old Inns, their names, their appearance, and their lore. A.M.
BABY AND THE FOOD PROBLEM.

A pr,b!em that is no longer a problem, for every authority in the world agrees that the only way to ensure baby's health and strength in the fitture is by natural feeding. In many cases the use of the bottle ;s prejudicial, not only to baby's laralth, but to his very life. The only difficulty, then, is how natural feeding may become possible for every mother, and that difficulty, also, science has completely overcome. Let every mothei, desiring thus to do her duty by her baby, buy a few ounces of lactagol, which almost every chemist has in stock, taise a teaspoonful three times a day, and in mest cases the result will be quickly appuent (though in a few uses it may be somewhat delayed) in the excellent supply of breast milk, con- taining its due proportion of fats and albumens. The result naturally is a contented and htalthy babe. Another immense advantage in the tare of lactagol, which is quite pleasant to take is that it prevents all nurs'ng pains, being an exo take, tonic for those weakened by illness or overs train. As no cue doubts the immerse advantage of breast milk over the very best of aotificial foods, lactagol should be more largely used, and as it is simply a pure extract of cotton seed, and not a manufactured compo• 'salon, mothers may have every ooefidence in taking it.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. GEORGE HENRY LEE.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. GEORGE HENRY LEE.

The death has occurred at Torquay of Mr. George henry Lee, onl of the Inunders of the well-known establishment of George Henry Lee and Co., Ltd., drapers, Basnett-street, Liverpool. In partnership with his brother, Henry B. Lee, who, however, retired early from business, Mr. George Lee was largely instru- mental in establishing the concern which has had so successful a career. In 1874 Mr. George Lee retired in order to devote himself to scientific pursuits, to which he had for many years strong leanings.

ITS QUAINT SHOPS AND INNS AND HISTORIC

A VISIT FROM T.

By the kindness of Mr. James Carter we are able to give to our readers a picture of a fragment of old Bridge-street which dis- appeared nearly sixty years ago and which will, therefore, be beyond the memory of all save the very oldest of our readers. The picture from which our illustration is taken is a water colour painting and repre- sents the buildings with great accuracy. For the interest of our readers Mr. Carter has promised to exhibit the picture in the window of Messrs. Carter and Son, Bridge-street during the coming week. The three shops which appear stood upon the site of the shop of Mr. Grimes and filled the space between the shop of Mr. Bailey and the National Provincial Bank. The gable and wood cornice of Mr. Bailey's shop may be traced in the picture and it will be noted that the two storey building only reaches to the cornice, a-height of about eleven feet. This curious old place of business, flavour- ing of Elizabethan days, was occupied sixty years ago by Mr.Shaw,a name still associated with beef and butchery though now on the other side of the street.

div.head: MORE NEGRO PROVERBS AND STORIES.
div.p: MORE NEGRO PROVERBS AND STORIES.

Last week I copied out for my readers a I few interesting negro proverbs collPcted by a missionary in "The Land of Mud." This country, which has so unpromising a title, proves to be a very attractive place to read about, and not the least interesting things are written about the negros•and their ways. flere is a little tale to begin with. It is told to illustrate a native proverb. One of the wise sayings of the negros of Guiana is that " Tuddyderation is better than edication." Tuddyderation is pretend- ing to know when you are ignorant. We should call it "Bluff," and the proverb is used by those who are too idle to learn. One of such was a Massa Sammy who was so ignorant that he did not even know the alphabet, but who used to place a pencil behind his ear to make people believe that he was a learned man. One day a boy arrived with a letter for Massa Sammy which required an immediate answer, for which the boy pressed mercilessly in spite of Sammy's protest that he could not read " a running hand." The messenger urged "Try see, if you can't read little bit, and see what de letter say." But Sammy replied "As soon as we try fo' read me eye bun (burn) me." Pressed still further by the boy for an answer, he had to adopt different tactics, explaining in a learned manner that "Eat you see, dis letter write wid lef' handed pen, and me eye is a right-handed eye." Lazy natives would argue that Sammy came out of the difficulty splendidly, and would quote the proverb with approval, " Tuddyderation better dan edication." Another native proverb will be understood by all who know how hard it is to regain strength after illness, "Sickness ride horse come, tak' walk boot, go away" (Sickness rides on a horse when he conies, but he wa.ks away on foot.) They use this not only of illness but or''. evil and calamity in general. Where we say 'Birds of a feather flock together" they have in Guiana something more picturesque " When cockroach hab dance, him nebber ax (ask) fowl." They also improve on our "Rolling stone gathers no moss" by saying, "Dog wid too much master goes to bed widout supper." (The dog with too many masters goes to bed without supper.) Going after many he belongs to none, and so does not get fed. A very attractive proverb of which we have no equivalent in English says "Cow dat belongs to butcher nebber say him berry well." This is used by people who have trouble hanging over them, and who in con- sequence are depressed or ill. Where we say of an argument " It cuts both ways," they say "Same knife dat kill sheep, will kill goat." We say " Beauty is in the eye of the beholder" or else " Every mother's child is the prettiest." They say " Carrion crow tink him own pickney white" (the carrion crow thinks his own chick white). As the carrion crow is black and the ugliest bird in the Colony the proverb is very forcible. Instead of "It's an ill wind that blows nobody good" they have the homely word "Kitchen dresserlfall down, little dog laugh." The kitchen dresser holds the food and when it falls it is the little dogs opportunity to steal Another tiny proverb is often passed across the table to selfish boys or girls and indeed for selfish folks of all kinds. My readers will undershnd it without any explanation. "Greedy choke puppy." And when boys and girls begin to show themselves independent of their parents and think they are clever enough to manage for themselves the old folks say "If you no' done climb bill, don't trow away you stick."

div.head: AN EDITOR'S HOME TROUBLES.
div.p: AN EDITOR'S HOME TROUBLES.

Editors have troubles at home as well as in the office, and part of the trouble arises from the fact that people always take it for granted that they know every thing. Here is a conversation between the Editor's small boy and the Editor. "Father, if a lion had a fight with an elephant which would win ?" "I don't know, Sonny." " Father,are there any people on the stars?" "I don't know." "Father, has a sea serpent got any legs." "I don't know." " Father, what does it look like at the North Pole ? " "I don't know, Sonny, really "-- In desperation and with withering emphasis, "Fathet,how did you get to be an Editor?" WHY JOHNNY FAILED. Johnny had a little mind It was his very own, And nothing could be put in it Except by him alone. It wasn't very big, it's true, But there was room inside For lots of tine things, chosen out As Johnny shoull decide. Mother and fs.her gave to him All sorts of good ad ‘ice, But Johnny never put it in, Or thought about it twice, But all the ugly things the boys Upon the corners said, Why, Johnnie picked them up at once, And put them in his bead. At school the teacher tiled her best To give him facts and Jules Of every useful sort—but, no ! For Johnny hated schools. He picked up brag and vulgar slang, And novels, too, ten deep, And filled his mind till it was like A tainted rubbish heap. So when the day of manhood came, When Johnny searched his mind For skill and power, it played him fulse, And nothing could he find But worthless trash and ugly thoughts, And so be failed, alas! Is any other boy who reads Ccming to Johnny's pass?

div.head: DEATH OF MR. EDWARD BECK. One of the Founders of Dallam Forge
div.p: DEATH OF MR. EDWARD BECK. One of the Founders of Dallam Forge

News was received at Warrington on Monday of the death of Mr. Edward Beck, lleddon House, Isleworth, Middlesex, who was at one time prcminently identified with the commercial and industrial life of the town. Mr. Beck, who was in his eightieth year, was one of the original founders and directors of the Dallam Forge Co. Ltd., which in 1858 took over the business of Nield and Co., ironmasters, Warrington, and which in 1874, by amalgamation with the Warrington Wire Iron Co., and Messrs. Pea' son and Knowles consti- tuted the firm of the Pearsen and Knowles Coal and Iron Co. Ltd., as it exists to-day—now the largest iron and coal producing concern in the country. Mr. Beck served his apprenticeship as an engineer at the loco- motive works at Crewe and Wohcrhampton, and afterwards at the engineeting works of Messrs. Gilkes, Wilson and Co, Middlesborough. He was successively a director of the Dallam Folge Co. Ltd., and the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co. Ltd., and only retired from the board in 1906. At no time a politician or a public man, he was, however, one of the old Tories by conviction. His purse was always unostentatiously open for the benefit of the unfortunate or of any good cause which recomtueaded it3ell to his judgment. The funeral took place on Wednesday.

Military people are very proud of F. E. Bacon's 52-43 45 in 1895 and Sergeant 0' Neill's 52-41 25 in 1902 and great interest was centred in the doings of the three soldier competitors of whom Sanderson was disappointing. Hutson reached the length of his tether before half way, and at 5 1-4 mil, s O'Neill retired although he was then quite close to Glover. The Irishman was feeling the effects of an overnight journey and his winning race, on the Wednesday previous, for the Army Championship Cross C.runtry (on which the War Office authorities are now very enthusiastic), otherwise he, probably, would have troubled the Midland champion for the second place. The cinder track, 4 laps to the mile, was in good con- dition, but, owing to a rough wind, the weather, although lair, was not favourable to fast time. For the first two laps, however, Wallach set a very hot pace. Then Glover took the lead and, running with fire throughout,he repeatedly lapped many of his opponents of whom all except Baldwin were lapped before reach- ing 7 miles,where Glover was a mile to the good with some of the opposition, The first three to finish were: -1, E. Gloxer, Hallbmshire 11, titre 51min. 56 4-sseco.; 2, H. I). Baldwin, Derby and C.A .C., 52min. 44 2-ssec..; 3, W. J. Tucker, Reading AC., 53min. 44 4-ssecs.; Glover's official times were :- 1 mile 444 4-5,2 miles 9 50 1-5, 3 miles 15 2 3-5, 1 mile 20 16 1-5, 5 miles 25 26 3-5, 6 miles, 30 40, 7 miles 35 571-5, 8 miles 41 19 2-5, 9 miles 46 45 1-5.

div.head: WORLDS BEST TEN-MILER,
div.p: THE WORLDS BEST TEN-MILER,

To appraise this performance at is prorer value an analysis of the previous 34 races, which constitute the record for this event, is Lot only necessary but inter- esting because of the world famous men concerned. Two men, Sid Thomas and Alfred Shrubbs, world's record holder, have each won it on four occasions. Thomas' average time was 52 18 3-1 and his best (51 31 2-5) is the record for this rr.c,.. Shrubb's average was 53 5 4-5 and his hest (51 55 4-5) is only one second better than Glover. Six men have won it twice and their :,verage times, in chronological order, viz : —C. H. Mason 56 19 2-5, W. G George 54 21 1-2, W. Snook 55 33, S. J Robinson 53 13 1-5, A. Aldridge 52 58, and W. Scott 52 38 2-s—place the theorists who di scribe us as retrogade people at a serious discount. If other nations ars getting ahead of us in athletics it is bee luse of their greater keenness and enthusiasm, in high places, nct to speak of the lethargic kind of interest taken by the British "man in the street" who offers so little encouragement for really high class performances. The Britisher, generally, wants the "best in the world," only, and whilst he has been already satisfied w ith it other peop'e have not been "waiting for the best in the World." Nu! they have appreciated, and by encouragement, have develop.d. Whether the world's best 10 miler is a Frenchman or a Finlander is a debatable point, but personal opinioi. favours the international Cross Country Champion, Jean 11,,uin, who is Glover's only conqueror this season.

Glover is a strong runner cf just the stamp to put down a fresh record for ten miles on grass, 0) it is hoped that local people will endeavour to provide him with opportunity by having the Warrington Fo.tball ground track in as good condition as possible for the Saturday before Whit-Monday. There is not much timo, but systematic rolling will be advantage- ous in every respect. A re-count of Glover's previcus performances and other items concerning 10 miles running, rec9rds, will be dealt with next week.

div.head: WARRINGTON ATULETIC CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON ATULETIC CLUB.
Social and Prize Distribution. •

On Saturday, at Atkinson's Calii, Mr. Henry Hope (vice-president) presided over an enthusiastic company. Apologies for non-attendance were received from Major G. R. Crosfield, Messrs. T. Locker, 11. Ashton, T. P. 13radslat,w, and Councillor E. Osborne. The toasts of the evening were " The King," by Mr. Dagnall, and " Warrington Athletic Club" by the Chairman, the latter evoking replies which ascribed the club's success to its splendid organisa tion, and the hard work of the officials. This culruinattd in votes of thanks being moved to the hon. secretary, Mr. C. Berry, and the hon. treas., Mr. R. Bennett, both of whom replied in suitable terms and pointed out the necessity for whole-hearted support by the members and kcal sportsmen generally. A very enjoyable musical evening was spent, Mr. A. Brayshaw, acting as accompanist. Messrs. W. Clayton, R. Bennett, B. Greaves, B. Warburton, J. Greaves, W. Beaman, T. Walker, and T. Reddish as a glee party were very successful in "Sailors' chorus,' "In absence," and " Wake Little Kate." Mr. J. Nurse's character sketches of "Henry the Eighth" and "The Registrar" brought encores. Mr. R. Bennett sang " Good Company " in good style. Mr. E. Reddish scored with " King's Champion." Mr. 0. Dickenson's rendering of "The Admiral's Broom and Ship- mates " was splendid. Mr. E. Walker sang very eff-ctively Oh, oh, hear the wild winds blow " and "Young Ttm O'Deven."

Mr. Hope presented the prizes to the successful members as follows : West Lasi.cashire Novice Championship: J. I-Imam (champton) made up the champion team with J. Nurse, H. Wocds, and W. Walters. St. Helens Novice Championship: N. Stafford (champion) with J. Watson, G. Wakefield r,nd J. Ihorniley formed the champion team. West Lancashire Junior Championship: A. Gregson (champion), J. Hanson, J. Nurse, J. Watson, W. Walters and N. Stafford formed the champion team which brought the " Express " Cup to Warrington. West Lancashire Senior: C. Vose (champion), 11. Holbrook, W. Bolton, F. Antrobus, J. Parsonage and F. Shadwell were the winning team. Northern Senior Championship : C. Vose (second to Glover), H. Holbrook, W. Bolton, F. Antrobus; J. Parsonage and A. Burgess were the team which won the "Fattorine shield." National Champion- ship: C. Vose (second to Glover), F. Antrobus (fifth), W. Bolton (sixth) earned the tight to represent England in the international. IL Holbrook (whcse misfortunes undoubtedly caused the club to miss the cup) J. Hanson and J. Parsonage formed the counting six who were placed second, only six points behind the winners.

The club competitions provided keen racing and resulted thus.— Championship : 1, C. Yost) ; 2, H. Holbrook ;3, W. Bolton. Points competition : 1, A. Gregson ; 2, C. Vose ; 3, J. Nurse. Junior Champion- ship: 1, A. Gregson ; 2, J. Watson ; 3, J. Nurse. The winners in the three novice races were : J. Hanson, J. Watson and F. Price. Attendance medal, H. Payton. During the season the club established several records and a reputation which will require the enthusiastic support of all to live up to. The phenomenal success of the novice section is clear proof that great care has been taken in their preparation and the club must, optimistically, look forward to a very large increase of new members next season. " More the merrier" is a cross country motto and that additional club competitions can always I e arranged, for the intermedittte classes and the raw material, were the axioms of those who moved votes of thanks to the chairman and artistes.

One of the most successful seasons in the history of local schoolboy football has just terminated. Eight teams representing Warrington and District elementary schools, joined the League, and though one was obliged to withdraw shortly after the season had begun, the remaining seven enjoycd what proved to be a most interesting competition.

The play (1 the boys reached a very high standard ; and we can assure those interested in football, and indeed all who take an interest in sport of any kind, that an hour spent in watching the youthful exponents of the game would be far from wasted.

The boys of the Wycliffe, Arpley-street and St. James's schools, are to be heartily congratulated on the great fight they made to carry off the handsome shield which was presented for competion by the late Mr. James Dodds. The teams from Evelyn-street and Penketh showed very promising form, and, as the boys are young, there is no dcubt that they will figure prominently next seas(l3.

div.head: BOWLING GREEN.
div.p: THE BOWLING GREEN.
Warrington Works_ Competition Opens
in Half a Gale.
WIND PLAYS HAVOC WITH THE WOODS.

Saturday last could not in any way be termed a decent day for bowling, but nevertheless five games in the first round of the Warrington Works Associa- tion's competition were decided on the Horse and Jockey green.

Half a gale was blowing all the afternoon which threw may y puticipants off their mark and luck accounted for a number of successes. One could never make adcquate all ,wances, for when the woods topped the cr,,wn, the wind seemed to catch them and turn them off to a rnalk directly away fcom the one they were intended to find.

After the rains of the previous week, it was gener- ally (xpecttd that the green would be in a sodden state, but the wind bad dote good, for the turf was practically dry, although running rather on the heavy side.

We have seen far more spectators witnessing games in this c mpetition than wcre present on Saturday. One cannot expect crowdel "gates " for a week or sq, but really the games in this and the subsequent draws should prove attractive to numerous lovers of the sport and we should like to see the sides of the green thronged csith more people.
When the first game had been decided, Mr. Willett announced the result, and afterwards tendered advice to the secretaries of the various teams.

If any team are a man short, the secretary must advise Mr. Patrick before hand whom they are going to play so that the association secretary can look up and enter the reserve man's handicap. No unregis- tered player can take part in the competition.

Mr. Willett also aslicd the players not to part with their tickets for the green to anyone, but to destroy them after use. Mr. Ruihworth did his best for the association, and it was only right that the players should reciprccate the kindnesses he extended to them.

Concluding his speech, Mr. Willett referred to the success of the association since its inauguration at the King and Queen Hotel. More interest was being taken in the game now, and he could say with certainty that there was more bowling in Warrington than in any town of its size for a considerable distance.
The individual handicapping system has proved most beneficial to the novices and, as Mr. Willett put it, there is now no such thing as walking off the green with the scores 15- 0.
Scme old favcutites made a welcome re-appearance and the games on the whole were fairly interesting.
The best victory of the afternoon was that of Rylands No. 1 team who, although having to concede 20 points on the total handicap to their oppments from Houghtons, won by 54 pints.

div.head: NOTES ON THE GAMES.
div.p: NOTES ON THE GAMES.
Wiredrawer's Splendid Win.
The St. Helens Cable team had an advantage of 30 points on the total handicap, but the Whitecross men made a determined stand and only three of their men had to knuckle under.

But where could one except the sheep to be without the shepherd ? The Cable team were like a ship without a rudder for their worthy captain, H. Brown, failed to put in an appearance although he received the handsome start of six pints against W. Ball (1).

J. Spilsbury (3), who it will be remembered won the second prize in the individual handicap competition last year, played a splendid game against G. Sargenson i (6). After having been n arrears 4-10 at the fifth end, he improved wonderfully for he peeled with 13 on the 13th length. Two singles on the next two ends placed the wiredrawer the winner.

J. Cartwright (6) Cable, alth )ugh by no means an expert at the game, only lost to J. Horton (1) by one point. Cartwright was exceedingly lucky and led 12-6 at the 9th end. Horton stuck to his man and, after two exciting final ends, ran home the winner.
W. Melia (5) could not be termed "the hope of his side "for he only scored one point against W. Shaw (2), Whitecross.

R. Woods (6) Cable would have been in a sorry plight had it not been for his big handicap, for G. Warburton the Whitecross skipper was out for blocd and although only receiving one point handicap just lost by the odd chalk in 17 ends.
The Whitecross men were by far the superior team and thoroughly deserved their victory.
There was a round of applause when J. Bell (6) Cable triumphed over P. Gleave (2) by four points in 17 ends for the Cable man was extremely fortunate to send the winning woods.

JAMES FEARNLEY,
[BUILT BULLET-HEADED FOR PENETRATING THE DEFENCE. Vide DEWSBURY.]

61, Laira-streot, Orford-lane. A native of Warrington born in 18S9. Employed by Messrs. Bylands Bros. Played for Cadisheaci who won the Manchester League competition, Ist division, twice while he was a member of the team. He also assisted them to win the Lancashire Junior Cup. Warrington " spotted " him and the season 1911-12 found him playing for the second team. Formerly played Association for Messrs. P. Walker and Son. Proud of having got the two tries against Dewsbury in the semi-final and hopes to add to that record to-day against Hudders- field. • Has not played in the N.U. final. Single.

ALBERT REN WICK,
[A CRACK COLONIAL CENTRE AND SKIPPER OF THE TEAM -j

Hume-street. Born, Auckland, New Zealand, 1881. Came to England in 1910 to play for Wtgan. Joined arrington last December twelve months, and was made captain of the team this season. Engaged at Messrs. Rylands' Bros. works in the joiners' depart- ment. Has been much handicapped this year throucth being injured has been twice under the care of Dr. Jones, of Liverpool, and is not yet properly recovered. Is a good all-round player and especially clever at " adding the goal points." When in New Zealand was captain of the Grafton team for four years. It epre- sented Auckland Province In inter-Provincial matches. Is married. Has not played in the N final.

div.head: ERNEST BROOK ES,
div.p: ERNEST BROOK ES,
[FISH'S SUCCESSOR ON THE LEFT WING, AND A GOOD BUSTLER."]

Gladstone Arms, Church-street, is a native of Warrington where he was born in 1883. Played in the Works Competition for Monks Hall & Co., and, upon a merit rions performance in a serni-final, was selected for Warrinpton purposes. Played for Warrington first in 1902. Had his toes broken in 1903 and was" off" 24 weeks as the result of the accident. Has played in two Northern Union cup Finals for Warrington, against Hull Kingston Bovers and Oldham, Warrington being the victors on each occasion. Has played International, against the Australians, England v. Australia, Lancashire v. Australians, and the pick of the Northern Union v, Australians. Always had an idea as a lad that he would like to p:ay in the Works Competition. Had an ambition to play with Fish. Achieved his object aud has played centre to Fish and to Harris. Has played in three finals and would like to add another winner's medal tc-day to his number before he retires. Married.

div.head: BERT BRADSHAW,
div.p: BERT BRADSHAW,

[RIGIIT WING. PRODUCES A " STAR" 11:RN AT THE RIGHT MOMENT.] 31, Priestley-street, born in Warringten 25 years ago. Played Rugby Union football for Stockton Heath beforejoining Warrington in 1909. Played for them on the right wing as he does for Warrington. Has played for Messrs. Crosfield and Sons (at whose works he is employed as a chemist) in the Works Competi- tion which they won one year, being runners-up the next. Has not been in the N.U. Cup final, but intends to assist the team "to go all the way " at his first effort. Has been hurt this year, which has largely accounted for some of the poor form in the League which misled the critics into thinking poorly of War- rington cup prospects. The return of Bradshaw and others has somewhat modified their opinion during the progress of the cup ties. Holds two works competition medals, a Combination medal, and a South-West Lancashire medal.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION LEAGUE.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION LEAGUE.
Warrington Defeated at Hull.

The visit of Warrington to Hull provided one of the most brilliant matches of the season on the Hull Boulevard. It attracted a crowd of 10,000 spectators, 1 and was noteworthy in its initial stages for the attrac- tive play of Batten who after smart individual play scored first, placing the ball between the posts for E. Rogers to add the goal. This however was equalised in a few minutes when Dainteth receiving from a scrumm- age, threw himself over the line, and Renwick cleverly kicked the goal. A try by Gilbert placed Hull three points in front at half-time. During the second half there as a wonderful change. While Warrington appeared to be doing their best, it was evident that they were being out-played by their more brilliant i opponents. They never scored, and in the last quarter they certainly were let down by their centres. Bull were all the time piling up a score. Darmody took a fine pass from C. Rogers and scored under the posts, and tries followed by Herridge. Grice. Harrison, and Merry, three being improved by E. Rogers, who was in good form. Result :—Hull 5 goals\7 tries (31 points), Warrington 1 goal 1 try (5 points). Teams : Rogers, back ; Cottrell, Gilbert, W. Batten, and Harrison. three-quarter backs ; Anderson and G Rogers, half-backs ; Ilerridge, Holder, Chloe, Darmody, Merry, and Taylor, forwards. Warrington.—Jolley, back; Jordan, Tranter, Renwick and Waywell, three-quarter tacks ; Nicholas and Dainteth. half-backs ; G. Thomas, Charters, Skelhorne, Fearriloy, Cox, and R. Thomas, forwards. Referee, C. Platt, Swinton.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIELD.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIELD.
SEMI-FINAL. RYLANDS' RECREATION v. CADISREAD.

Great interest was taken in this match on the Gorey- Jane enclosure and the home team delighted their supporters with another fine victory. The visitors were unable to place their full side in the field. A high wind prevailed and the players experienced the grPate't difficulty in controlling the ball. Eventually Bramhall secured on the half-way line, and dodging splendidly, he elMed man after man in surprising fashion and scored behind the posts, Warren landing the goal. Following on this,the Recreation continued to have the major portion of the attack, and a fine passing display' initiated by Warren, and taken part in by Leah and Carter, sent F. Horrocks over for a good try at the right-band corner. Although playing with the wind in the second half, Cadishead could make no headway against the resolute work of the Recreation forwards and the skilful tactics of the backs. A fine breakaway by Warren and A. Horrocks ended in Leah scoring a try, which Bramhall converted. From this point onwards the visitors were outclassed,and after Griffith:, F.Horrocks and Carter had been checked near the line,A Horrocks completed two good tries, but in neither case were the extra points added. Result: Rvlands Recrea- tion, two goals, five tries 19 points) ; Cadishead, nil.
The League Final between Huddersfield and Wigan will be played at Wakefield on May 3rd.

div.head: BROADITHATH v. LOSTOCK GRALAM.
div.p: BROADITHATH v. LOSTOCK GRALAM.
At Altrinchran. Fiial :—Lostock Gralam, three goals ; Broadtkeatb, one goal.
OUGHTRINGTON PARK V. LOSTOCK GRALANI.

The Park brought their season to a close at Heatley with a victory over the Champions. lostock wore the first to 330 re, but Tnornason equalized from a penalty. Half-time :—One goal each. N‘ith the wind in their favour, the home team now had matters their own way. Thomason ran through the defence, but finished by putting wildly over the bar. At last the Park were rewarded. Alec Lord put in a splendid drive and although Davies got his bead to the ball he could not prevent it passing into the net, Oughtrington Park thus maintaining the unbeaten borne record with the score:— Oughtringtou Park, two goats ; Lostcck Gralam, one goal.
ALTRINCHAM JUNIOR COMPETITION. FINAL TIE.

MERSEY ATITI.F.TIC V. STOCKTON EIEATIL—The above final tie took place at BroAlands. At the end of 25 minutes Cummings shot into the net from a capital centre by Royle. At the interval Mersey Athletic led by a goal to nil. In the second half although having more of the game, the Heathens were never really dangerous—their forwards could not control the ball. Mersey again took up their running, and following some good work by their forwards, Jackson easily defeated Vernon for the second time. Stockton Heath strove desperately to reduce the lead, but met a sound defence. A brilliant individual effort by Royle (out- side left) settled the issue. He received the ball just, in his own half and teating man after man, coolly placed the ball into the net and gave his side a welt- deserved victory with the score :—Mersey Athletic, three goals ; Stockton Heath, nil.

div.head: SCRIPTURE IN SECONDARY SCHOOLS.
div.p: SCRIPTURE IN SECONDARY SCHOOLS.
Canon Stevenson Suggests a School Bible.

The Head Master of Elartow, the Rev. Lionel Ford, presided at a conference on Scripture teaching in secondary schools opened on Tuesday in the Examina- tion Schools, Oxford. There was a numerous and rapresen tative attendance. The Chairman explained that there was a desire on the part of public schools and preparatory schools to obtain a sort of co-ordination in their arrangements for divinity teaching in their classes.

Canon Morley Stevenson, principal of Warrington Training College, spoke on the question of a" School. Bible," stating that be should like to do away with chapter and verse and arrange in paragraphs and chapters,like an ordinary book,the story of the Creation the story of the Flood, and so on. Mr. H. Cradock Watson, head master of Merchant Taylors'School,Crosby,introduced the subject of the teach ing .of the miraculous in the school lesson. Hesaid that

if -their teaching was to have any moral or spiritual value it must be absolutely sincere. Coercion was no remedy. They could not compel belief by a reference to:an infallible Church or even an linfallatle Book. At this stage they wanted to encourage discussion and not to stifle it. The critical habit was forming. It had to be trained in the right direction. Let it be granted at once in their teaching that there was a possibility of error in their records as in all human documents, that to discredit one miracle was not to discredit all, just as, on the other band, belief in the miraculous did not necessarily involve a belief in all miracles recorded. They did not want a " flabby" credulity which accepted all it received, to succumb later only too easily to the first breath ot vain doctrine and unbelief. They must. inoculate with criticism to avoid the disease of scepticism. The miracles of the Gospel were unique phenomena, but they were the manifestations of a unique personality, _
Aiter.a short disCussion the conference adjourned.
BULBS AFTER FLOWERING.

Much as we appreciate the flowers of daffodils, hyacinths, tulips, and other bulbous plsnts in the early spring months, we are .111 ready to tire of their foliage when the blossoms have departed. But we must have patience, as the leaves have a most important part to play. After the bulb has flowered, it sets about prepar- ing for next spring, and the flowers that are to come from it then are actually formed in embryo before the foliage dies off naturally this year. By extracting carbonic acid gas from the air and converting it into plant food, which is sent down to build up the bulb, the leaves are doing valuable work, so leave them well alone until they have finished their task and die a natural death.—" Agricultural Economist and Horticul- tural Review.

div.head: OUR FORWARD POLICY.
div.p: OUR FORWARD POLICY.
SAVING THE CHILDREN AND FIGHTING CONSUMPTION.

Dr. J. emote Hibbert, who, after six years' service as medical officer of health for Warrington, has just been appointed to a similar position at Blackburn, is one of the most progressive of public officials. His adminis tration of the health department has been marked by the concentration of effort upon some of the most pressing problems which confront the sanitarian and s mat reformer, and also by a welcome quickening of public interest in measures of vital import to the well being of the community. The impending departure of Dr Elibbert presents a favourable opportunity for taking stock of War- rington's position from the health standpoint. Accordingly a represerdative of the " Examiner " yesterday waited upon Dr. Hibbert to invite his Opinion on what the Health Committee has been able to achieve in its campaign. against disease and insanitary surroundings. As the doctor's annual report will shortly be issued, he was siymewhat reticent in discussing the latest developments of certain phases of the question, but he courteously gave some outstanding impressions.

Saving Child Life. "There is no doubt" said Dr. Ilibbert " that the last few years have been a time of special activity in sanitary matters in Warrington and that decided improvements have been brought about. I wish to make it clear that I do not claim personal credit for this, but that I am proud to be associated with a ccmmitte which has adopted a forward policy and nay justly claim to have done pioneer work in certain d.rections." Asked to indicate the principal lines on which an a cgance bad been made, Dr. Hibbert first referred to t trt- question of infantile mortality. " The figures themselves," be said, " are sufficient to st ow that much has been done to reduce the sacrifice of young life in our town. Ido not wish to ant)cipate my report to the Health Committee,but think it is already known that for the year 1912 we had an infantile mortality rate of 92, which is highly creditable to a
(Photograph by Birtres DR. HI BBERT.

manufacturing town like Warrington—in fact it is con- siderably below the aserage tor the large towns of 'England and Wales." "How does that rate compare with the previous local records ?" !Laken be interviewer.

"It is the lowest figure ever touched in Warrington" replied the doctor, " the next lowest being 113 which 'was reccrded in 1910." Dealing with toe causes of the reduction, Dr. Hibbert sAid the weather conditions in 1912 were unciubtedly lavotfrable to a low rate. Apart trom those, however, the #fforts recently made to improve the general sanitary conditions of the town, by more extensive paving and better scavenging, and the s)s,ematic work &no by the health visitors in inducing people to pay more heed to home sanitation and the proper up-bring- ing of their babies, must have had considerable effect.

Housing of the Poor and Slums. Dr. Hiboert went on to speak of the work which had been done in improving the.housing conditions ot the poor. There was a long list of houses which had either been closed or put into a habitable condition, on the Health Committee's initiative.

There is, however, one serious drawback to which Dr. Hibbert called attention. "We are now beginning "he said "to feel the need for further cheap housing accom- modation for the poorest classes of inhabitants. Families, on being turned out of insanitary dwellings, have in some instances gone to live with other families in houses which should only accommodate one family, thus aggravating the overcrowding evil." " Do you advocate a municipal housing scheme as a solution? " asked our reporter. "There are many unskilled labourers in Warrington " said Dr. Hibbert " whose low wages do not allow them to pay more than a very small rental. I don't see how self-contained holves can be provided at a rent within their means, and therefore the only solution seems to be the erection of tenement dwellings, such as the Liver- pool Corporation has provided in certain areas." "Then how, briefly, does Warrington stand with regard to its slum problem ?" I think at the present time it can be said that the worst property has been entirely dealt with, and that Warrington is practically free from slums—that is, from houses that are unfit for habitation."

The Pail System. Dr. Hibbert has always been a strong advocate of the adoption of more up-to-date sanitary conveniences in place of the generally discredited pail system. Asked for his views on this question, the doctor said : "One can only say that the recent satisfactory death rates make one chary in definitely condemning the pail closet system, but it is, from a public health point of view, a very undesirable one, contravening as it does, the fundamental law that no refuse or collections of organic matter should be allowed to accumulate in the vicinty of dwellings. My personal feeling is that the pail closet system is, to a certain extent, responsible for those rises in the infantile death-rate which occur during hot summers. I have only to instance the hot summer ot nu w hen the rate rose to a fairly high figure,as compared with the cooler summers of 1910-11" Dr. Hibbert expressed the view that the necessity for adopting the water carriage system, on a larger scale than at present, was realised by the Health Committee. Fighting Consumption.

Wtat LTr. Hibbert regards as the outstanding work of recent years is the endeavour of the Health Committee to fight the scourge of tuberculosis. "The question" be said "bas been tackled from the standpoints of dealing both with the animal and the human sources of infection. The milk supplies of the borough have been systematically examined and, under the special powers obtained by the borough some years ago, an attempt has been made to prevent the supply and distribution of tuberculous milk. The inspect. rs, too, have kept a thorough watch on the slaughtering of aniu.als and this, combined with the co-operation of the butchers, has resulted in our meat supplies being practically beyond suspicion. As regards the human source of infection, the work done at Sankey sanatorium has been most valuable. Patients in the more advanced stages of the disease have been taken away from their homes, where they were a danger to the other inmates and to their neighbours, and isolated in suitable surroundings. Moreover, early cases have been placed under more or less ideal conditions, at the sanatorium, for bringing about a cure of the disease. My .1013111M1 report will, I believe, show that very excel- I lent results in the way of apparent cure have already I been obtained at the institution."
"Then you tire a strong believer in the efficacy of sanatoria ? "

"Sanatorium treatment is certainly of great assist- ance in the cure of early cases, but it must be followed up by helping patients, on leaving the sanatorium, to obtain suitable employment and to live under good, healthy conditions. lam strongly of opinion that the proposed extension of the Sankey sanatorium will meet .11 the needs of the borough for dealing with both classes of cases."

Dr. Hibbert emphasised the educational value of sanatorium trea meet. He pointed out that, after a short stay in the institution, patients, although they might not be cured, were able to return to their home and continue the treatment, as far as their environment would allow. They were also taught how to prevent themselves becoming a source of danger by spreading the infection.
"are there any figures in existence to show, in a

definite way, the outcome of the committee's effcrts with regard to tuberculosis?" "1 ain afraid the good results of the work will be slow in showing themselves in actual figures, as so many factors are involved in deal- ing with a disease like tuberculosis. But the sum total of all the efforts—improved housing condi- tions and home sanitation, the measures to ensure sound and pure meat and milk supplies, and the provision of sanatorium treatment—must tend, in the near, future, greatly to reduce the death roll from this disease."

General Health Highly Satisfactory. • Asked for an opinion on tue general health condition of the town, Dr. Hibbert replied : 'Warrington's health condition is a highly satisfactory one, as shown by its vital statistics for recent years. Its death iates compare quite favourably with those of similarly situated manufacturing towns." Dr. Hibbert concluded with a warm acknowledgment of the support he had received from members of the Council. He bad been exceedingly fortunate, in the first place, in having the help of the Mayor who, as a medical practitioner and a former medical officer of health, had such a thorough knowledge of the health conditions of the town that his leadership had been invaluable. Any work he (Dr. Ilibbert) had been instrumental in carrying out, had been greatly facili- tated by the unfailing support of the Health Com- mittee, and he wished especially to thank the chairman (Alderman James Evans) for tne sound advice he ht.d imparted on any quAstions on which it had been necessary to consult him. "I would not like you to go away," added Dr. Hibbert," without my making some reference to the loyal and efficient help of my stair- In particular I would acknowledge the services of Dr G W N Joseph, my assistant, and Mr. W. T. Flood, chief inspector of nuisances. In Mr. Flood the Corporation has an. invaluable servant and the medical officer of health a bard-woraing and absolutely reliable colleague."
PLEASURE AND DI SCONTENT. The Modern Craze for Sport and Amusement.

SPEECHES AT PHILOMATHIC SOCIETY'S DINNER. The Warrington Philomathic Society's fourth annual dinner, which was held at the Patten Arms , Hotel on Wednesday evening, happily synchronised with St. George's day and the anniversary of the birthday of William Shakespeare. The coincidence , inspired the watchword "God and Saint George! Philoinaths and Victory ! " which appeared on the menu card. There were also the following appropriate lines from the pen of the hon. secretary (Mr. T. E Knowles) :- 0 philomathic youth! Thy yearnings bold Make thee impatient with toe things of old ; And yet, doth tried and trusty wisdom give This choicest r.eArl from out her aged sieve : Waste not in striving to be new ; He wisest is who would be true. A disappointment was in store for the company as the Right Rev. Dr. Casartelli, Roman Catholic. Bishop of Salford, who had consented to be the principal guest was compelled, by doctor's orders,to cancel the engage- ment. Be sew a telegram profoundly regretting his absence and wishing the members a delightful evening. The Rev. Father Wilsc,n, who waa asked to take Dr, Casartelii's place, was also unable to attend, and a cr nference in London detained the Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph). Despite these drawlyieks, the function proved most successful end enjoyable and the speech-making, is usual, reached a high standard of interest. Mr. James Ball, president of the society, presided and among others present were: The Rev. Dr. Stanley A. Mellor, Drs. Bowden and Muir ray, Councillor J. Haw- thorn Mr. J. Moore-Murray (director of education), Mr. H. B. Roberts (assistant director), Mr. C. Sawkit,s Burgess, Mr. 0. Loithouse, Mr. E. Gord n Burgess (vice-president of the s iety), Mr. D. J. Dunn (hon. treasurer), end Mr. 'l'. E. Knowles (hon. secretaiy). After an excellent dinner had been servea by Mr. Burleigb, tt e toast of " The King" was honoured on the proposition ot the President. WARRINGTON AS A SHIP-BUILDING CENTRE. Mr. J. A BnooKes propmed *".1.1e County Borough of Warrington." He said casual visitors to the town invariably went away with a poor impression of the place and its surroundings. A lady whom he met on his holidays referred to Warrington as " that beastly smelly place." (Laughter.) Be tried to explain that our taste in smells migt,t tot be very high (laughter)—but that did not cover the whole ground. -Sometimes he got a bit weary of the constant chorus of condemnati, n and began to ask: What do our friends want? Warrington was not the Garden of Eden; it was an old-fashioned, plain manufacturing town,and some of them took a wicked delight in seeing factory chimneys erected and smoke emitted. (Laughter.) Those people who were uisposed to grumble at our legacy of narrow streets, which had necessitated so much expenditure on improvements, ought to bear in mind the long history of the town and the troublotis times in which it had borne its part. When we were asked what we in modern times had done for the town, we could, with modest pride, point to Victoria Park, Queen's Gardens, the Secondary School, Gymnasium, the Parr Hall, the enlargement of the Infirmary, and the extension of the baths. THE HOBBY OF BRIDGE-BUILDING. Then there was toe widening of Bridge-street and no allusion to Warrington's advancement was com- plete without a reference to the bridge. It was singular that the bridge, like King Charles's bead, could not be kept out of anything. At the time of the Conquest they were building a bridge, and from time to time the bridge had bteu washed or blown away, with the result that, down to the presest moment,we had always had the little hobby of bridge- building in hand. When the crack of doom came, other towns might be in the midst of their merchan- dise, but he wagered that Warrington would be build- ing a bridge. (Laughter.) Under the town planning scheme provision was made for three other bridges,so that posterity was all right, and all was well. (Laughter.) Referring to the Town Council, the ' speaker said they had their ups and crowns and tough times, but, speaking generally, they deserved generous appreciation for their work. The trade of Warring- ton was absolutely good, and that embraced every- thing. (Applause.) They hoped that a few years hence Warrington woulu be a prosperous and proud city. There was one trade yet to be welcomed into our midst, and that waa shipbuilding. (Hear, hear.) Some day in the near future Warrington would make the great uiscovery it ought to have made years ago,and then the commercial prosperity of the borough would be assured. If they were to make an imperish- able name for the town, they must not be wholly absorbed in business and material pursuits, but must encourage the higher side of life. The speaker con- cluded by expressing satisfaction that when the King and Queen visited Warrington the Mayor would have the honour of receiving them on behalf of the towns- people. (Applause.) POLICIES, NOT PERSONS. Mr. J. MOORE MURRAY responded. He said that Warrington, like Sheffield, was a very fine place to get out of —(laughter)—aed all would agree that it was fortunate in its suburban surroundings. He appealed to the members of the Philomathic Society to justify their existence still further by taking a more prominent part in the social and municipal life of the town. They spent their time largely in the realms of controversy ; they bed high ideals and talked about them. That, however, was not sufficient. Somebody must work out their ideals, and who better than those who knew what they were aiming at? While much had been done in the town, a great deal more could be accomplished with the ateostance of the thoughtful men who belonged to that society. They had already in the Town Council many men who sacrificed much of their leisure and money in the interests of the well-being of the town, and not one of them did more devoted service than their worthy Mayor. (Applause). PLEA FOR CONSTRUCTIVE CRITICISE. As to the public life of Warrington at the present time, it was noticeable to bim how often matters of policy, which concerned the social and municipal welfare of the town, were criticised, not from the point of view of the principles involved, but solely with a regard to the persons who brought them forward. Personally be did not care who was responsible for a proposition, if it were going to be for the benefit of the great number. That attitude might, with advantage, be more generally adopted in con- sidering the proposals of the Town Council and other bodies. Let them put on one side destructive criticism which was not always helpful but often very harmful, and brieg forward constructive alternatives. Then the town would advance in its position among the . towns of South Lancashire and the time might again come when they would refer to "Liverpool, near Warrington. " (Applause). THE BREADTH OF THE SOCIETY.
The Rev. Dr. Mellor, in proposing' Our Guests" said that whatever else the Philomathic Society stood for, it at least stood for fellowship. In no field waa
Too Late for Classification__.

fellowship more real or valuable than in the desire fot learning and the search for truth; and ir should also be their object to develop that feeling of friendliness in the wider world. Within the bounds of their society, they had DO limits of party or sect. There were very few societies in the world to-daywhich could say that, with entire truth. It so often happened that di&rences on politics or religion meant exclusion from fellowship. It was a matter of very great regret to him that the Bishop of Salford was not present, because there would have been witnessed the unique spectacle of a Unitarian minister proposing the health of a Roman Catholic bishop. tApplause.) If the society cccasionally admitted into their midst, members of a revolutionary frame of mind, who were sometimes regarded as playing" those old Socialist tricks "- (laughter) -it was still another tribute ta the extent and splendour of their fellowship. (Applause.) Mr; C. SAWKINS BURGESS responded. He said that although he was not a memier of the s ciety, be might in one sense call himself its father, inasmuch as two of his;sons were among the few who founded it- The society was now, an institution in the town and he hoped it would do a greAter work in the future. (Applause). THE CRAZE FOR SPORT. Mr. 0. LovritousE (president cf the Literary and Philossphical Society) proposed " Tne Philoinathic Society." He commended the efforts which the society was making to fit its members tor the duties and res- ponsibilities of citzenship. In these days, he continued the cultivation of the intellectual life was far too, much neglected. The tendency of the age was to con- centrate itself upon the physical and, as an illustrua- lion of that, he would point to the patronage that was given to all kinds of sport. He had nothing to sal against participation in sport—he had been a sports- man all his life -but he did blame the tens of thousands of people who, week after week, watched games without attempting to take part in them. The decadence of Rome came about when the Romans got meicenaries to fight for them and gladiators to play for them. If ever the day came when the people of England would pay foreigners, to fight for them and people to 2lay for them, the ruin of the country would not be far distant. The. intellectual life was something too vast to contemplate,. for the garnered wiscl, m of the world, the deepest. thoughts of the mightiest intellects of the Fast had. been preserved for us to-day. The more one learned,. the more one realized one's ignorance. AMUSEMENTS AND DISCONTENT.

Mr. NORMAN NIELD, in responding, said the society, might do much to develop that strength of character% and true manliness, which was being undermined to such a regiettable extent by so many artificial condi- tions of life. They were told that individuality was - decadent, that in its place we were getting an uninteresting, stereotyped, conventional kind of char- acter. Nobody would deny that we had lost a great deal of that spirit of self-assertion,that personal dignity and thoroughness, that confidence in self-discritnination, so characteristic of the Englishman of a century or two ago. There was a growing teadency to ignore or consider useless all knowledge that did not lead to' material gain. Business was becoming more exacting. and the leisure time of many people was thereby con- siderably curtailed. We had only to observe tbe' increasing desire for amusement in all grades of' society, the growing inability or reluctance on the, part of the individual to cater for himself, to realize bow small was the desire for that knowledge aria learning which philomaths held in such high esteem. There never was an age when the facilities for enjoyment and amusement were s) lavish as in these days, but, in spite of that fact, we bad more discontent, more real unhappiness, more dissatisfaction with life generally than ever before. The reason was perfectly obvious. There was no virtue in that frivolity; it failed to satisfy and never would satisfy, because it was tc o empty. Com- pare that, concluded Mr. Nield, with the wonderful interest and enjoyment they obtained from the pursuit. of knowledge! (Applause). The health of `• The President" was honoured with, enthusiasm, on the proposition of Mr. A. J. NEWTON.. During the evening songs were admirably rendered; by Mr. J. W. Bibby. The following personal paragraphs, giving at a glance the leading faots concerning the members of to-day's Warrington cup team, will be of great interest : BENJAMIN JOLLEY, "STAR" CUSTODIAN, AND NEPHEW TO THE FAMOUS "JIM " JOLLEY OF RUNCORN. i nO, Norton-street, Runcorn. Born at Runcorn twentY- two years ago, and is employed there as a crane driver. Played for Runcorn White Star. and last season assisted that club to beat Rylands Bros. at St. Helens in the final of the Lancashire Junior Cifp. Has played for two or three teams in Runcorn and the local works competition, and thinks it a distinction to reach the final for the N.H. cup in his first complete season with Warrington. Single.

JAMES TRANTER, [FORSOOK FORWARD FOR CENTRE, AND GIVES " CHECKS " TO TIIE OPPOSITION.] 22, Warburton-street, is a native of Warrington. This is his second season for Warrington. Played for Newton in the Wigan and District League and for Pearson and Knowles in the Works Competition. Was in the team that ran up for the watches. Employed at Pearson and Knowles as a fitters' labourer Not been in a final for the great cup before but thinks he has "a rare god chance" of appearing among the winners at. his first effort. Did some fine work against Hull Kingston Rovers in the second round. JAMES DAINTITH, [THE EVER-READY. LIKES " MUD " BUT CAN MANAGE ' WITHOUT.] 10, Clifton-street, Latchford. A native of Warrington. Originally olayed Association football for Latchford hut now prefers Rugby. Played in the Woik-s Competition for the Locos who got into and won the final in 1905. Joined Warrington in 1906. Is employed in the signalling department of the I . and N.-W. Railway. Has not played in a N.C. Final. Single. Thinks "we shall win to-day." SIDNEY NICHOLAS, [THE " BABY" OF THE TEAM. A HAT.F BACK, HALF PLUCK AND HALF GLII.E.] 64, Chester-road. Played for Ebbw Vale and came to Warrington last October. Is only 21 next December and is the youngest member of the team. Played for the County of Monmouth twice last seas, n and once this. Has not been in Northern Union finaL JOHN WILLIAM CHESTER, LTHE HEAVY MAN OF THE PACK. WEARS A BROAD SMILE AND SHORT PANTS.] 26, Charles-street. Born in Warrington in 1887. Played for Whitecross in the Works Competition and joined Warrington in 1908.
